articles.title: UNGA: World leaders discuss AI, global conflicts
articles.body:
Zelenskyy namechecks Trump, Putin at UN General Assembly
Published September 22, 2026last updated September 24, 2026
What you need to know
- Artificial intelligence, the Iran war, and climate change are also set to dominate debate on Day 2 of UN General Assembly
- Syria's President Ahmed al-Sharaa, Iran's Masoud Pezeshkian and Ukraine's Volodymyr Zelenskyy were among those who spoke, with others including Spain's Pedro Sanchez and Venezuela's Delcy Rodriguez to follow
- US President Donald Trump was among the first speakers to take the stage on Tuesday and said he had a 'big decision' to make on Iran, to either make a deal or 'annihilate' the country
- The gathering of world leaders takes place against a backdrop of global conflicts, environmental crisis and massive technical disruption
Read below for all the top headlines, videos and analyses on the 81 UN General Assembly from September 22-28, 2026:
Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.
Venezuela to hold elections, Rodriguez tells UNGA
Venezuela's acting president, Delcy Rodríguez, delivered her first address to the UN General Assembly since coming to power, promising her country would hold elections when the nation's people determine the "right moment."
"I want to make this very clear at this General Assembly: there will be elections in Venezuela," Rodriguez said, adding that the country "has initiated the process of democratic transformation for its rebirth" following two blows this year.
First, "strangulation of its internal political life and the heightened confrontation with the United States" and second, the earthquakes on June 24 that caused the deaths of more than 6,500 people.
Rodriguez took power after the US toppled the then-president Nicolas Maduro in January.
Rodríguez briefly met US President Donald Trump at the UN General Assembly as well.
Ukrainian foreign minister met with Iranian delegation on the sidelines of UNGA
DW's US Correspondent Misha Komadovsky reports that the Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha met with the Iranian delegation on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly.
Sybiah earlier in the day told a UN Security Council meeting that Ukraine was ready for an immediate and complete ceasefire without preconditions, if Moscow did too.
German FM calls on Iran to end Hormuz blockage
In a meeting on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly, German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul called on Iran to end its closure of the Strait of Hormuz.
"It is up to Iran to engage constructively in negotiations and to loosen its stranglehold," Wadephul told journalists ahead of the meeting.
Wadephul also urged Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi to engage seriously and credibly in sustainable negotiations with the US and neighboring states in the region, sources in the German delegation were cited by the DPA news agency as saying.
"There must now be an overall willingness to compromise in order to bring about a solution to the deadlocked conflict in the region," Wadephul was quoted as saying.
He stressed the readiness of Germany and the so-called E3, which also includes France and the United Kingdom, to support mediation efforts.
Wadephul also stressed in the talks the need for Iran and militias it supports in the region, namely Yemen's Houthi rebels, to halt attacks on civilian ships. He added that Berlin expects free transit through the Strait of Hormuz to be restored immediately, stressing the rejection of any fees for passage through the critical waterway.
"Not only the Gulf States, but large parts of Asia, Africa and also Europe are suffering under this blockade," Wadephul said.
He added that Germany welcomes renewed talks between the US and Iran on the sidelines of the General Assembly, adding that he planned to speak to his counterparts from Jordan, Pakistan, Iraq and Oman.
Zelenskyy announces defense deals with Finland, Australia
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy also announced fresh deals with Finland and Australia related to defense, adding that another deal with Canada will follow.
Kyiv's defense experience against Russian drone strikes has now made it a world leader in the field.
"We are already working with partners in the Gulf, the South Caucasus, and across Europe through drone deals. Today, I signed a drone deal, a serious drone deal, with Finland," he said.
"Also today, I signed [a] security agreement with Australia, and drones are part of it too."
Zelenskyy calls Putin 'patient zero,' from whom 'this idea of war keeps spreading further'
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy also addressed the ways the war in Ukraine had spread, not least North Korea sending troops to fight on Russia's behalf.
"Recently we sent two North Korean prisoners of war the the Republic of Korea," Zelenskyy said, referring to South Korea by its formal name. "And these guys are not easy to capture alive. One of them, when he realized he was going to be taken prisoner, tried to kill himself."
He said this spoke to how personnel in North Korea were trained and an attitude that "they must die, no matter what."
"Do you really want to give such a force more time to learn how to wage war?" he asked.
Zelenskyy said that North Korea's leader Kim Jong Un provided troops to Russia in a transactional way. He said he presumed North Korea's neighbors must have noticed what he said was the country's recently-improved missile capabilities.
Zelenskyy alleged that Putin never seemed satisfied in his territorial ambitions and argued that this pattern applied beyond Ukraine.
He said that many around the world, in the south Caucasus, in Syria and across Africa "also know very well what Russian killers are."
"After all of this, can you even imagine [Putin] without war?" Zelenskyy asked. "He is patient zero, the one from whom this idea of war keeps spreading further. And wherever it spreads, it brings only pain, instability, new risks and of course new crises."
The more space Putin has to operate, he argued, the more dangerous the world became for everyone else.
"That is why patient zero must be stopped. He must be denied the space to act and the space to spread this evil further," Zelenskyy said.
Ukraine's Zelenskyy opens speech with critique of Putin, overture to Trump
Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy opened his speech not just with a message targeting Russia after more than four and a half years of open war, but also aimed squarely at the sensibilities of his host in New York.
"This morning on my way to New York, somewhere in the sky over the big and beautiful Atlantic Ocean, I read President Trump's post on Truth Social," Zelenskyy began.
He relayed how Trump had written that Russia lost control of its diesel oil industry due to its war with Ukraine, an embarrassment for a UN Security Council member so proud of its oil industry.
"And this is true, Russia messed up," Zelenskyy said. "And the conclusion of the post is also right: this ridiculous and never-ending war with Ukraine must be ended. I do not know a single world leader who would say otherwise. I do not know anyone who is openly for this war: except one man."
He said that Russia had been trying to carry out what he called Putin's "crazy orders" to seize eastern Ukraine for more than four years.
"Just this year, from January through August" the Russian army "lost" 248,964 people on the battlefield in Ukraine, Zelenskyy said. He later clarified that this constituted military casualties — so soldiers "killed and badly wounded" and said "we have video confirmation for every one of these losses."
He said that amid these losses, Russia had only managed to capture "around 1,000 square kilometers (380 square miles) of our land this year," adding that "we have already liberated a significant part of it." He compared this to Russia's own vast territory spanning some 17 million square kilometers.
He said of the continued fighting: "It's madness, but they still keep going there to die, because that is what Putin wants."
Palau says UN exclusion of Taiwan 'marginalizes' 23 million people
Palau's President Surangel Whipps began his address with thanks to outgoing UN Secretary General Antonio Guterres, who is nearing his term limit.
"Your climate leadership, steadfast defense of multilateralism, international law, human dignity and the voices of the vulnerable carries a special meaning for small island developing states," said Whipps, who leads an archipelago of more than 500 islands but only around 17,600 people, which only completed its independence process in 1994.
However, he also issued a stern criticism of the UN later in his address, arguing that there was one small island state whose sovereign rights the UN did not honor.
As one of just a dozen countries to have formal diplomatic relations with Taiwan, partly as a result of its historic and current ties to the US, Whipps also made the case for its inclusion in the UN.
"In Palau we say we are a friend to all," he said. "We choose our partners based on our shared values of democracy, human rights and a rules-based international order: principles that underpin our friendship with Taiwan."
He described Taiwan as "a trusted partner that can contribute even more fully if given the space to do so."
Taiwan is not a member of the United Nations and has been excluded from the organization since 1971 — when the Communist People's Republic of China took over the Chinese seat and the veto rights on the Security Council that came with it. This happened amid the normalization of ties between Beijing and much of the West, roughly two decades after the Chinese Communist Revolution.
"The UN marginalizes Taiwan's 23 million people," Whipps said. "We stand with likeminded partners in calling for the reversal of misinterpretations of the rules and procedures that have constrained Taiwan's meaningful participation in this body."
The leader of the island nation on the front lines of the battle against climate change and rising tides concluded with a traditional adage he said offered a lesson to the wider UN.
"Be strong, and do not give up. The shore is near," Whipps said, translating the saying. "The promise of multilateralism is that even the smallest can be heard, and that the many voices — shaped by different histories and experiences — can move toward a common shore."
Venezuela's Rodriguez, Trump hold brief but 'important' talks on sidelines
Venezuela's acting president Delcy Rodriguez — in office since the US abducted her predecessor at the start of the year — and US President Donald Trump met in person for the first time on the sidelines of the assembly.
Rodriguez first announced the meeting on social media, calling it "historic" and saying they discussed "strengthening the bilateral relationship" and enhancing cooperation in "strategic areas such as energy, mining and security and other matters of common interest."
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Wednesday described the meeting as brief but important.
One issue the pair discussed was the South American country's large debt load, Rubio said.
"There's a lot that needs to be fixed in order for Venezuela to be successful," Rubio told reporters. "Debt restructuring is key to that."
He described the country as having "probably the world's largest debt that has to be restructured," and said the US wanted to help to ensure this is done "in the right way."
Rodriguez also thanked Trump and his administration for their support following a pair of severe earthquakes at the end of June.
Venezuela's former President Nicolas Maduro and his wife Cilia Flores are both being held in a New York prison a short distance from the UN building. They are set to face trial on charges of alleged involvement in drug trafficking.
Argentina's Milei lambasts UN as 'useless organization'
Argentina's President Javier Milei issued a fiery rebuke not just against the UK, amid renewed tensions with the UK over the Falkland Islands, but also against another pet peeve of his — the UN itself.
He said he wanted to highlight the shortcomings he perceived in the UN "in a constructive spirit," decades after it undertook to "uphold international law, defend the sovereignty of nations and provide a forum through which conflicts could be resolved through cooperation, rather than immediately through the force of arms."
That, he said, was the original contract member states signed, but this "sacred covenant" had in practice been broken.
"That's to say it's become a useless organization whose only purpose is to sustain a cast of fatally arrogant parasites masquerading as well-intentioned bureaucrats," Milei said.
He said they had failed in their task of ensuring collective global security and human rights: "Instead, they allowed chaos, violence and international terrorism to flourish."
Milei accused these "alleged defenders of human rights" of sheltering "bloodthirsty dictators and regimes that stone women in the streets" and of "systematically" voting against Israel "while remaining silent in the face of Islamic terrorism and the genocide of Christians in Africa."
From this point, he turned his gaze directly to the isolated Falkand Islands of some 2,000 residents, some 550 kilometers (350 miles) off Argentina's coastline. He referred to them using their Spanish name, the Malvinas.
"And, as if that were not enough, an organization established to defend the territorial sovereignty of its members decided to look the other way with regard to the situation of the Malvinas Islands, South Georgia Islands and South Sandwich Islands and the surrounding maritime areas," he said of the disputed British territory that Argentina's defunct military dictatorship invaded in the 1980s, just a matter of months before it collapsed.
"For us, the Malvinas are a national cause," he said, before repeating for emphasis. "They are also a test of the gulf that can exist between the words of international institutions and the reality upon which they purport to act."
He complained, for instance, about UK oil extraction operations in waters that Argentina claims, saying this violated a past UN resolution designed to prevent further tensions in the dispute. Milei said that "for far too long" Argentina had opted for a "rhetorical" and "peaceful" defense in this dispute, and said his country again called on the UK "to resume negotiations with a view to finding a peaceful solution to the sovereignty dispute, as required by international law."
Pezeshkian say Iran can't let others use Hormuz Strait to 'impose their aggression on us'
Iran's president also to defend his country's moves to restrict commercial shipping through the Strait of Hormuz in his speech, in part by citing the US military's attempt to blockade Iran's ports.
"We cannot let some have free access and bolster their interests from the waterway, while at the same time using that waterway to impose their aggression upon us," Masoud Pezeshkian said.
He went on to mention efforts to close access to "our waterway" for Iran in his comments.
The speech did not make any solid proposal or suggestion for how to resolve the impasse in the key commercial shipping lane — where Iran is trying to restrict international shipping and the US Navy is trying to restrict access to Iranian ports in an uneasy and costly standoff.
Pezeshkian concluded by saying that Iran was not and never had been averse to negotiating, but at the same time said that President Donald Trump should have learned that it would not "bend the knee" when faced with "bullying" and military pressure.
Iran stands by desires for 'peaceful nuclear technology'
Iranian President Madoud Pezeshkian said during his speech that Iran was not prepared to give up its nuclear program, which it says is for peaceful power generation purposes.
This follows the US government and Donald Trump repeatedly insisting that one of its terms for a potential peace deal with Iran is that the country "can never have a nuclear weapon."
"For our country, peaceful nuclear technology is part of our inherent progress," Pezeshkian said. "For our sick people, it's cure and treatment. For our agricultural sector, it's food security. For industry's advancement and progress and supply of electrical energy. Iran does not accept for nuclear technology to be at the exclusive disposal of some, of a handful."
He said that the country would not "bow our head and give up the right that is inherently ours."
Pezeshkian summed up his country's position on the nuclear question as: "no nuclear weapons and no limitations to peaceful nuclear technology."
This has been Iran's public position for years. However, various US governments have been at least somewhat skeptical of the stated stance, while Israel has openly labeled it dishonest — Benjamin Netanyahu famously brought visual aids of his own to the UN General Assembly in 2012, as Pezeshkian did on Tuesday, showing how close to attaining a nuclear bomb he thought Iran was at the time.
Iran's Pezeshkian: 'We have been the victims of terrorism'
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian took the stage at just after 10 a.m. local time in New York, wearing an Iranian flag pin on his lapel.
"Yesterday, the United States president described us as terrorists," Pezeshkian told the chamber. "We have been the victims of terrorism."
Holding up a portrait of Ali Khamenei, killed in US-Israeli airstrikes at the start of the war, he said, "I come from an Iran in which our esteemed supreme leader was assassinated without any legal framework or reason."
He then mentioned the bomb attack that struck a school early in the attacks on Iran, again holding up various images he said showed "innocent children who in truth had committed no crimes."
Only one member of the US delegation was in the chamber amid the speech, and he stood up and left after these opening statements, as Pezeshkian was accusing the US and Israel of being "terrorists" and of training and protecting terrorists, only to describe Iran as such. However, both governments reject these accusations.
"We have only defended ourselves, we are not terrorists," he asserted. "Our innocent people have been the targets of cowardly attacks and aggressions imposed on our country. And we defended ourselves with utmost strength."
Pezeskhian said Iranian people "stood steadfast" in response to the attacks, claiming that Iran retaliated but did not hit "civilian populations," accusing Iran's attackers of targeting "our universities, our healthcare centers, our schools, our hospitals, our infrastructure, all of it against international law."
Later in his speech, Pezeshkian claimed that "in the past seven months our people have been in the streets every night demonstrating in support of their land, of their homeland." He made no mention of the Iranian regime's violent suppression of major public protests in the weeks prior to the attacks on the country.
Latvia's Rinkevics: Different threats, 1 lesson — 'none of us can face them alone'
Latvia's President Edgar Rinkevics sought to stress the value of the UN and its charter in his speech, alluding to the much-trodden warnings that "the world order is breaking down" and that "the rules-based order is under growing strain."
"The world has changed. International trade, mobility, technology — what happens far away is no longer far away. Instability travels. Conflicts cross borders. What happens in Ukraine does not stay in Ukraine. What happens in the Middle East, in the Red Sea, in Sudan, does not stay there."
Similarly, Rinkevics said, technology was also making "distance matter even less."
"And nature respects no borders either. Heat waves do not stop at checkpoints," he said after a record-breaking summer in Europe. Rising sea levels, he said, were another climate change threat, but not the only one: "In the mountains, a river may turn into a deadly flood. It can happen in seconds," he warned, referring to the flooding in Nepal in which 33 Latvian citizens died.
"Different threats, the same lesson: none of us can face them alone. We are in the same boat. Perhaps Noah's Ark is no longer just a biblical story," Rinkevics said. "And when we share the same boat, we need something that holds us together. And we already have it: the United Nations charter and its principles."
These principles, he said, "were not written for an easy world, quite the opposite." Rinkevics said they had emerged from the devastation of the second World War and from the determination not to repeat it.
"Peace was its purpose then. Peace remains our responsibility today. And peace will be relevant tomorrow," he said.
Rubio meets with Lavrov to discuss Ukraine war
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio met with his Russian counterpart Sergei Lavrov on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly on Wednesday.
Lavrov had previously indicated that the war in Ukraine would be a major topic of discussion with Rubio, according to Russia's Interfax news agency.
Ahead of the meeting, the Kremlin said that its stance on Ukraine peace talks had not changed.
"For now, there are no prerequisites for moving onto a peaceful negotiating track, although we, as the Russian side, remain open to peace talks," Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters.
He reiterated Russia's position that Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy would need to travel to Moscow for talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin. Kyiv has suggested that talks place in a neutral country.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy is set to address the United Nations later on Wednesday.
Zelenskyy met with US President Donald Trump the previous day, saying that both Kyiv and Washington want to end the war with Russia "before winter."
Al-Sharaa hails Syria's reconstruction, criticizes Israeli 'aggressions'
Syria's relatively new President Ahmed al-Sharaa said in his second appearance at the assembly since toppling Bashar Assad that the civil war-torn country's reconstruction was gathering pace.
"Last year I mentioned that Syria had come back, today I say to you that Syria is rising," he told the audience, before listing a series on achievements in what he termed "our journey in the struggle between good and evil."
"The country was united. We controlled arms. We rebuilt military and civilian institutions, sanctions were lifted, projects for reconstruction have continued," al-Sharaa said, also hailing moves to combat drug trafficking, bring "transitional justice" to Assad regime members and reach out to the international community diplomatically.
He paid special tribute to the initiative dubbed "the Breath of Freedom" his administration launched with six regional partners to dispose of chemical weapons stores in conjunction with international bodies like the OPCW and IAEA.
The Syrian president, formerly the founder of the Islamist terror group known as the al Nusra Front, said this outreach with the international community stood in stark contrast to his administration's ties with Israel since taking over in December 2024.
"The world is overjoyed about our return but Israel is launching attacks against Syria," he said. "There have been 500 airstrikes, more than 1,200 incursions and 300 detentions."
He said that "any attempts that violate our sovereignty, violate international law will be stopped," adding that the "will remain Syrian territories," in accordance with UN Security Council Resolution 497 from 1981, which deemed Syria's occupation of the Golan Heights to contravene international law.
Israel retained de facto control of the area despite the resolution and has taken up more advanced positions in the aftermath of al-Sharaa's forces seizing power, citing security concerns.
"It is reminiscent of an era that we thought was long gone," al-Sharaa said. "We call for the withdrawal of Israeli forces to the lines of December 8, 2024 [when the Assad regime fell]. We reject Israeli attempts to impose a fait accompli, we reject their aggressions."

Senator confirms ‘eight suicide attempts’ by US navy personnel assigned to USS Abraham Lincoln carrier group – live
Kirsten Gillibrand says acting US navy secretary told her of attempted suicides after carrier strike group’s lengthy deployment as part of US war in Iran
Senator Kirsten Gillibrand confirms 'eight suicide attempts' by US Navy personnel assigned to the USS Abraham Lincoln carrier strike group
Senator Kirsten Gillibrand, a New York Democrat, has confirmed to the Guardian an earlier report from CNN, that the acting US Navy secretary, Hung Cao, told her in a letter on Tuesday, that there have been “eight suicide attempts” by US Navy personnel assigned to the USS Abraham Lincoln carrier strike group since the start of their lengthy deployment as part of the US war on Iran.
The revelation about the attempted suicides came in response to the fifth of the senator’s 12 questions. Here is the full text of the exchange:
5. Have there been any suicides aboard the ship during this deployment? How many instances of detected suicidal ideation or attempted self-harm, including attempts to go overboard, has the Department recorded?
There have been no suicides onboard during this deployment. Since the beginning of LINCOLN’s deployment, there have been a total of eight suicide attempts across the strike group - this number includes the LINCOLN crew and Sailors from the carrier air wing, strike group and destroyer squadron staff, escorting destroyers, and all embarked aviation squadrons.
In a statement to the Guardian, Gillibrand said: “What Trump and Secretary Hegsethdismissed as ‘fake news’ turned out to be serious and deteriorating conditions for our service members. Our troops and their families make immense sacrifices every single day, yet the president dismissed them with open disrespect. That this administration can find endless taxpayer dollars for bombs, ballrooms, and billionaires, but cannot take care of our service members, is completely unacceptable.”
Here is the complete text of Cao’s response to Gillibrand’s questions:
A US district judge on Wednesday heard arguments in the extraordinary showdown between Donald Trump and CNN, MS Now and Politico, suggesting in comments that he was more inclined to side with the media plaintiffs who sued the president on Monday.
Lawyers representing the media organizations have asked Timothy J Kelly, a district judge, to force theWhite House to return the press badges that were taken over the weekend after Trump banned their journalists from the building. While the judge declined to rule on Wednesday, he acknowledged that due process had not been followed in revoking access.
The three news organizations were not given advance notice that they were in violation of any set of standards and only received formal notice – in letters sent to each news organization on Tuesday – that they “exhibited behavior in violation of the standards of professionalism and decorum expected of those given access to the White House Complex, including by trafficking in verifiable falsehoods about national security and other issues, and publishing sensitive or classified information”.
When he originally announced the ban in a Friday post on Truth Social, Trump cited “their constant ‘reporting’ FAKE NEWS”, rather than any violation of national security protocols.
During a tele-hearing on Wednesday afternoon, Kelly cited past case law that clearly laid out the need for a distinct process that involved advance notice of an infraction and the opportunity to plead one’s case.
“I think it is fair to say that the processes that the circuit laid out in those two cases wasn’t followed here,” the judge said, referring to two similar cases involving journalists who had either lost access or were denied access to the White House. The judge said that the cases made clear that “before a journalist’s White House hard pass was suspended or revoked, that the journalist was entitled to pre-deprivation notice and an opportunity to be heard”.
Congressman Ro Khanna, the progressive Democrat whose California district sits across a swath of Silicon Valley, has called for an agreement between the US and China to pace and monitor AI development as he led a “shadow hearing” on Thursday of Democrats on the House select committee on “the Strategic Competition Between the United States and the Chinese Communist Party”.
“The American people are deeply concerned about the future of AI and the potential risks,” Khanna said in a statement. “We urgently need an agreement with China on basic inspections and safety standards.”
The virtual hearing included testimony from Geoffrey Hinton, British-Canadian computer scientist and Nobel laureate often called “the godfather” of artificial intelligence, on what kind of US-China agreement might be possible. Khanna said OpenAI and Anthropic had not agreed to testify.
The progressive Democrat also said he’d sent letters to leading Chinese AI companies, including Moonshot AI, Alibaba, and DeepSeek requesting commitments to join American AI labs in a binding international agreement to responsibly pace the development of the technology.
On Tuesday, members of the committee sent a letter to the White House saying that US calls to “pace the frontier” of AI “do not need to conflict with ensuring American AI leadership and maintaining our strategic edge against the PRC, which is also an imperative.”
The signatories called on Donald Trump to use his summit with Xi in Washington tjis week to press for “a binding, enforceable, and verifiable international accord to prevent any country from losing control of AI or unleashing misaligned superintelligence on the world.”
The letter acknowledged that when engaging with China on the issue, “the US cannot assume commitments will be upheld unless there are clear mechanisms for verifying compliance. We recognize that this is a complicated topic and there are no easy solutions.”
The letter also requests that Trump meet with committee members after his sit-down with China’s leader. “Just as humans must be kept in the loop of this technology, Congress must be kept in the loop of your diplomacy,” it says.
In remarks earlier this week at the Asia Society, Khanna addressed the issue of US-China AI competition, days after Trump proposed an “AI Force” and an AI czar as the issue of data centers have become a potent midterm issue.
Kahnna was asked how managing competition between the two AI superpowers would be possible if the stated goal of the US is to win the AI race, leaving China with little incentive for China to co-operate.
“Winning the AI war is like winning a nuclear war – it would just lead to devastation,” Khanna said. “I don’t think the US should be trying to win an AI war – I think we need to come to an agreement about basic safety and basic standards to prevent a loss of control and misuse.”
The US, he added, could continue to have the best chips and researchers. “It’s like nuclear weapons,” he said. “Both sides want to have the most advanced weapons, but there are still arms control agreements.”
The call for US-China co-operation comes after the congressman published a bill of rights proposal for managing data centers in the US.
At the the meeting in New York, he told the Guardian that levies on data centers he proposes would not affect US competitiveness.
“The data issue is about economic balancing at home. There are a lot of places in the US you can build data centers that are away from residential communities, but big tech has just been lazy in building them where its easy but they need to build them only where communities want them and where there is real community benefit.”
“I believe we need to tax agentic AI and robots,” he added. “There should be a tax to have neutrality in our tax code so that we are not incentivizing the replacement of human beings.” Workers, he added should also benefit from increased productivity as a result of AI.
“There has to be a value to social cohesion in this country,” he added. “We need to be on the side of workers more than tech billionaires in terms of how this AI revolution takes place.”
Khanna said that in keeping with regulations and safeguards in place for the nuclear power industry, the AI industry should embrace oversight and monitoring. “If something negative should happen the call would be for total nationalization,” he warned. “It’s a reasonable proposal that the private sector should get behind.”
A bill of rights around AI should include investment in communities around data centers because most of what was currently proposed in the US amounts to “data center extraction”.
“There should be a fund of $10m per 100 megawatts of data processing power to invest in schools, parks, jobs programs and infrastructure” and that “could easily be paid by the companies setting these data centers up.”
Trump mocked for wincing during loud flyover, as Xi, and the wives of both leaders, remained impassive
Commentators and news outlets on the left and the right of the US political spectrum mocked Donald Trump on Wednesday for visibly wincing during a loud flyover of US military jets he staged for his Chinese counterpart, Xi Jinping, at Joint Base Andrews in Maryland.
Video of the US president recoiling as the jets flew overhead, as Xi, his wife, Peng Liyuan, and Melania Trump all remained calm, was captured in a live broadcast on Britain’s Sky News.
The leftwing streamer Hasan Piker, who featured the Sky News broadcast on his live Twitch stream, exclaimed “What the fuck was that face! Xi didn’t even flinch!” After replaying the moment, Piker added: “Oh my god! Fucking mogged! Trump, it’s your air show! How do you get scared at your air show?”
Lindell TV, the partisan rightwing news outlet published by Mike Lindell, a Trump supporter and 2020 election conspiracy theorist, which was chosen by the White House to provide pool video, zoomed out at exactly the moment Trump winced, so did not capture the president’s startled reaction in its video.
The United States has invited Vladimir Putin to take part in the meeting of the G20 scheduled in Miami in December in what would be the first major summit with the Russian leader present since he launched his invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
The invitation, which marks a significant reversal by the Trump administration of Russia’s international isolation, was announced by Marco Rubio, the US secretary of state, during a press conference on the sidelines of the United Nations conference in New York.
“We’ve invited President Putin to the G20,” Rubio said in a televised press conference following a meeting with Russian foreign minister Sergei Lavrov. “We think it’s an opportunity for him to engage not just with [Trump] but with other world leaders. We hope that’s an invitation he’ll accept.”
The Kremlin has not yet responded publicly to the invitation, which is likely to raise concerns from Ukraine and other European leaders who have recently accused Russia of launching hybrid attacks to disrupt logistics and spread political uncertainty among Kyiv’s allies.
Russia remains a member of the G20 but Putin has not attended a summit of the body since 2019. He did attend one session virtually in 2023. The December summit is set to take place at the Trump National Doral golf club.
Trump greets Xi at start of Chinese leader's state visit to US
Donald Trump just greeted China’s leader, Xi Jinping, at Joint Base Andrews in Maryland.
The US president rolled out the red carpet for his Chinese counterpart, and a ceremony is ongoing – in which a very loud flyover of jets just punctuated the US national anthem.
Reuters provided live video of the ceremony, in the absence of the US pool cameras, which are boycotting the event in solidarity with three news organizations banned by Trump on Friday over what he sees as overly critical coverage of his performance as president.
According to an update from the pool’s print reporter at the base:
Staff from Fox, CBS and NBC are here but not shooting, as journalists wait to see whether the judge will issue a ruling after hearing arguments today. Some of the networks appear to be breaking down their cameras.
There are signs in front of other tripods/cameras that say: NewsNation, Newsmax, RSBN, One America News and Lindell.
Trump and his wife, Melania, have just ushered Xi and his wife, Peng Liyuan, into limousines to leave the airport, and boarded a helicopter to return to the White House.
According to the White House, the arrival ceremony also featured:
a 100-foot-long red carpet
a salute battery
a 21-Person honor cordon
two three-person color teams to include the
US and Chinese flags
a US air force band playing fanfare and the U.S. and Chinese national anthems
Senator Kirsten Gillibrand confirms 'eight suicide attempts' by US Navy personnel assigned to the USS Abraham Lincoln carrier strike group
Senator Kirsten Gillibrand, a New York Democrat, has confirmed to the Guardian an earlier report from CNN, that the acting US Navy secretary, Hung Cao, told her in a letter on Tuesday, that there have been “eight suicide attempts” by US Navy personnel assigned to the USS Abraham Lincoln carrier strike group since the start of their lengthy deployment as part of the US war on Iran.
The revelation about the attempted suicides came in response to the fifth of the senator’s 12 questions. Here is the full text of the exchange:
5. Have there been any suicides aboard the ship during this deployment? How many instances of detected suicidal ideation or attempted self-harm, including attempts to go overboard, has the Department recorded?
There have been no suicides onboard during this deployment. Since the beginning of LINCOLN’s deployment, there have been a total of eight suicide attempts across the strike group - this number includes the LINCOLN crew and Sailors from the carrier air wing, strike group and destroyer squadron staff, escorting destroyers, and all embarked aviation squadrons.
In a statement to the Guardian, Gillibrand said: “What Trump and Secretary Hegsethdismissed as ‘fake news’ turned out to be serious and deteriorating conditions for our service members. Our troops and their families make immense sacrifices every single day, yet the president dismissed them with open disrespect. That this administration can find endless taxpayer dollars for bombs, ballrooms, and billionaires, but cannot take care of our service members, is completely unacceptable.”
Here is the complete text of Cao’s response to Gillibrand’s questions:
Lawyer for media outlets banned by Trump tells court he thought White House letters citing national security grounds were fake
Ted Boutrous, a prominent First Amendment lawyer who represented CNN, Politico and MS NOW in court on Wednesday, reportedly told the judge that, when he first saw three unsigned letters sent to the news organizations on Tuesday, four days after they were banned from the White House by Donald Trump, which attempted to justify the bans on national security grounds, he “didn’t think they were real”, the legal journalist Adam Klasfeld reports.
Boutrous pointed out that the three letters – to CNN, Politico and MS NOW – were unsigned and not on White House letterhead. All three cited articles published by the outlets months ago, most of them written by reporters who do not have passes to the White House.
The letters, Boutrous said, looked a “post hoc” attempt to justify the bans that the president himself told reporters on Friday were in response to overly negative coverage of his performance as president, by grafting on national security grounds.
In a supplemental declaration filed with the court Sudeep Reddy, MS NOW’s Washington bureau chief, pointed out that only one of the three articles cited in the White House press office letter, a report published on 11 June 2026 by Jake Traylor, “was written by a journalist who held a White House hard pass.”
Reddy also noted that the broadcaster submitted a request for the renewal of Traylor’s hard pass on 18 June 2026, a week later, “and his hard pass was subsequently renewed.”
Acting US navy secretary says 8 personnel assigned to USS Abraham Lincoln carrier strike group attempted suicide - report
There have been “eight suicide attempts” by US Navy personnel assigned to the USS Abraham Lincoln carrier strike group since the start of their lengthy deployment as part of the US war on Iran, the acting US Navy secretary, Hung Cao, revealed in a letter to senator Kirsten Gillibrand obtained by CNN.
“Since the beginning of Lincoln’s deployment, there have been a total of eight suicide attempts across the strike group,” Cao wrote to Gillibrand, a New York Democrat who is a member of the Senate armed services committee, the broadcaster reports.
“This number includes the Lincoln crew and sailors from the carrier airwing, strike group and destroyer squadron staff, escorting destroyers and all embarked aviation squadrons”, Cao reportedly wrote in a letter this week responding to written oversight questions from the senator.
The Guardian has asked the US Navy for comment on the report.
RFK Jr. accepted millions in book advances, gifts from MAHA allies: report
Robert F. Kennedy Jr., Trump’s secretary of Health and Human Services and a figurehead of the Make America Healthy Again movement, has taken millions of dollars in book advances and gifts from personal allies active in that movement outside of the government, The New York Times reported on Wednesday.
Kennedy received $4 million in book advances for a pair of books forthcoming from a company belonging to one of his friends and business partners, Tony Lyons, who runs several MAHA-related organizations.
Mr. Lyons also helms a nonprofit that paid $210,000 in consulting fees to Mr. Kennedy’s wife, the actress Cheryl Hines.
And Gavin de Becker, a friend of Kennedy’s who donated to his presidential campaign, provided him with $126,000 worth of lodging in a Washington, D.C. residence de Becker owned.
Ethics experts who spoke to the Times warned the payments may violated rules preventing government officials like Kennedy from leveraging their offices for profit.
Federal court hearing on Trump's 'ban on the free press' concludes
A federal court in Washington just finished hearing arguments in the lawsuit over Donald Trump’s self-described “ban on the free press,” in which he barred three news organizations – CNN, MS Now and Politico – from the White House over what he considers overly negative coverage of his work as a president.
C-SPAN posted an audio stream of most of the court hearing on YouTube, which has now, sadly, been removed, but before it was, the judge overseeing the case promised to issue a ruling soon on the request from the media organizations to have the credentials of the outlets restored while the court case goes on.
Judge Timothy Kelly, a former federal prosecutor nominated to the US district court for the District of Columbia in 2017 by Trump, is hearing the arguments from the government and the news organizations. In 2018, Kelly ordered the White House to restore the press pass of a CNN reporter, Jim Acosta, after he challenged Trump at a news conference and was briefly banned.
CNN’s chief media correspondent, Brian Stelter, reports that Kelly “began the hearing Wednesday by telling attorneys that the White House did not give reporters appropriate due process before revoking their access to the building, running against previous court decisions.”
Kelly himself previously held that the White House cannot suspend or revoke a journalist’s access without notice or giving them a chance to appeal that decision on due process grounds.
That process “wasn’t played out here,” Kelly said. “I just say to both sides that’s where I am,” Kelly said. “Before we get to any core First Amendment issues, there is a due process claim and a due process issue that seems to me the first stop in figuring out how to resolve the motion.”
Trump is set to meet with Chinese leader Xi Jinping in a major diplomatic summit. Xi, the long-serving leader of the Chinese Communist Party, will land at Joint Base Andrews in Maryland for a three-day visit. Trump plans to receive him with a red carpet and a personal greeting on the tarmac — a warmed welcome than Trump has ever given the Chinese leader.
The Trump administration’s White House ban on three news outlets will go to court today. The Trump administration will have to defend the president’s ban on CNN, Politico and MS Now from the White House before a Trump-appointed federal judge. Trump himself has said he isn’t optimistic about the outcome.
The Iranian president addressed the United Nations, a day after Trump’s apocalyptic threats. A day after Trump threatened to “annihilate” his country and drive its people “into Hell,” Iran’s President Masoud Pezeshkian issued a forceful rebuttal to the gathered world leaders. He accused the US of engaging in terrorism, and vowed Iran would “never bow” to American threats.
Volodymyr Zelenskyy, in his address to the UN, pushed for global pressure on Russia. He sought greater economic pressure on Russia to end its years-long invasion of Ukraine, and warned that continued attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure would be met with similar strikes in Russia. That might worry the Trump administration, which is trying to bring down gasoline and diesel prices before the midterms.
Susan Collins’ alleged pay-for-play scheme is providing fuel to Maine Democrats. The alleged corruption, detailed in a ProPublica investigation published yesterday, is providing campaign fodder for the state’s Democrats, including Collins’ challenger for a key Senate seat.
Zelenskyy, speaking to the United Nations, tries to rally support for a grinding war
Taz Ali
Speaking to the United Nations annual assembly of world leaders for the fifth time since the invasion of his country, Volodymyr Zelenskyy sought to rally global support for the defense of Ukraine from Russia.
Zelenskyy warned that Putin would not be appeased by a partial victory in Ukraine, and would continue pursuing conquest in Ukraine even if granted a piece of its territory.
He also asked world leaders to help end the conflict by pressuring Russia financially, stepping up sanctions to pressure Russian President Vladimir Putin to seek peace.
“When someone gives Russia more money through trade, they give this war more time. And that is exactly why we insist on limiting trade with the aggressor, and why we are burning Russia’s revenues ourselves,” he says.
In one particularly relevant comment for the Trump administration, Zelenskyy warned that continued Russian attacks on Ukraine’s energy system would result in retaliation in kind. “Ukrainians understand that this winter could be very hard for us,” he said. “But in response we will have no choice but to make it painful for Russia too”
The day before, Zelenskyy met with President Trump, who was quick to point out while speaking to reporters that Ukraine’s latest efforts to take out Russian oil infrastructure had impacted global fuel prices. Those prices (which have been worsened by Trump’s military campaign against Iran) have become a burden for Republicans ahead of the midterms.
Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022 threw Europe, and the international order, into crisis when it began more than four years ago. What was predicted to be a swift conquest has devolved into a grinding war of attrition reminiscent of World War I.
It has also since become just one unfolding crisis in a world increasingly at war. Since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, Hamas’ Oct. 7 attack on Israel has sparked a devastating Israeli retaliation against Gaza and renewed war between Israel and Lebanon; the US-Israel joint strikes on Iran, downstream of the Gaza war, have turned into a protracted conflict that has set the Persian Gulf ablaze; and a tenuous transition to democracy in Sudan has spiraled into a vicious civil war, each side backed by foreign allies.
Zelenskyy used his appearance at the UN General Assembly to remind delegates of the scale of devastation facing Ukraine, as just today Russia launched a punishing round of bombing on its capital, Kyiv.
“Russia has used over 2100 missiles against us. More than 950 of them were ballistic missiles,” Zelenskyy said, adding: “They launch jet-powered Shahed [missiles] every hour… We are fighting them 24/7”.
He said this is “to make life harder for the economy and to disrupt our lives. They disrupt children at school. Would your country survive something like this?”
Bernie Sanders introduces bill to “ban artificial superintelligence”
Bernie Sanders, the left-wing independent Senator from Vermont who has quickly become one of the loudest AI-skeptical voices in US politics, announced on Wednesday new legislation that would, in his words, “ban artificial superintelligence.”
“The leading experts are clear: AI is rapidly escaping our control,” Sanders wrote in a post to social media announcing the bill. “Congress must act NOW. Today I’m introducing legislation to permanently ban artificial superintelligence and pause advanced AI until clear safety rules are in place.”
The Associated Press reported earlier this morning that the legislation – backed in the House of Representatives by Texas Democrat Greg Cesar – would pause the development of frontier AI until a new “Department of Artificial Intelligence” could establish guardrails around the industry.
It would also ban, in perpetuity, “artificial superintelligence,” a category that includes AI systems that exceed the limits of human intelligence or have “sufficient capabilities to plan and execute the destruction or disempowerment of humanity,” per AP.
Maine Democrats seize on pay-for-play donation allegations against Collins
The allegations, first reported in a ProPublica story yesterday, were the latest development in an already chaotic Maine Senate race: that Maine GOP senator Susan Collins’ campaign had accepted large donations from a defense contractor in return for Collins steering government funds to the company.
A day later, Maine Democrats are centering those allegations as they seek to win Collins’ seat in the November midterm elections.
“I cannot stress enough today the seriousness of these allegations,” Devon Murphy-Anderson, executive director of the Maine Democratic Party, said at a party press conference called to highlight the investigation.
Collins, Murphy-Anderson said, had “sold us out yet again, and gotten bailed out of trouble by the President of the United States. It is not the first time she has betrayed us. However, this November we have the opportunity to ensure it is one of the last.”
Collins’s team has fiercly denied the allegations, which emerged from an FBI investigation into Martin Kao, former executive of the defense contractor Navakek. Kao, who detailed the alleged scheme to the FBI, has since been convicted and sentenced to prison on unrelated charges.
ProPublica reports that the FBI has been investigating Collins as part of a wide-ranging probe into members of Congress, but that the inquiry died as part of the Trump administration’s restructuring of the FBI.
Troy Jackson, Collins’ opponent for her Maine Senate seat in November, has also seized on the corruption allegations, implying that Collins has been deferential to Trump because his FBI helped kill the probe into her conduct. (Jackson was chosen by the Maine Democrats to replace their previous nominee, one-time progressive darling Graham Platner, after allegations of sexual assault led him to terminate his campaign.)
“This is corruption of the highest order,” Jackson wrote in a post to social media. “Susan Collins delivered millions in taxpayer dollars for a corrupt donor bankrolling her campaign, and then Donald Trump helped her cover it up.”
Trump administration drafting up plans for 90-day embargo on diesel exports: report
The Trump administration is readying to launch a 90-day ban on diesel fuel exports from the United States, following mounting calls from his party to take action to bring down the fuel’s price ahead of the midterm elections, POLITICO reported Wednesday.
Several people with inside knowledge of the conversations told POLITICO (currently one of three outlets banned from the White House by Trump) that the plan has created a schism within pro- and anti-embargo camps in the administration. It’s also prompted furor from the oil and gas industry that has broadly supported the president.
One oil industry executive privy to the conversations told the outlet that Trump seemed intent on announcing a ban by the end of the week.
The price of fuel has weighed heavily on Republicans in the lead-up to the midterms, which will determine whether Trump’s party retains control of Congress for the second half of his term. Trump ran in 2024 in part on bringing down the price of gas, but the war he helped kick off between the US and Iran, and the closure of vital oil shipping arteries it prompted, has sent the cost of fuel skyrocketing.
Diesel, in particular, has become a sore spot. The fuel for everything from semi-trucks to tractors to heavy machinery, it has surged in price even more than standard gasoline, to more than $6.50 per gallon.
That’s prompted some Republicans, especially those representing farming-heavy states, to publicly call on the president to take drastic action to lower the price of diesel.
The pushback, POLITICO reports, is coming from oil and gas executives and administration officials who warn that the embargo could raise fuel prices in the long run.
Yesterday, Britain’s new prime minister Andy Burnham navigated his way through a first high-stakes meeting with DonaldTrump at the UN general assembly in New York. His aides were delighted with how the meeting went, as Trump praised the US-UK relationship and described Burnham as a “natural businessman”.
The anticipated sticking points – theChagos Islands, WestBank settlement sanctions and Ireland – appear not to have derailed the talks nor cast a shadow over the future relationship.
In today’s edition of The Latest podcast, Lucy Hough speaks to the our policy editor in London, Kiran Stacey. You can also watch on YouTube.
'I am the code': Trump reportedly clashed with White House ballroom architect after dismissing safety concerns
The Washington Post (paywall) reports today that James McCrery II, the first architect on Donald Trump’s controversial $400m White House ballroom project, resigned after repeatedly clashing with the president, who dismissed his warnings that design features Trump was insisting on violated building safety codes.
McCrery withdrew from the project last October after warning Trump that a preliminary design he wanted “did not provide adequate emergency exit routes or fire-containment measures”, according to the Post’s report, which cites two people with knowledge of the discussions and corroborating documents reviewed by the paper.
The sources said Trump brushed off the architect’s concerns, and argued that no building codes apply to White House construction. “I am the code,” Trump reportedly said.
The Post previously reported that they had also clashed over the size of the ballroom. One document obtained by the paper features an image of a planned data center overlaid on a map of Manhattan, with a note that appears to be poking fun at McCrery’s concerns. “James,” it reads. “And you think we are big.”
Another note made in Sharpie makes clear Trump’s preference for Corinthian-style columns.
When approached by the Post, McCrery didn’t say why he stepped down. A White House official said it was “factually false and totally inaccurate” to suggest he left the project over issues with the code, and said he was a “valued member of the initial design team.”
Discussions about the safety issues continued for months after McCrery’s departure, according to White House records reviewed by the Post.
It is not clear from those records whether the safety issues he identified have been resolved in more recent designs by Shalom Baranes Associates, the architecture firm that took over McCrery’s firm’s role in the project late last year.
The ballroom project is – unusually – being overseen by the Executive Residence, rather than the General Services Administration or National Park Service. The small office is exempt from rules that require federal agencies to solicit competitive bids and disclose details to the public, the Post previously reported. Typically, it’s responsible for routine repairs, entertainment expenses, and the purchase of furniture, art and other items for the executive mansion.
Rubio, in his press conference, also touched on the war in Iran at several points, including on the surprise negotiations that took place yesterday between Trump administration envoys and the Iran delegation.
“I don’t want to mischaracterize this as a major breakthrough,” Rubio said. “But at the same time I think it was significant that at least there was a conversation.”
Little detail has been shared about what was discussed at that meetings, though Rubio framed the conversation as a continuation of the earlier back-and-forth between the two sides.
Rubio also notably insisted that Trump would be able to see through his campaign in Iran acting on his authority alone, even if Republicans lose control of Congress in November and if Democrats were to oppose the continuation of US operations against the country.

articles.title: Poland scrambles jets after Russian helicopter breaches its airspace
articles.body:
A Russian Mi-8 helicopter flies toward Novosibirsk in Russia during a Victory Day parade rehearsal in May 2020. | Rostislav Netisov/AFP via Getty Images
A Russian Mi-8 helicopter briefly violated Polish airspace near the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad on Wednesday, prompting Warsaw to scramble its fighter jets.
The Operational Command of Poland’s Armed Forces said in a statement on X that the helicopter had entered Polish airspace at 11:08 a.m. from Kaliningrad in the country’s north, remaining there for 42 seconds.
“The flight of the machine was observed by the radio-location systems” of Poland’s military, the command said in a statement, adding that ground forces remained on standby. “The nature of the incident indicates that Russia is once again testing the readiness of our air defense.”
Advertisement
The incident comes as Polish prosecutors revealed that a Russian Gerbera 2 drone found in the Baltic Sea last week had been carrying a high-explosive fragmentation warhead. Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk warned Sept. 17 that Russia could launch drone or missile strikes against countries that support Ukraine, and try to pass them off as accidents.
European officials have accused Moscow multiple times this year of using sabotage, cyberattacks, espionage and drone operations to pressure Kyiv’s backers as Russia continues its grinding full-scale war on its neighbor.
In August, Germany blamed Russia for an attempted explosive-drone attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport, while earlier this month Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen accused a Russian frigate of firing two flares at a Danish military helicopter. She called the incident an attempt to test NATO and said it was part of Russia’s increasingly aggressive strategy of hybrid warfare.
In an address to the United Nations General Assembly on Wednesday, Polish President Karol Nawrocki accused Russia of “ruthless persistence” in its efforts to “conquer a neighboring state and destabilize the entire region.”
“We are not the ones seeking confrontation,” he said.
Russian President Vladimir Putin has said Moscow doesn’t plan to attack NATO countries, but Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov has warned that any European attack on Russia would trigger a different — and “very short” — war.
Tusk’s office and the Russian Embassy in Warsaw did not immediately respond to POLITICO’s request for comment.
This story has been updated. Cheyanne M. Daniels provided reporting from New York.

articles.title: Russian Drones Over Kyiv – War of Speed and New Deep Strike Tactics
articles.body:
Russia’s “Shahed / Geran” drones are attacking Ukraine’s civilian cities almost continuously. Their targets of choice include shopping malls, gas stations, energy infrastructure, food warehouses, office centers and other civilian facilities. They increasingly deploy jet-powered Geran 4 and 5 variants of the drones that have replaced the so-called “mopeds” – powered by piston engines.
Ukraine recorded around 180 uses of jet-powered drones in the whole of 2025. In August this year alone, they launched around 2,800 – Russia used 15 times the annual total of jet-powered drones in a single month. Russia’s once experimental weapon, that it occasionally launched to test Ukraine’s air-defense capabilities is now one of mass deployment.
nd this creates new challenges for Ukraine. Having learned relatively quickly to effectively intercept conventional Shaheds – open-source data shows interception rates reached 90-95%. These jet-powered targets present a more complicated challenge for Ukraine with currently only around 60% interception rates.
The success Russia is currently achieving with jet-powered drones clearly demonstrates one of the fundamental principles of modern warfare – the race to implement new technologies faster than the enemy. Each side constantly probes the other’s vulnerabilities and can rapidly scale up a technology or tactic that works.
Russian Drone Attack on Kyiv Kills 2, Injures 22 as Explosions Rock Central Kyiv
Changes in Russian tactics
Russia has not simply increased the number of attacks; it has constantly changed how those attacks are conducted. These changes likely have several objectives: to overwhelm Ukraine’s air-defense system, forcing it to use expensive missiles against relatively cheap targets, create prolonged panic, and ultimately identify areas where Ukrainian defenses are weaker.
Where Ukraine’s defenses are thinnest, Russia tries to scale up its attacks. Constant attacks on civilian as well as military infrastructure in major cities serve to disrupt the functioning of the country. When air-raid alerts last for hours, logistics are disrupted, people move to shelters and businesses suspend operations. Even if a drone does not hit its target, the threat itself creates an economic impact and reduces the country’s financial capacity.
This effect is especially visible in Kyiv. When air-raid alerts are repeatedly declared, the capital simply cannot operate in a normal way which, in my view, is one of Moscow’s objectives: not simply to destroy something, but to gradually paralyze normal life. Russia is also trying to destroy residents’ morale by striking warehouses in an attempt to cause shortages and disruption to food and other essential supplies.
There is another aspect to these air attacks. They do not necessarily have to end with a strike against a specific target. The use of aircraft for reconnaissance can provide data about Ukraine’s response: where and how air defenses operate, which routes are being blocked, how quickly Ukraine responds to a target, and which systems are used to intercept it.
Even though not every drone launched by Russia is designed to explode, the objective ultimately remains the same: to destroy Ukraine.
Energy infrastructure, military and government facilities, communications towers, telecommunications infrastructure, media offices, gas stations, shopping malls – the list of potential targets is endless. Drones can be manually controlled and switch between targets in real time.
Every single attack can serve several purposes simultaneously: inflicting physical damage, overwhelming air defenses, collecting intelligence or simply keeping up constant psychological pressure. Nighttime attacks disrupt sleep and reduce productivity of Ukrainians throughout the following working day.
Why jet-powered drones are difficult to Intercept?
Conventional Shaheds fly relatively slowly allowing Ukraine’s air-defense forces time to detect them and assign the appropriate weapon system to destroy them. A jet-powered that flies twice as fast or more aircraft significantly reduces that window.
Speed is not the only factor; flight altitude, trajectory, terrain, buildings and the number of simultaneous targets present air defense with an entirely different and more complex problem.
Jet-powered drones operate at altitudes above 3.5 kilometers (2.2 miles), meaning that some of the conventional tools – mobile fire teams, machine guns, Gepard anti-aircraft systems and MANPADS – become ineffective. This leaves three main tools: fighter aircraft, surface-to-air missile systems and interceptor drones.
Russia does not rely on a single design with various types of jet-powered drones emerging, with some already approaching the capabilities of cruise missiles.
The Geran-5, for example, reportedly has a range of around 950 kilometers (590 miles) and a warhead of up to 90 kilograms (198 pounds). The Bandrol develops a speed of approximately 500-560 km/h (310-350 mph) and can go even faster during an attacking dive. The Dan-T drone-missile has a payload of up to 135 kilograms (298 pounds).
“Mother Drones” – another new Russian tactic
Recent attacks on Kyiv involved the use of so-called “mother drones.” These are Shaheds acting as carriers for smaller, faster and more maneuverable first-person view (FPV) drones which are released closer to and can be directed on to a potential target deep behind the front lines – distances that would otherwise be beyond the FPV drone.
The limited use of the tactic so far suggests it is yet another Russian testbed prior to mass deployment
What new threats could emerge?
Ukrainian defense engineers today must identify trends, understand the direction of technological evolution, and anticipate the direction Russian technology might take and develop countermeasures before they become a “game changer.”
When assessing the threat, it is not just technical or tactical capability that is important – scale. We have already seen that Russia was able to rapidly increase the production of relatively inexpensive guided munitions. It is not solely important to be able to effectively intercept a particular target but also in sufficient numbers.
Even the world’s best interceptor will not suffice if production is limited while the enemy can manufacture thousands of cheaper targets.
We need asymmetry.
The countermeasure should preferably cost significantly less than the target it faces or Ukraine could literally be exhausted by the financial cost of war. Ideally Ukraine should make mass attacks economically unattractive to Russia.
The future will be largely defined by a war of quantity – more missiles, more UAVs, more types of munitions opposed by more countermeasures – with lower cost being essential for both offensive and defensive systems.
Just as essential as quantity and price alone the decisive advantage will see a struggle for quality and autonomy with artificial intelligence (AI) inevitably becoming part of that process.
As the number and type of munitions increase, they will by necessity become “smarter,” requiring fewer external commands for guidance. They will be able to analyze their surroundings, adjust their routes, and independently select the moment or direction from which to approach a target.
With hundreds or thousands of different targets flying simultaneously, it will be impossible to train and field the same numbers of pilots. Both sides will rely on decisions being delegated to algorithms.
AI will be used to both strike targets and launch countermeasures. Systems will be able to analyze the airspace more quickly, predict flight paths, filter out decoys, allocate weapons to genuine targets, and operate without constant human intervention.
Future warfare will increasingly see humans defining the rules, while machines perform most of the work. This is already happening in civilian life. Vehicles can now operate without drivers, and AI systems are capable of independently analyzing enormous volumes of information. The next logical step is greater autonomy in military systems.
What Ukraine needs to do to protect its skies
The technological race is already underway – at full speed. If Ukraine is not to lose, it needs to prepare for this race now.
In 2023, when the first Shaheds appeared Ukraine could only counter them effectively by using expensive missiles, which were already in short supply. Kyiv went through a rapid and productive evolution – from detecting drones with searchlights to effectively destroying them over Ukraine. When conventional “mopeds” stopped delivering the results Russia needed, jet-powered unmanned aircraft began to appear.
Ukraine cannot afford to simply catch up with Russia every time it introduces a new technology. It needs to develop its own solutions in advance – both offensive systems and countermeasures. In no time at all fast, high-flying drones will be able to independently decide where to fly, what to attack and how to circumvent its defenses.
Several Ukrainian companies are already developing and combat testing jet-powered interceptor drones. The next steps will be scaling up production which should significantly improve Ukraine’s ability to intercept jet-powered UAVs.
Ukraine needs to think more broadly. It needs domestic production of jet engines and to avoid becoming dependent on third countries, including China. Similarly it should also increase the number of radars, protection for aircraft and strike drone bases and production facilities to manufacture its own jet-powered drones combined with strong intelligence capabilities and sufficient strike assets.
At the same time, Ukraine will have to adapt to the new reality of round-the-clock air threats and attacks. It is impossible to live for months in a situation where every air-raid siren automatically means a complete halt to normal life. It needs a much more precise system for understanding where the danger actually exists and how immediate it is. Where life can safely continue, the country should keep working. Where there is an immediate threat, people should receive a clear warning and be able to move to shelters.
Kyiv has already introduced different levels of air-raid alert. The same principle applies not only to protection, but to active defense as well. This calls for the introduction of a range of countermeasures as new types of target appear. Air-defense effectiveness is not only about the number of targets destroyed but also the cost of interception.
If an attacking munition costs $10,000 while the defensive system used to destroy it costs $100,000, the engagement may be won but the overall economic race will be lost.
Electronic warfare is another critical element of this development. For example, BlueBird Tech is constantly improving its Hrets systems in close cooperation with the military to respond quickly, because tactics and technologies are changing every day. As long as electronic communications exist, there will be ways to detect, intercept, jam or protect against them. Even if some systems become autonomous, warfare will not become fully automated overnight.
In addition electronic warfare itself will gradually move toward greater automation. Systems will be able to analyze the electromagnetic spectrum independently, identify signals, determine their source and select an appropriate response. AI will be an integral part of the electronic warfare system itself.
However, it is important to understand that Russia will not stop with jet-powered drones. By the time we learn how to intercept them effectively, Moscow may already have the next iteration: cheaper weapons, greater numbers, new tactics or increased autonomy.
Ukraine’s task, therefore, is not simply to catch up with every new threat as it emerges. It is to build a system capable of adapting faster than the adversary – and staying one step ahead.
