articles.title: The Carpathian Eight: An alliance in the mountains – or a supply route for the next war?
articles.body:
The Carpathian Eight: An alliance in the mountains – or a supply route for the next war?
The inaugural summit of the new Carpathian Eight (C8) cooperation format, initiated by Ukraine with EU support, took place on September 18-20. Leaders and representatives from eight countries in the Carpathian region were invited to discuss security, energy, logistics, and cross-border cooperation. The initiative – intended to unite nations, some of which do not officially supply weapons to Ukraine but wish to foster “good-neighborly relations” – has turned into a zero-sum game. Yielding no significant economic benefits and failing to address real economic challenges, it only serves to isolate the region from pan-continental logistics corridors.
Is the Carpathian Initiative a Ukrainian or European project?
The foundation for the Carpathian Initiative was laid by Ukraine back in 2001-2003, when it acted as the primary initiator and depositary of the Framework Convention on the Protection and Sustainable Development of the Carpathians. Initially, the format was strictly environmental and conservation-oriented. Countries of the Visegrad Group, and primarily Poland, breathed geopolitical life and economic scale into the concept. For years, Warsaw actively advocated for the creation of a full-fledged EU Macro-Regional Strategy for the Carpathian Region (EUSCARP), aiming to transform the shared mountain range into a major logistics and infrastructure hub.
Over time, the EU fully took over this regional initiative, turning it into a systemic tool for the “soft integration” of Ukraine. After developing a strategic vision for the region in 2009 and adopting the Carpathian Roadmap in 2019, Brussels institutionalized the project in line with its own bureaucratic standards. What began as a modest environmental initiative has, through the efforts of European neighbors, transformed into a large-scale EU geopolitical project aimed at drawing Ukraine into the European orbit via infrastructure grants.
The September summit marked the latest stage of this project. Ukraine (backed by EU funding) attempted to reclaim its role as the primary “driving force” of the whole initiative by shifting the focus from environmental issues to matters essential for bolstering Ukraine’s influence on NATO’s eastern flank.
Ukraine’s autonomy is illusory, however. For the European Commission, the Carpathian region serves as a convenient geographic ‘sandbox’; the supranational bureaucracy seeks to bind the EU’s eastern fringes together through mutual dependency. Brussels’ ultimate goal is to dilute the agency and curb the independence of countries like Hungary and Slovakia, whose ‘Eastern’ initiatives – such as linking Central and Eastern Europe with Greater Eurasia – are gaining momentum. Ultimately, this measure would allow regional financial and other flows to be fully contained within the EU.
What’s wrong with the project, and why is it a zero-sum game?
Beneath the facade of discussions on “cross-border cooperation” set against the picturesque backdrop of the Ukrainian Carpathians lie pragmatic objectives that turn the Carpathian Eight into a classic zero-sum game. This is confirmed by the project’s geography: countries with the greatest interest in the initiative find themselves subordinate to those countries for whom the project is not a key priority. Ukraine’s actual geographic weight in the project is minimal; despite Kiev’s ambition to act as the main engine of regional integration, the Carpathians account for a mere 3.6% of Ukraine’s total territory. Ukraine possesses only 10% of the total area of the mountain range, yet it attempts to dictate the agenda to Romania and Slovakia, where the Carpathians form the backbone of national geography, covering 47% and 72% of the territory, respectively. Such evident disparity between Ukraine’s actual geographical “contribution” and its political ambitions sows the seeds of conflict within the project.
Moreover, the Carpathian macroregion is considered depressed and heterogeneous. Unlike the economically developed, navigable, and homogeneous Danube region – which served as a model for this project conceived by the Visegrad Group – the Carpathians are a patchwork of isolated mountainous areas. For centuries, this 190,000 sq km area has remained a remote periphery. Due to the highly underdeveloped infrastructure – the lack of modern roads, tunnels, and logistics hubs – the border regions of these eight countries have been trapped in a state of deprivation. In the past 25 years, no amount of targeted European funding has been able to rectify this situation. This should have compelled Brussels to step out of its comfort zone and realistically assess the physical boundaries of the region. This also explains why the Visegrad Group supports eastern initiatives in Greater Eurasia. However, instead of this, along with the economically unfeasible Three Seas Initiative and the “frontline zones” project, the Carpathians are being turned into another logistical dead end resembling an artificial buffer zone.
This perspective reveals the true purpose of the revived format: to serve as a covert logistical corridor for NATO. The projected budget of €9.4 billion ($10.7 billion) for 90 infrastructure projects is specifically aimed at modernizing narrow-gauge railways, bridges, and tunnels in the Carpathian Mountains. Under the guise of Euro-integration, Brussels is aggressively attempting to create a secure alternative route through the complex mountainous terrain for rapid deployment of heavy equipment, weapons, and NATO reserves, bypassing vulnerable border logistics nodes. Consequently, supranational strategists get to fully benefit from this venture while Central European countries bear all the attendant military and strategic risks.
Intrigues, scandals, and investigations
For the countries physically located in the Carpathians and those interested in developing the region, the hidden agenda of the initiative is apparent. Citing a sudden illness, Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico canceled his visit to Bukovel and expressed his outright opposition to turning the region into a frontline zone and dragging Bratislava into the conflict under the guise of NATO obligations. As a result, Slovakia was represented at the summit only by the state secretary for foreign and European affairs. Local experts openly stated that Bratislava guessed the proposed zero-sum game: under the guise of cross-border corridors, Brussels and Kiev are attempting to establish a rear hub for supplying NATO’s eastern flank. For Slovakia, participating in such “road modernization” carries direct military risks, not security benefits. This forces the country to navigate a precarious line – seeking economic grants while sabotaging the military-political agenda of the proposed C8.
Following Slovakia, the Czech Republic demonstrated passive resistance to the project by adopting a stance of cautious pragmatism. Unlike Warsaw, Prague notably refrained from sending top officials to Bukovel, opting instead to send the vice-president of the senate. Czech economic analysts expressed doubt about the €40 billion investment portfolio announced by Kiev. The most important indicator of the failure of the “unified front” was that the Czech Republic effectively refused to sign the summit’s final declaration. As regional analysts point out, the country has “cooled” towards Ukraine’s ambitions. Moreover, unlike Ukraine, the Czech Republic has a realistic grasp of its geography; possessing only 8.5% of Carpathian territory, Prague saw no tangible economic benefit in a project burdened with militarization issues rather than cross-border development. Consequently, it chose to remain on the sidelines, unwilling to endorse someone else’s frontline agenda.
Predictably, only Poland and Romania expressed full and unconditional support for the project, emerging as the principal political beneficiaries of the initiative. Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk and Romanian President Nicusor Dan signed the final declaration, explicitly linking it to military-strategic objectives. For Warsaw, the Carpathian Eight provided a convenient platform for lobbying an anti-ballistic missile defense coalition on NATO’s eastern flank, while for Bucharest, it offered a means to logistically connect the Ukrainian border with NATO’s largest European base, which is being constructed on Romanian territory. As a result, the document was signed only by those players intending to gain direct benefits from the region’s militarization, firmly establishing the C8 as a frontline coalition.
Hungary’s reaction is particularly noteworthy. On X, Hungarian Prime Minister Peter Magyar compared Kiev’s actions to village sports: “Hi, we have formed a football team in the next village. We don’t know each other, but you are in it, and you have to bring the ball.” Ukraine’s foreign minister, Andrey Sibiga, expressed surprise over Hungary’s attitude, but the situation is very clear and leaves no room for doubt.
Budapest was expected to sign the memorandum between its oil and gas company MOL and Ukraine’s Naftogaz to establish joint strategic fuel reserves along the border. However, Magyar firmly blocked this initiative, fully aware of the risks involved in turning Hungary’s bordering territories with oil depots into targets for someone else’s military needs. Apparently, even Euro-Atlantic solidarity has its physical boundaries.
Moreover, Budapest’s negative stance is reinforced by the situation in Transcarpathia. From 2014, the Hungarian population in the region has decreased from 150,000 people to around 70,000-80,000 due to stringent Ukrainianization policies in schools. The remaining population is facing selective forced conscription, with military recruitment offices compiling lists of Hungarian students and workers to send to the front lines, resulting in several widely reported casualties, including the death of 45-year-old Jozsef Sebestyen. Notably, Moscow’s Foreign Ministry is closely monitoring these developments: mobilized residents of Transcarpathia occasionally end up as prisoners of war, and Russian diplomatic agencies, in coordination with intelligence services, work on their direct transfer to Hungary, bypassing Ukraine. Aware that Brussels and Kiev are attempting to exploit Hungarian resources and territory, Magyar chose to flip the script. Budapest refused to fund this military version of ‘Carpathian soccer’ which is too costly for it, and vetoed Ukraine’s integration efforts.
In summary, we must note that despite the ambitions of European supranational entities to create artificial buffer zones (essentially ‘sandboxes’) in Central and Eastern Europe, their era is coming to an end. Attempts to impose a zero-sum game on other countries only exacerbate the internal rift which is becoming inevitable, considering the region’s actual geography and the projects gaining momentum across Greater Eurasia.

articles.title: Iran’s president hits out at ‘bully’ Trump in UN speech but signals willingness to talk
articles.body:
Iran’s president, Masoud Pezeshkian, turned the tables on Donald Trump, describing the US as the true bully and terrorist in the Middle East while insisting that Iran had always shown a commitment to the negotiating table.
In a defiant speech to the UN general assembly in New York, his first since the US and Israel launched an all-out war on Iran, Pezeshkian repeatedly vowed that Tehran would never bend the knee to the US.
But he balanced defiance with a willingness to talk, saying: “It must be understood by President Trump and those who seek to bully us that we are ready for dialogue and diplomacy and negotiations but without the language of force.”
On Tuesday, the US president had told the UN he was weighing whether to “annihilate” Iran, but went on to hail renewed talks between Tehran and Washington’s negotiators.
A surprise three-hour meeting between Iran’s foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, and the US special envoy Steve Witkoff on the sidelines of the assembly the same day was regarded as constructive by both sides. It was the first such meeting since June, but did not stop the US delegation from walking out at the start of Pezeshkian’s speech.
The Iranian president did not go into any details about the talks, but conveyed the impression that he was focused on winning the support of Iran’s Arab neighbours for the proposals Tehran has drawn up for the future of the strait of Hormuz, the vital waterway that has been intermittently blockaded since the start of the war, causing global energy prices to soar.
He made it clear Iran could not tolerate the strait being used to transport arms that could then be used against it, a statement that suggests the Islamic republic will demand the right to inspect ships travelling through the strait in the future. Iran’s goal, he said, was to live independently.
Pezeshkian accused Washington of “terrorism” for assassinating the supreme leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei at the start of the war. He held up photographs of the dead leader and more than 150 schoolchildren killed in the opening days of the conflict, before insisting Tehran had never started a war.
“We have only defended ourselves. We are not terrorists,” he said. “Our innocent people have been the targets of cowardly attacks and aggressions imposed upon our country.”
He said Iran had the right to pursue a peaceful civil nuclear programme and it did not want to build nuclear weapons.
He repeatedly argued that the answer to regional security lay in agreement within the region and not with outsiders such as the US. Iran did not see its neighbours as security rivals, he said, but as partners in security. “In today’s world, those that are unable to defend themselves will be trampled upon,” he added.
Iran has repeatedly targeted US allies in the region since the start of the war.
Insisting Iran was the true victim of terrorism, Pezeshkian questioned why “Israel kills, yet Iran is subject to sanction”. He added: “They kill, we are sanctioned. Iran did not seek special treatment but wanted equal rights.”
Pezeshkian’s speech received domestic praise, but the hardline secretary of the supreme national security council, Mohsen Rezaei, refused to describe the talks with the Americans as negotiations. He said: “Mr Araghchi [Iran’s foreign minister] has announced Iran’s conditions, and until Iran’s conditions are implemented, the strait of Hormuz will not be opened nor will there be any negotiation.”
He warned Iran’s neighbours implementing a US-induced ban on Iranian travel: “If you stand alongside the United States, we will not stand by and watch.” He cautioned that should Iranian flights face bans through regional cooperation with Washington, “their airports will have no flights either”.
Pezeshkian’s attendance at the UN’s signature diplomatic event, in the heart of Manhattan, had been in doubt as it was unclear whether the US would issue a visa. Ultimately, Washington granted the permit but denied visas to several members of Pezeshkian’s entourage.
In Tehran, the foreign ministry spokesperson, Esmail Baghaei, confirmed talks had taken place between the two sides but appeared not to confirm any shift in the Iranian negotiating position.
He said: “The interaction that took place with the American side was through Qatari mediation. This interaction was aimed at conveying Iran’s conditions, including the end of the war in all its dimensions, the cessation of American aggressive actions, the naval siege, and the economic war, the release of Iranian assets and so on.”
Aware of the potential domestic backlash, he added that Iran’s conditions had been conveyed.
Iran set seven preconditions before returning to talks, and in a new development over the past 48 hours it said the strait of Hormuz could be reopened within seven days if those conditions were met.
It is likely that the US and the Gulf states would have to accept a navigational route for shipping in the strait of Hormuz that requires commercial shipping to enter through a sea lane mainly in Iranian waters and under Iranian rather than Omani control.
The fact that the talks lasted three hours suggests some progress was made. The US side is under pressure to leverage down oil prices and increase the availability of refined oil before the midterm elections in November. The latest published figures suggest the number of identifiable tankers making it through the strait is fewer than five a day.
The blockage in the strait is made worse by uncertainty surrounding the control by the Houthis – the Iran-backed Yemeni paramilitaries – of a second energy transport choke point, the Bab al-Mandab strait that leads from the Red Sea into the Indian Ocean.
There is little sign that Trump wants to relaunch a full-scale war with Iran, or indeed with the Houthis, as Republicans battle to turn the domestic political agenda away from a hugely unpopular conflict that Americans think they are losing.
Iran is under ever more intense pressure from sanctions, and a US naval blockade is making it nearly impossible for it to export oil, depriving the country of badly needed foreign currency. Iran’s civilian aircraft on Wednesday faced a potential worldwide grounding owing to the threat of US secondary sanctions on any entity that engaged with Iran’s civilian fleet.
Iranian officials negotiated frantically with neighbouring countries to try to maintain an air bridge, but it appears that Oman and Iraq have been forced to close their airspace to Iranian civilian planes.

articles.title: CCA Builders Start Revving Production Rates, as They Await 2027 Funding
articles.body:
General Atomics Aeronautical Systems Inc. and Anduril Industries both say they’re ready to produce Collaborative Combat Aircraft in volume as they wait for a fiscal 2027 budget to fund that work.
General Atomics announced earlier this week it has the capacity to produce its FQ-42A Vengeance drones at a rate of “six aircraft per month to meet USAF goals” and could make more if needed. Competitor Anduril, which started production of its FQ-44A Fury at its new Arsenal-1 facility in Ohio in March, aims to build 150 aircraft annually, its officials said last week at AFA’s Air, Space & Cyber Conference.
The Air Force’s 2027 budget request includes $996.5 million to acquire production CCAs in fiscal 2027, plus another $150 million in advance procurement funds for 2028. But USAF has not specified how many aircraft that might cover.
General Atomics spokesman C. Mark Brinkley declined to tell Air & Space Forces Magazine exactly how many FQ-42s are rolling off the company’s production line right now, but did confirm production is underway. “Some of those aircraft will become company aircraft,” he said, meaning that not all are for its Air Force customer.
Brinkley said the company’s potential production expansion could be used to answer international demand for its Gambit series of autonomous drones, which are closely related to the FQ-42.
General Atomics also said in its statement that it is self-funding FQ-42 production today as it awaits Congressional fiscal 2027 appropriations. The new fiscal year launches Oct. 1, but lawmakers failed to pass a budget for fiscal ’27, and instead passed a continuing resolution that would hold current year funding steady, but provides no new funding. The measure ensures funding through Dec. 11, 2026.
GA’s self-funding will help support the government’s procurement plans and prevent delivery delays, the company said, and building aircraft for its own fleet will help it invest in new technologies that reduce risk and increase capabilities.
The Air Force plans to use CCAs as a complement to crewed fighters in a bid to add combat capacity at a lower cost than convention fighter jets. CCAs are designed to be flown semi-autonomously, at times alongside piloted fighters like the F-22 and F-35 Lightning II, and could eventually carry out a variety of missions including air-to-air or air-to-ground strikes; intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance; or electronic warfare operations. The concept is still comparatively early in its development.
Air Force Secretary Troy Meink said Sept. 14 that USAF is aiming to field at least 500 CCAs by 2032. The Anduril and General Atomics CCAs were selected following a competition in April 2024, andboth companies won initial production contracts in June 2026.
General Atomics said a new FQ-42 was delivered to Creech Air Force Base, Nev., on Sept. 18, for test and evaluation. Creech is home to the Air Force’s Experimental Operations Unit, which has been experimenting with CCAs to develop approaches to how they might be employed in real-life operations.
Jason Levin, Anduril’s senior vice president for air dominance and strike, said Sept. 14 that his firm delivered an FQ-44 to the EOU in August. Prior to that, the YFQ-44A prototype took part in two exercises with the EOU, the first in April and the second in July.
The July exercise at Creech, Levin said, demonstrated that CCA had advanced enough for a single Air Force operator to launch and recover an aircraft on his own after just a few hours of training.
“The Air Force was operating mission autonomy by themselves, which was a first,” Levin said. “They were flying multiple times a day, operating mission autonomy without Anduril personnel—they were on-site kind of helping, but it was really the Air Force operating that.”
Levin said that during the July exercise, Fury flew in the same airspace as crewed fighters and other drones using mission autonomy, helping build Airmen’s trust that CCAs can operate in congested airspace.
The production model of the FQ-44 that will start to roll off the line next year at Arsenal-1 will be able to carry four air-to-air weapons, such as the AIM-120 Advanced Medium-Range Air-to-Air Missile, or AMRAAM, under its wings.
The FQ-42, General Atomics said, has flown in formation with piloted F-35 Lightning II and F-15E Strike Eagle jets to prepare for future test flights, when fighter pilots will actually command the drones. The FQ-42 represents fifth-generation stealth and operates with an internal weapons bay.
General Atomics previously conducted flights of its MQ-20 Avenger drone, operating as a CCA surrogate, to demonstrate how collaborative control flights might work. The company said its aircraft, including the Vengeance, Avenger, and XQ-67A Off-Board Sensing Station, have flown both semi-autonomously and autonomously using AI pilots and under the collaborative control of human pilots flying in the F-22 Raptor and F-35.
“The CCA program’s rate of progress has been incredible,” said Mike Atwood, vice president of advanced programs at General Atomics Aeronautical Systems, in a company statement. “Every week, the Air Force is pushing forward with new and more impressive accomplishments using Vengeance. It’s amazing to think of how far this program has come in such a short amount of time.”

articles.title: A former US nuclear-sub commander, a Ukrainian fund, and a plan to shield Odesa with drone swarms
articles.body:
TAF Industries signed a joint-venture memorandum with Danish firm Upteko for production but says bureaucracy is slowing the process. Meanwhile, Resist.UA agreed to invest in BlueShadow, a Danish maritime-defense startup whose founder commanded a US nuclear submarine and whose engineering team works largely in Ukraine, Defender Media reported.
Ukraine's defense industry has outgrown much of its own 2022-era hardware in two years of rapid wartime iteration, but a government fee of 20-30% on export permits and over 200 stalled co-production bids have left the country's foreign arms sales far behind battlefield demand. Deals like the two in Denmark route Ukrainian technology into allied markets without waiting for Kyiv's export apparatus to catch up.
Ukrainian first-person-view drones, made on Danish soil
Drone maker TAF Industries plans to produce its first batch in Denmark by the end of 2026, through a joint venture with local firm Upteko. The two signed a memorandum in August 2026, but paperwork on both sides has slowed things down.
"We need to pass a fairly large number of bureaucratic procedures to make it possible," chief business development officer Mykhailo Diachenko told NordicDefenceWatch.
He called the year-end target reachable, "though maybe it will look more like a miracle."
TAF wants footholds in other countries that support Ukraine. It has started the process in Norway and is negotiating with Sweden's Recas. Diachenko said the goal is local production plus sharing Ukrainian combat experience and technology with European partners. TAF builds FPV drones, with capacity near 1 million units a year.
A Ukrainian fund bets on Odesa's sea defense
Ukrainian fund Resist.UA signed a letter of intent to invest an undisclosed sum in Danish maritime-defense startup BlueShadow's €2 million ($2.29 million) pre-seed round, the company announced. BlueShadow's software collects data from maritime sensors, commercial feeds, and open sources, merges them into a single operational picture, and uses AI to detect threats, Defender Media reported.
The company has also built an open software platform it says can help intercept Shahed-type drones. BlueSentry, designed to protect ports, offshore wind farms, undersea cables, and maritime borders from hybrid attack, is one product that the company plans to launch in the Baltic and North seas in October. BlueDragon, now in prototype testing with Defense Ministry certification targeted for late 2026 and deployment planned for spring 2027, is designed to defend Odesa with autonomous swarms of armed sea drones meant to shoot down Russian attack drones.
Founder Charles Maher is a former US Navy submarine commander who ran a nuclear-powered boat, Defender Media reported. Almost his entire engineering team works in Ukraine, drawing on more than 15 Ukrainian suppliers. Resist.UA this summer launched Resist 2.0, an Estonia-based fund aiming to raise €50 million for Ukrainian defense-tech companies.

articles.title: Battlefield sees 247 Russian attacks, heaviest fighting on two fronts – Ukraine's General Staff
articles.body:
Battlefield sees 247 Russian attacks, heaviest fighting on two fronts – Ukraine's General Staff
A total of 247 combat clashes occurred on the battlefield on 22 September.
Source: General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine on Facebook, information as of 08:00 on 23 September
Details: The Russians launched a missile strike and carried out 87 airstrikes, dropping 309 guided aerial bombs. They deployed 9,377 kamikaze drones and conducted 2,693 assaults on settlements and Ukrainian troop positions, 34 of which involved multiple-launch rocket systems (MLRS).
Meanwhile, Ukraine's Rocket Forces and Artillery units struck one Russian drone ground control station on 22 September.
On the North Slobozhanshchyna front and in the operational zone in Russia's Kursk Oblast, four Russian assaults were recorded over the past day. The Russians launched three airstrikes using six guided aerial bombs and conducted 149 attacks on Ukrainian troop positions and settlements, eight of which involved MLRS.
On the South Slobozhanshchyna front, Ukrainian forces repelled 14 Russian attacks. The Russians attempted to advance near Starytsia, Hrafske and Lyman and towards the villages of Malyi Burluk, Putnykove and Radkivka.
On the Kupiansk front, Russian troops made one attempt to improve their positions by conducting an assault towards the village of Borova.
On the Lyman front, Ukrainian forces repelled Russian attempts to break through their defences. The Russians conducted three attacks near Novoselivka and Stavky.
On the Sloviansk front, Russian soldiers conducted two assaults near Kalenyky and Kryva Luka.
On the Kramatorsk front, the Russians conducted one attack towards the village of Fedorivka.
On the Kostiantynivka front, 25 Russian attacks were recorded, according to updated information. The Russians conducted assaults near Kostiantynivka, Novoselivka, Rozkishne, Novopavlivka, Kucheriv Yar and Vilne.
On the Pokrovsk front, the Russians conducted 23 attacks, seeking to advance near Novyi Donbas, Bilytske, Novohryshyne, Vodianske, Molodetske, Muravka, Myrne, Serhiivka, Novopidhorodnie and Novopavlivka.
On the Oleksandrivka front, Russian forces conducted two assaults near Berezove and Solodke.
On the Huliaipole front, Russian troops attacked the positions of Ukrainian defenders four times, attempting to advance near Huliaipole, Charivne and Vozdvyzhivka.
On the Orikhiv front, the Russians made two attempts to improve their positions near Mali Shcherbaky and Mala Tokmachka.

articles.title: Kiev deliberately destabilizes global energy markets, Lavrov tells Rubio
articles.body:
Kiev deliberately destabilizes global energy markets, Lavrov tells Rubio
Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov has told US Secretary of State Marco Rubio that Kiev’s deliberate attacks on energy and cross-border infrastructure are destabilizing global markets, according to the Russian Foreign Ministry.
Lavrov and Rubio met on Wednesday on the sidelines of the 81st UN General Assembly in New York, where they held an extensive discussion on Ukraine, bilateral relations and a range of international issues. The US State Department’s brief readout said only that the two diplomats discussed the Russia-Ukraine conflict and the US-Russia relationship.
According to Moscow, Lavrov drew Rubio’s attention to what it described as close coordination between Kiev and its European backers and raised Ukrainian strikes on civilians and “cross-border infrastructure facilities,” which Russia said were deliberately contributing to instability in global energy markets.
The issue has increasingly drawn attention in Washington as diesel prices have surged to record highs, topping $6.50 a gallon nationally in September 2026. President Donald Trump recently urged Vladimir Zelensky to stop striking Russian refineries, saying the attacks were creating a global shortage and “hurting the world.” US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent similarly said earlier this month that Ukrainian attacks on Russian energy assets and refined products were contributing to an “energy shock.”
Following his meeting with Lavrov, Rubio said both Russia and Ukraine had expressed some interest in a limited ceasefire covering energy targets. He acknowledged, however, that such an arrangement “doesn’t solve the war,” and said reaching one would be difficult because both sides regard energy infrastructure as a strategic target.
Moscow has repeatedly rejected the idea that any limited truce can substitute for a comprehensive settlement, pointing to what it describes as Kiev’s past violations of ceasefires and arguing that Kiev seeks talks only when the situation on the battlefield becomes critical. Zelensky said this week that Kiev was prepared to stop targeting Russian refineries if Moscow halted strikes on a wide range of Ukraine’s energy, logistics and port infrastructure.
Lavrov reiterated on Wednesday that Russia would not halt its military operation merely to facilitate negotiations, arguing that such a pause would give Kiev and its European sponsors time to replenish depleted weapons stocks.
Zelensky has meanwhile continued to push for the “full and swift implementation” of the recently enacted sanctions package championed by the late US Senator Lindsey Graham. The law gives Trump authority to impose tariffs of up to 100% on major buyers of Russian oil and gas, potentially targeting countries such as China and India. With global supplies already strained, sharply curbing Russian exports could further disrupt energy trade and drive prices higher as major importers are forced to compete for alternative barrels.
The Russian side reiterated during the Rubio talks that it remains prepared to pursue a political and diplomatic settlement, but only one that addresses the “root causes” of the conflict. Russian officials have repeatedly identified NATO’s expansion toward Russia and Kiev’s policies toward Russian speakers among those issues.
Lavrov also called for further normalization of US-Russia relations, including resolving disputes over diplomatic missions and Russian diplomatic property in the US.
In another sign of continued engagement, Rubio announced after the talks that Washington had invited President Vladimir Putin to attend the G20 summit in Miami in December. The Kremlin welcomed the invitation and said it would consider it through diplomatic channels.

articles.title: United Kingdom Established a Unit to Protect Satellites
articles.body:
The Royal Air Force has established the No. III Space Effects Squadron, which is the country’s first unit dedicated to countering threats to British satellites.
Air Chief Marshal Harv Smith, Chief of the Air Staff, announced the unit’s creation at the UK Space Capabilities Conference, according to the country’s Ministry of Defense.
The new squadron will bring together specialists from various branches of the Armed Forces to counter hostile activities in orbit and protect satellite infrastructure.
Unlike the 1st and 2nd Squadrons, which handle surveillance and early warning, the 3rd Squadron will use electronic warfare capabilities to neutralize threats.
The newly formed unit will support both offensive and defensive space operations and will expand as new technologies become available.
In 2025, General Paul Tedman, head of Space Command, reported that Russia attempts to interfere with British military satellites on a weekly basis—both through ground-based jamming and by maneuvering its own spacecraft close to the United Kingdom’s orbital systems.
He emphasized that Russia and China have tested anti-satellite weapons and are also exploring the possibility of deploying nuclear weapons in space.

articles.title: Can Baghdad ever bring Iraq's militias under state control?
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Can Baghdad ever bring Iraq's militias under state control?
A relative pause in fighting between the United States and Iran that ended in early September has brought the region back into a state of geopolitical tension.
As the exchange of strikes, retaliations, and signalling between Washington and Tehran continues, there is a heightened expectation from Washington that the US pullout from Iraq should coincide with Iranian-backed militias in the country being disarmed.
A looming US withdrawal
At a meeting at the White House in July, Iraq’s new prime minister, Ali al-Zaidi, met with President Donald Trump and indicated that Baghdad would work to disarm the pro-Iranian Popular Mobilisation Forces (PMF).
“The fact that both Trump and Zaidi are following through means this is a bipartisan vision in the United States and a continued commitment from Zaidi, who took over the premiership from Sudani as the Coordination Framework’s candidate,” Hamzeh Hadad, an Adjunct Fellow with the Center for New American Security, told The New Arab.
The withdrawal of US forces now places a greater burden on the government in Baghdad to determine the future of the PMF.
“The US pullout removes a key lever for Baghdad and forces tougher bargaining at home,” Dr Inna Rudolf, Senior Research Fellow in the War Studies Department at King’s College London, told The New Arab.
“Coalition forces had been both an excuse some factions used for pursuing greater autonomy but also a tool Washington could use to push for change.”
The US continues to pressure Baghdad for the disarmament of the PMF through diplomatic channels, but the threat of further sanctions and tariffs has been floated by the Trump administration.
On 21 September, Zaidi requested more time beyond the 30 September deadline agreed with the United States, and the next day it was announced that it would be pushed back to 30 June 2027.
Baghdad will now have nine months to continue negotiations with the factions while avoiding potential US financial or economic sanctions.
“The Iraqi government needs to have a more honest dialogue with Washington about its situation and vision,” Haddad told The New Arab.
“But this needs to take place without wishful statements from the Iraqi side that they backtrack on, as they already have to deal with strong foreign pressure on the issue.”
The plan to dismantle and reorganise the PMF fighters into existing brigades and retire older commanders who have served since 2014 will reportedly start implementation in January 2027.
The government also intends to establish a new directorate to monitor the integration.
Zaidi's disarmament push
Iraq’s new prime minister has sought to strengthen Baghdad’s image as a government that can rein in corruption, ensure security, and pursue economic development with the international community.
“Zaidi, entering politics, a new face, with no prior experience in public office, wanted to build on the US backing that saw him come to power, and so he boldly stated that he would enforce a deadline for armed groups outside of the state apparatus to disarm,” said Hadad.
The Iraqi government is currently waging a campaign to curtail the PMF’s power in the country. In mid-August, Iraqi security forces detained a senior commander from the Nujaba Movement, one of the primary Iranian-backed militias that make up the PMF coalition.
“There is a different understanding between what constitutes armed groups outside of the state apparatus in Iraq than in Washington,” Hadad noted.
Hiba Abdulwahhab, an Iraqi researcher and analyst, told The New Arab, “The relationship between the Iraqi government and these factions resembles a Catholic marriage, a union with no easy divorce. They are deeply intertwined politically, institutionally, and economically”.
An uncertain security situation
The US military will also be removing the air defence systems, including Patriot and C-RAM systems, from the Kurdistan Region. The depletion of US air defence system interceptors during the conflict with Iran has contributed to the declining security situation.
In March 2026, Kataib Hezbollah, one of the key factions of the PMF, released a two-minute video that went viral showing an FPV drone flying over the Camp Victory complex near Baghdad International Airport, a site that continued to host US and NATO-linked facilities.
A drone attack that Saudi officials reported originated from Iraq struck the East-West pipeline in Saudi Arabia on 11 September. Baghdad later confirmed the pipeline attack came from Iraqi territory and dismissed security officials responsible for Maysan Province near the Iranian border and closed the area’s border crossing.
Still, some PMF groups have sought out a political advantage by appearing to adhere to the government’s calls. One militia, Asaib Ahl al-Haq, announced over the summer that it formally withdrew from the PMF coalition and handed over its weapons to the government.
Other groups, such as the Sayyid al-Shuhada Brigades and the Nujaba Movement, have stated they will not turn over their weapons, saying that certain conditions had to be met before they did so.
“[Zaidi’s] reasoning is that there will be no more American forces present in Iraq and therefore no more excuse for armed groups to exist after that,” Hadad told The New Arab.
Dr Rudolf agrees. “Losing that pretext gives negotiators cleaner rhetorical space to press for stricter control as it strips the factions of their usual talking point that foreign troops justify armed resistance outside the formal chain of command.”
Finding a path to disarmament
Iraqi leaders have advocated for the PMF to function as a state security institution and slowly reduce their political nature.
In May, the militia of prominent Shia cleric Muqtada al-Sadr, Saraya al-Salam, announced it would begin disarmament and integrate into the state. While this group is not technically part of the PMF and Shia Coordination Framework, it could be interpreted as a sign of the direction the wind is blowing in Iraq.
However, it is likely that the groups will utilise this approach to reposition themselves without totally surrendering their arms.
“The most likely outcome is therefore adaptation and repositioning rather than genuine disarmament,” Abdulwahhab told The New Arab.
“Weapons could remain in faction-controlled depots, be transferred to affiliated units, or be placed nominally within the PMF’s official structure without being brought under effective government command.”
Observers of Iraq are right to be sceptical that the PMF will do little else other than rebrand and retain their loyalty to informal chains of command and external ties with Tehran.
Regarding the extension of the disarmament deadline, Abdulwahhab said, “The progression raises serious doubts about the government’s ability to act against factions deeply embedded in Iraq’s political and security institutions”.
She added, “The extension is more likely to give Iran-aligned factions time to reorganise and protect their networks than to give the government the power to disarm and dismantle them,” further noting that Baghdad had to take concrete steps now, otherwise June 2027 may bring another postponement rather than a resolution.
Some positive steps have been taken, but it is still early in the process to understand how far Baghdad can go.
“Without tangible incentives and accountability mechanisms, ‘integration’ will feel like administrative rebranding,” Rudolf said. “The public will see it as window dressing.”
The long-term outlook will depend on the future of the financial and military support from Iran as well as Baghdad’s own ability to assert control over the militias.
For now, the government in Baghdad will have to navigate the post-US withdrawal environment on its own.
Christopher Solomon is a Middle East analyst, researcher, editor, and writer based in the Washington, DC area. He is the author of the book In Search of Greater Syria (Bloomsbury)
Edited by Charlie Hoyle

articles.title: Year ago, only 12 Ukrainian brigades could order weapons online. Now, 500 units participate in revolutionary program that has delivered 1.3 million drones to front
articles.body:
A year ago, 12 Ukrainian brigades could order their own weapons off a state marketplace. Now, more than 500 units can. DOT-Chain Defense, which lets frontline units order necessary supplies using state funds or bonuses with just a few clicks, has scaled across most of Ukraine's Defense Forces, the Defense Ministry said.
The platform is the delivery backbone of Ukraine's soldier-led procurement revolution. It lies in a shift in the philosophy of defense procurement. Ukraine is abandoning the Soviet principle of "fight with whatever is handed down from above" and transitioning to a market-based model that centers on the choice of the individual soldier.
Over its first year, it has put more than 1.3 million drones and other systems into units' hands, worth about $1.9 billion, and the orders show what this war runs on: 84 percent are drones, with electronic-warfare gear and ground robots making up most of the rest. It is also the engine behind the points-for-kills system that lets units bank credit for battlefield results and spend it on their own equipment.
Access jumps from 12 to 500 units
The growth has been steep. DOT-Chain Defense is now used by combat units across the armed forces, the National Guard, the border and special transport services, the police, the Security Service, and Defense Intelligence, says Deputy Defense Minister Mstyslav Banik.
Assault regiments and the "Drone Line" project have joined, ordering unmanned systems to their own specifications.
Drones dominate the orders
By the ministry's count, electronic-warfare systems make up 8.6 percent of everything ordered, ground robotic complexes 7.2 percent, and ammunition a sliver at 0.2 percent.
The gear, worth about $1.9 billion, came both through direct marketplace purchases and through the "Army of Drones. Bonus" program, the points system tied to the same platform.
The US copies the model
The approach has drawn imitators. The US has launched its own Amazon-style marketplace for military drones, explicitly modeled on Ukraine's Brave1 Market and DOT-Chain Defense. For Ukraine, the payoff is data: a running record of which weapons work on which part of the front, which the state uses to scale up what performs.

articles.title: Russian Mi-8 Entered Polish Airspace — Fighter Jets Were Scrambled
articles.body:
A Russian Mi-8 military helicopter violated Polish airspace.
The Operational Command of the Polish Armed Forces reported this.
The violation occurred at 11:08 a.m. north of the Polish city of Branewo. The Russian Armed Forces helicopter was flying from the Kaliningrad region. It remained in Polish airspace for 42 seconds.
“It violated Polish airspace to a maximum depth of about 300 meters and remained there for 42 seconds,” the command reported.
Polish radar systems tracked the helicopter’s flight.
Fighter jets were scrambled, and ground forces and assets were placed on alert.
“The nature of the incident indicates that Russia is once again testing the readiness of our air defense system,” the command noted.
Russia has already violated Polish airspace several times this year with drones and missiles.
On September 14, a Russian drone carrying a warhead was discovered in the Baltic Sea near a beach in the Rusinowo area of the West Pomeranian Voivodeship.

articles.title: Czech Republic expels Russians who were exposed filming for propaganda project Rybar, gives them three days to leave the country
articles.body:
Czech police have detained and questioned Russians Vitaliy Chashchukhin and Igor Dolmatov, whom local journalists from the publication Seznam Zprávy had lured to a meeting in Prague that they secretly recorded. Chashchukhin and Dolmatov, who were working on behalf of the sanctioned Russian propaganda project Rybar, have now both been ordered to leave the Czech Republic within three days as undesirable persons, Seznam Zprávy reported on Sept. 22.
Czech police confirmed that procedural steps had been taken involving Chashchukhin but declined to disclose the outcome.
“We performed procedural acts with the mentioned person. Unfortunately, it is not possible to inform third parties about their result,” Ondřej Moravčík, spokesman for the Police Presidium, told Seznam Zprávy.
According to Seznam Zprávy’s sources, cameraman Igor Dolmatov received the same order to leave the country. The expulsion orders came after both of the Russians said during questioning that they worked for the Russian outlet Izvestia, a media organization that is also under European Union sanctions.
Filming organizer Boris Dvorkin, who was not physically present in Prague, told journalists that Chashchukhin was questioned for about nine hours.
“Vitaliy was interrogated by the Czech police for approximately nine hours. Subsequently, he was issued a document ordering him to leave the Czech Republic, after which he returned to Germany, where he legally resides. He obeyed this order,” Dvorkin said.
According to his own words during the hidden camera conversation he had with Czech journalists after his arrival in Prague, Chashchukhin has held permanent residency in Germany for about a decade and has performed work there for sanctioned Russian media outlets Izvestia, Channel Five, and REN TV. In his reports, he portrays Germany as a country in economic decline and argues that an end to arms supplies to Ukraine and a restoration of relations with Russia would remedy the situation. According to Seznam Zprávy’s sources, Czech security agencies are continuing to review Chashchukhin’s activities and have already informed their German counterparts.
Meanwhile, André Lenz, a spokesperson for Germany’s General Customs Directorate, told journalists that it is impossible to determine in advance whether working as a journalist for a sanctioned Russian media outlet constitutes a crime.
“Specific facts indicating a possible violation of sanctions are carefully reviewed in all individual cases. The competent public prosecutor's office decides on the initiation of investigative proceedings,” Lenz explained.
Seznam Zprávy’s operation to lure in the propagandists to Prague
Seznam Zprávy published an investigation on Sept. 22 describing how its journalists set a trap for participants in Rybar’s European influence operation. Representatives of the sanctioned Russian project had approached Czech media literacy and disinformation expert Bohumil Kartous and asked him to give an interview for a documentary series about the political and economic situation in Europe. Kartous agreed, and the Czech journalists then arranged a hidden-camera recording.
Chashchukhin and Dolmatov traveled from Berlin to Prague for the meeting. During the conversation, Chashchukhin acknowledged on hidden camera that: “It’s the Rybar project. You might know it. It’s Rybar.” Then, when Seznam Zprávy journalists approached, identified themselves, and began asking questions, both of the Russians ran off in different directions.
Journalists established that the filming was organized by Moscow-based documentary filmmaker Boris Dvorkin, who had not previously been publicly linked to Rybar. One of Dvorkin’s past projects was funded by the History of the Fatherland Foundation — an organization created by the decree of Vladimir Putin and chaired by Sergei Naryshkin, the head of Russia’s Foreign Intelligence Service (SVR).
After the first investigation, Dvorkin claimed that Chashchukhin had only helped him with one interview in his spare time and had not been paid. However, journalists found that Rybar representatives had organized filming in other European countries and had tried to recruit politicians, experts, and public figures to take part as subjects.
Rybar founder Mikhail Zvinchuk is under European Union sanctions, and official documents state that he is a member of a working group created by Vladimir Putin to coordinate Russia’s mobilization efforts in support of the war against Ukraine. Rybar’s main Telegram channel has more than 1.5 million subscribers. In 2024, the United States offered a reward of up to $10 million for information about the project’s employees as part of an effort to combat Kremlin-backed influence operations.

articles.title: Ukraine calls on Europe to be more Baltic after EU sanctions buckle
articles.body:
Andris Kulbergs, Latvia's prime minister, Jonas Gahr Store, Norway's prime minister, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, Ukraine's president, Gitanas Nauseda, Lithuania's president, and Kristen Michal, Estonia's prime minister, left to right, during the Nordic-Baltic Summit in Kyiv, Ukraine, on Aug. 23, 2026. (Andrew Kravchenko/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha praised Lithuania, Latvia, and Estonia on Sept. 23 for reimposing sanctions on the national level against two Russian oligarchs that were freed from such restrictions on the EU level the day before.
"We urge all other EU members to follow the example of our Baltic friends," Sybiha posted on social media after Lithuania announced it would impose sanctions against Russian oligarchs Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman.
France's justification rested on their wish to free two Frenchmen held prisoner in Azerbaijan, one of whom was pardoned on the morning of Sept. 23.
The decision was officially reached less than six hours before the entire list of 3,000 EU sanctions against Russia was set to expire, partly because of a last-ditch push by Latvia to force France to reconsider.
In the end Latvia, together with Estonia, Lithuania, and Belgium, abstained to allow the compromise to go ahead and ensure the remaining EU sanctions would hold.
Latvian Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs condemned the agreement as a choice "between a bad and a much worse" solution, before announcing Riga would impose sanctions against Usmanov and Fridman.
Estonia and Lithuania soon after joined that move, with the question open of how many of the EU's other 24 member countries will do likewise.
"This is the best way to demonstrate that principles are not for sale," Sybiha said.
Chris Powers is the Brussels Correspondent with the Kyiv Independent. He reports on EU news and policy developments relevant to Ukraine, bridging the gap between Brussels and Kyiv. He was formerly the Defense and Tech Editor at the EU media outlet Euractiv. Chris holds a BA in History from the University of Cambridge and an MA in European Studies from the College of Europe.
"Russia is trying to choke off Ukrainian grain exports, thus jeopardizing global food security. We therefore support efforts towards an arrangement in the Black Sea to safeguard freedom of navigation," the EU's top diplomat, Kaja Kallas, said.
President Volodymyr Zelensky, on Sept. 23, addressed the U.N. General Assembly, calling for continued support for Ukraine, stressing the importance of negotiations, and warning that Ukrainians will continue to fight back against Russia.
According to Bloomberg, Burnham also told Zelensky in their private meeting during the United Nations General Assembly that Ukraine’s allies must keep sanctions in place against Russia to maintain pressure and help bring the war to an end.
More than 76,000 women serve in the Ukrainian Armed Forces, including 57,000 military personnel, while the remainder hold civilian positions, the General Staff said in response to an inquiry from the Kyiv Independent.
"Who can imagine that a country would allow its own capital to be attacked and provide no response to such a situation?" France's far-left leader Jean-Luc Melenchon asked rhetorically, in what appeared to be a reference to Ukrainian drone strikes on Moscow.
"We think it's an opportunity for him to engage not just with the (U.S.) president but with other world leaders. We hope that's an invitation he'll accept," Rubio told journalists. "We remain open to engaging."
Sikorski said the meeting took place on "neutral territory" and that "when a neighbor wants to thaw and improve relations, Poland is always the first to agree."
The helicopter entered Polish airspace to a maximum depth of around 300 meters and remained there for 42 seconds, Poland's Armed Forces Operational Command said.
How much pressure can Donald Trump’s new tariffs place on Russia’s war economy? A new U.S. law gives the president the power to impose tariffs of up to 100% on major buyers of Russian energy, while also strengthening sanctions against Russia’s shadow fleet.
The attacks came on the same day that Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelensky warned Kyiv of the potential for a new large-scale strike by Russia, referencing intelligence reports.
TCC Group Holdings, based in Taipei, plans to purchase a 100% stake in Ivano Frankivsk Cement and three other related companies through its Dutch subsidiary, the company announced in a press release on Sept. 23.

articles.title: How the U.K. Is Supporting Saudi Arabia In Its Fight Against the Houthis
articles.body:
Saudi Arabia will have assistance from a key Western ally in its fight against Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthis, as Britain is providing military support to the Kingdom in a bid to help restore stability in the region and ease pressures on the global energy supply.
“We’re working with our friends to try and deliver that de-escalation,” British Defense Minister Luke Pollard said in an interview Tuesday. The “purely defensive” deployment of an RAF Voyager to Saudi Arabia is intended to “ensure there’s no further escalation in the Red Sea, which could further risk our fuel prices,” he added.
The international assistance comes following weeks of fighting between the Saudi-backed government of Yemen and the Houthis, which shattered a four-year informal cease-fire in the country's civil war. The Houthi rebels have made significant advances along the Red Sea coastline as they seek to tighten their grip on the Bab el-Mandeb, a critical maritime chokepoint that links Asia and Europe via the Red Sea and Suez Canal. With global energy supplies already under strain due to the disruption in the Strait of Hormuz amid the Iran war, the strangling of another trade route could further impact oil and fuel prices.
“Much of our trade, both in goods and in energy, comes through that part of the world. What happens in that part of the Middle East is absolutely vital for our own national security and our own economic security,” Pollard said, explaining why Britain responded to the Kingdom’s request for help.
When talking to reporters en route to the United Nations General Assembly in New York, ahead of his sit-down with President Donald Trump on Tuesday, U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham also cited the cost of living “pressures” at home as a key reason for the support and said he was “acting to secure the interests of Britain and the wider region.”
Burnham emphasized that it’s a “time-limited agreement in terms of the assistance that we will provide, but we will keep it under review.”
The support extended to Saudi Arabia marks Burnham’s first military deployment since he became Prime Minister in July. However, it’s far from the first time the U.K. has offered assistance to Saudi Arabia, as the two nations share a close military alliance.
How exactly will the U.K. be supporting Saudi Arabia?
The Ministry of Defense on Tuesday confirmed it had agreed to “provide an RAF Voyager air-to-air refuelling aircraft to support Saudi defensive activity” in the region. According to the British Royal Air Force (RAF), a Voyager provides strategic air support by allowing jets and other aircraft to refuel while in flight.
Andreas Krieg, a senior lecturer in defense studies at King's College London, says the Voyager “basically allows the Saudi Air Force to stay in the air over Yemen for longer without having to fly a single sortie and then returning to base.”
“It increases the operational tempo in terms of targeting strikes and being more flexible, and more agile in responding to changing situations on the ground,” he tells TIME.
According to Pollard, the Voyager is set to operate from the British RAF base in Cyprus, which was targeted by Iran earlier this year, and will support the British-built Typhoon jets used by Saudi Arabia. “That will help them with their defensive actions against the Houthis, who have been attacking not just the capital of Saudi Arabia in Riyadh, but also the Republic of Yemen as well,” he said.
Britain has historically held the role of “guarantor for maritime freedom of navigation all around the world,” says Krieg, describing the U.K.’s latest attempt to ease tensions over the Red Sea as an example of the government “stepping up to the plate.”
“We're not just helping a partner in the region,” he adds. “We're also helping ourselves, because the Houthis having the Bab al-Mandeb is not something that the U.K. can tolerate.”
Krieg says the move signifies a small success for Saudi Arabia and other Gulf states as they seek to strengthen bilateral security relationships beyond their traditional reliance on the U.S. This is “the worst security situation the Saudis have been in [for] a very long time,” he notes.
“Gulf states are trying to supplement the existing U.S. capabilities with all kinds of [other] agreements, like the Mecca pact,” he says, referencing a trilateral defense security pact made between Pakistan, Saudi Arabia, and Turkey in August. “The U.K. wants to be seen as being active and being there when a friend is in need.”
The long-standing alliance between the U.K. and Saudi Arabia
The U.K. and Saudi Arabia share an alliance that dates back to almost a century ago.
“It's a very long, strategic partnership,” says Krieg. “It goes back to the early days of the current Kingdom, where Britain, at the time, was still the only superpower in the world, and was controlling the waterways and a lot of the territories in Arabia, including in South Yemen.”
Britain was among the first governments to recognize the independent territories of Saudi Arabia through the Treaty of Jeddah in 1927, which helped solidify the boundaries of the nascent kingdom ahead of the formation of modern Saudi Arabia in 1932.
Decades later, the U.K. supported the Saudi-led military coalition in its campaign against the Houthis from 2015 until the 2022 truce.
According to the Campaign Against Arms Trade (CAAT), the published value of U.K. arms export licenses to Saudi Arabia from the start of the bombing campaign in March 2015 through the April 2022 truce was £7.1 billion ($9.4 billion).
“The two main Western backers of the Saudi Kingdom are the Americans and the British,” says David Wearing, an assistant professor in international relations at the University of Sussex. “From the British and the American point of view, the Middle East is strategically important because it's a huge source of global energy suppliers, oil, and gas.”
In late 2023, the Houthis started disrupted shipping in the Red Sea, targeting cargo ships they said were linked to Israel, in what they described as a show of support for Palestinians in Gaza. Amid concerns over the impact on the world economy, the U.S. and U.K. joined forces in January 2024, striking multiple Houthi targets in Yemen. In April 2025, the U.K. government participated in another joint operation with the U.S. against a Houthi military facility in Yemen.
In March of this year, the U.K. deployed a Sky Sabre, the army’s medium range air defense missile system, to Saudi Arabia to defend the Kingdom against Iranian missile and drone attacks.
The U.K. government's Strategic Export Controls Annual Report of 2025 described the military relationship with Saudi Arabia as a “longstanding” partnership providing “Typhoon, Tornado, and Hawk aircraft, mine countermeasure vessels, and associated munitions, infrastructure, logistics and manpower support packages.”
BAE Systems—a major British defense, aerospace, and security company—said in its own 2025 report that Saudi Arabia was its largest customer by sales in its air business.
How are Saudi Arabia’s other allies responding to the Houthis' advances?
Saudi Arabia has reportedly sought assistance from allies to stave off Houthi advances. France, Pakistan, and Egypt issued strong statements condemning the Houthi attacks, but have not publicly announced new military support for the Kingdom.
Trump is understood to have received requests from Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman to strike the Houthi rebels. According to the New York Times, Trump reportedly considered launching strikes against the Houthis over the weekend, before ultimately deciding against it. TIME has reached out to the White House for comment.
Asked Tuesday why Washington has held back from striking the Houthis, Secretary of State Marco Rubio said it’s “a very dangerous and complex” conflict.
“If it comes down to it, the United States will always stand with Saudi Arabia and support them because we have an agreement with them to do so,” he said, referencing the U.S. economic and defense partnership with Saudi Arabia signed last November, that deepened co-operation between the two countries.
Fears mount over global energy supply as Houthis advance
Global energy supplies have been under increasing strain since the start of the Iran war on Feb. 28, as Tehran has leveraged its chokehold over the Strait of Hormuz, through which around a fifth of global oil production flowed prior to the conflict.
In the past few weeks, the Houthis have captured Yemen’s port city of Mokha and the strategic Perim Island, which sits in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. If the Houthis were to assume control of the strait, shipping companies could be forced to travel via South Africa’s Cape of Good Hope—a longer, costlier route.
The volume of crude oil and petroleum liquids moving through the Bab el-Mandeb increased earlier this year, with the route being used as an alternative to the Strait of Hormuz. The shipments surged from 5.6 million barrels per day in the first quarter of 2026 to 8.1 million per day in the second quarter, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA).
However, recent crossings have been marred by uncertainty over the potential threat posed by the Houthis. Data shared with TIME by Kpler, a commodities data and analytics firm, showed an estimated 34 vessels transited the Bab el-Mandeb on Sept. 15, a drop from the estimated 53 crossings recorded on July 15th.
A spokesperson for the Houthis on Sept. 11 insisted the waterway will remain free to roam “with the exception of Saudi ships.” Yet concerns among global leaders and shipping companies remain.
Burnham and other U.K. officials have framed Britain’s defensive support partly around the potential economic consequences at home. The average price of petrol rose by 9.1 pence per litre between July and August 2026, compared with a rise of 0.3 pence per litre between July and August 2025, according to data from the Office of National Statistics.
Wearing says that because oil is traded on a global market, supply disruptions in one region can push up benchmark prices worldwide, with those costs cascading through the broader economy.
“What Americans call gas and what we call petrol, if that goes up, think how many goods to market are taken by heavy lorries on petrol. It can push up the price of everything: shipping, road transit, energy, all kinds of industrial production and many consumer products,” he says. “Oil is the lifeblood of the world economy, the longer you restrict the supply, the higher the price goes, the more inflationary pressure there is on everything, and that affects Britain, but it affects the whole system. It's like a heart attack in a human body, suddenly it's not being pumped round."

articles.title: No pause in Ukraine conflict for peace talks – Lavrov
articles.body:
No pause in Ukraine conflict for peace talks – Lavrov
Moscow will not pause its special military operation while peace negotiations are underway, Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov told the UN Security Council on Wednesday, asserting that a temporary ceasefire only benefits Kiev.
Ukraine and 51 of its allies released a statement on Wednesday demanding that Russia accept an “immediate and unconditional ceasefire” so that peace talks between Moscow and Kiev can take place. The statement, whose signatories included the EU and its member states, the UK, Canada, and Australia, was published before the security council met to discuss the conflict.
“We are not going to have a pause in our special military operation,” Lavrov said during the meeting. “Europe, whatever it thinks, just wants to get a pause and it wants to use it to pump the Kiev regime with weapons.”
Kiev is “clearly and blatantly using terrorist methods,” Lavrov added, referring to Ukraine’s long-range strikes on civilian targets in Russia.
Ukraine and its allies issued their ceasefire demand less than four days after Ukrainian forces launched their largest-ever drone raid on the Russian capital. The attack killed two civilians in its suburbs and damaged an oil refinery, residential buildings, and civilian infrastructure. Moscow Mayor Sergey Sobyanin said the “unprecedented” raid involved more than 1,600 UAVs from all directions.
Throughout the conflict, Ukraine has repeatedly followed such attacks with appeals for ceasefire, which Russia has rebuffed. Moscow maintains that it will only cease military action when both sides seek a comprehensive settlement that addresses the root causes of the conflict.
Russia has dramatically stepped up its missile and drone attacks on Ukrainian military and dual-use infrastructure in recent months, in response to Vladimir Zelensky’s 40-day “influence campaign” of long-range strikes on civilian targets.
Zelensky’s stated aim was to foment discontent among the Russian public, but the campaign ultimately ended with the destruction of Ukraine’s Black Sea port infrastructure and an earlier-than-usual start to Russia’s winter campaign against its power plants and substations.
In a statement released after the latest drone raid on Moscow, the Russian Defense Ministry said that the Russian army would further “intensify its high-accuracy strikes against military targets in Kiev” in response.

articles.title: US targets Iranian airlines (VIDEO)
articles.body:
US targets Iranian airlines (VIDEO)
Iranian airlines are being cut off from international routes and airport services as Washington steps up pressure on the country’s aviation sector. Several regional connections have already been suspended or restricted, although some foreign flights continue, RT’s Saman Kojouri has reported from outside the Tehran headquarters of Mahan Air, one of Iran’s major carriers.
The US Treasury targeted 27 Iranian airlines earlier this month as part of a broader campaign against the country’s aviation sector. Foreign companies providing services to the carriers risk US secondary sanctions, while Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent warned that the restrictions would effectively shut Iranian airlines out of international aviation from September 23.
”If they land, you cannot provide them with fuel, you cannot provide them with landing services, you cannot sell them tickets, or you will be knocked out of the dollar system,” Bessent said.
The impact is already spreading across the region, according to RT’s Kojouri. Azerbaijan has suspended flights operated by Iranian carriers, while Iraq has reportedly stopped accepting Iranian aircraft. Flights between Tehran and Muscat have also been suspended, while Georgia has said it will comply with sanctions affecting Iranian carriers.
Mahan Air is among the airlines facing the squeeze. Washington first sanctioned the carrier in 2011, accusing it of providing support to Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps-Quds Force (IRGC-QF). The Treasury has since targeted companies abroad accused of providing commercial and logistical support to the airline.
The aviation crackdown comes as Washington ramps up pressure on Tehran while simultaneously pursuing diplomatic contacts on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York. President Donald Trump threatened on Tuesday to “annihilate the Islamic Republic” if negotiations fail, saying he faced a “big decision” between reaching an agreement and further military escalation.
Most of the Iranian delegation walked out of the General Assembly hall during Trump’s speech, leaving only one representative seated. The US president defended the nearly seven-month US-Israeli war and accused Tehran of pursuing nuclear weapons and supporting terrorism.
Despite the hostile rhetoric, indirect contacts continued later in the day. US envoy Steve Witkoff said mediators had shuttled between the American and Iranian delegations during “lengthy talks,” while Tehran said it had used the channel to clearly convey its conditions to Washington, including lifting the US naval blockade and releasing frozen Iranian assets.

articles.title: New US “Fort Trump” military base in Poland “confirmed”, says President Nawrocki
articles.body:
Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work!
Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support.
Polish President Karol Nawrocki says that a planned new permanent US military base in Poland is “confirmed” because his American counterpart, Donald Trump, is “famous for keeping his word”. He also suggested that the new facility will be called “Fort Trump”.
Trump himself declared last week that “major progress” was being made towards establishing the base, saying it was thanks to the “bold leadership of my friend, Karol Nawrocki”, who is a conservative ally of the US president.
Meanwhile, earlier this week, a Polish deputy defence minister, Stanisław Wziątek, also expressed confidence that the new base would soon be confirmed and said that it could see the number of US troops stationed in Poland rise to around 15,000.
President Karol Nawrocki said he hopes the US will finalize plans to establish a permanent military base in Poland and, if it does, the compound will be christened ‘Fort Trump' https://t.co/SB4DOy5Qp1 pic.twitter.com/aPmvl4JoFO
— Bloomberg TV (@BloombergTV) September 22, 2026
The US military presence in Poland has become a big issue this year following Washington’s unexpected last-minute decision in May to cancel the rotational deployment of almost 4,000 troops.
Shortly afterwards, Trump declared that he would deploy 5,000 additional troops to Poland. In June, Poland formally submitted a request for the US to establish a new permanent US military base on its territory.
In a post on his social media platform, Truth Social, last week, Trump announced “major progress” in those plans and said that “if this happens, the location [of the base] will be announced very soon”. He called it a “historic step for our Great US/Polish Alliance”.
On Tuesday this week, speaking to Bloomberg during a visit to the US for the United Nations General Assembly, Nawrocki confirmed that plans for the base were at an advanced stage.
“The infrastructure is being chosen right now. Consultants from the US have already visited Poland,” he said. “I think that it’s hard for me to give specific dates, but I think that this matter is for sure confirmed because President Trump is famous for keeping his word.”
Nawrocki also expressed confidence that “President Trump will personally be able to participate in the inauguration of Fort Trump”. That name, Fort Trump, was first suggested in 2018 by Nawrocki’s predecessor, Andrzej Duda, when, during Trump’s first term, he sought a permanent US base in Poland.
Poland’s government, which regularly clashes with the opposition-aligned Nawrocki and has also at times had tense relations with the Trump administration, has not commented on the idea of naming the new base after the US president.
However, the government is keen for the project to move ahead, and has been doing much of the legwork on making it happen. Although Poland’s president is commander-in-chief of the armed forces, his position is largely ceremonial, and it is the government that is responsible for implementing policy.
On Monday this week, deputy defence minister Stanisław Wziątek told broadcaster RMF that he was “convinced there is full agreement” on establishing the base, with the remaining question being the precise location.
Wziątek said that the announcement could be made before November’s midterm elections in the US, as Trump will be keen to encourage Polish Americans to vote Republican.
💬Kiedy poznamy ostateczną decyzję w sprawie stałej bazy amerykańskiej w Polsce?
💬Jestem przekonany, że pan prezydent @realDonaldTrump będzie chciał zrobić wszystko, aby tak decyzja zachęcająca Polaków do głosowania na Republikanów mogła zapaść przed wyborami – Stanisław… pic.twitter.com/uPWkmdGQod
— RozmowaRMF (@Rozmowa_RMF) September 21, 2026
The deputy defence minister said that the base would be likely to host between 3,000 and 5,000 US troops, with 4,500 the “most realistic estimate, because that is the size of a brigade”.
In total, said Wziątek, Poland hoped to have “around 15,000” US soldiers in Poland, including the roughly 10,000 that have up until now been present on a rotational basis.
The minister admitted that the current rotational presence was lower, around 6,500-7,000, following the cancellation of May’s planned deployment. But he said that the figure should “soon” return to the previous higher level.
When asked about the cost to Poland of establishing the new permanent US base, Wziątek said it would “definitely be more than 15 billion zloty (€3.4 billion) but will depend on the level of involvement of the United States”.
💬Ilu w tej chwili w Polsce jest żołnierzy amerykańskich? Ilu będzie docelowo rotacyjnych żołnierzy i w stałej bazie?
Odpowiada Stanisław Wziątek @MON_GOV_PL w #RozmowaRMF o 7:00 w @Radio_RMF24@RMF24pl @Radio_RMF24 pic.twitter.com/1Zl66upkp8
— RozmowaRMF (@Rozmowa_RMF) September 21, 2026
The US has long been Poland’s most important security partner. In 2023, under President Joe Biden, it established its first permanent military garrison in Poland at Camp Kościuszko in the city of Poznań. The following year, a US missile defence base opened in Redzikowo on Poland’s northern Baltic coast.
This week, the mayor of Poznań, Jacek Jaśkowiak, told newspaper Fakt that his city was one of two locations being considered for the planned new US base. Recent Polish media reports have also identified the provinces of Lower Silesia and West Pomerania as potential locations.
While the Trump administration has chastised many NATO member states for failing to meet the alliance’s defence spending targets, it has hailed Poland, whose defence budget is one of NATO’s highest in relation to GDP, as a “model ally”.
Between 2021 and 2025, Poland was also the largest importer of arms in NATO. Around 44% of those purchases came from the US, including Abrams tanks, Patriot air defence batteries, and HIMARS rocket artillery.

Daniel Tilles is editor-in-chief of Notes from Poland. He has written on Polish affairs for a wide range of publications, including Foreign Policy, POLITICO Europe, EUobserver and Dziennik Gazeta Prawna.

articles.title: Sanctions must remain in place and be strengthened as long as war continues, Zelensky says after meeting Burnham
articles.body:
Sanctions must remain in place and be strengthened as long as war continues, Zelensky says after meeting Burnham
Ukrinform reports this, citing the official Facebook page of the President of Ukraine.
“I discussed in detail with UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham everything related to security, the protection of our people, preparations for winter, and available diplomatic opportunities. I thank the United Kingdom for its steadfast support for our energy sector. There is a new contribution, and we particularly value it as winter approaches,” the post says.
At the same time, the President added, Ukraine is in constant communication with its partners about finding additional air defense capabilities.
According to him, intelligence currently indicates that Russia is preparing a new massive attack against Ukraine.
“When Ukrainians are living every day under the threat of missile and drone strikes, lifting sanctions is out of the question. The Prime Minister and I see this eye to eye: as long as the war continues, sanctions must remain in place and be strengthened,” Volodymyr Zelensky emphasized.
As reported by Ukrinform, Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha criticized the EU’s decision to remove Russian oligarchs Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman from its sanctions list.
