articles.title: Britain forms squadron to strike threats in orbit
articles.body:
The Royal Air Force is today forming No. III Space Effects Squadron, the first British unit dedicated to disrupting, degrading and denying hostile activity in space, the Ministry of Defence stated.
The squadron is being announced by the Chief of the Air Staff, Air Chief Marshal Sir Harv Smyth, at the first UK Space Power Conference today, and will bring together specialist personnel from across the armed forces to counter hostile activity in orbit and defend the satellites the country depends on.
Sir Harv will say: “Space no longer supports operations from the sidelines. It’s a domain of direct competition, where our military advantage can be won or lost. No. III Space Effects Squadron will safeguard the vital benefits that space gives to our integrated armed forces, and will be capable of denying those benefits to our adversaries.”
The new unit completes a trio of squadrons, since No. I Space Operations Squadron gives the Royal Air Force the ability to watch what is happening in orbit and No. II Space Warning Squadron provides warning of threats, while according to the department No. III will act against those threats using advanced technology including electronic warfare. It will support both offensive and defensive space operations and is expected to expand as new capabilities enter service.
The department describes the formation as contributing to developing British capabilities for space warfare, including electronic warfare and countermeasures against anti-satellite weapons, and delivering the Control of Space Requirement set out in the UK Space Strategy published earlier this month. That requirement covers maintaining freedom to operate in space while denying adversaries the same freedom.
Britain has formally ruled out destructive anti-satellite missile testing, the kind that generates long-lived debris fields, and the department says it continues to work through the United Nations Committee on the Peaceful Uses of Outer Space to promote norms and principles of responsible behaviour in orbit. The government describes itself as committed to the peaceful and sustainable use of space while protecting critical infrastructure.
Alongside the announcement, the department restated an £880 million investment between 2026/27 and 2029/30 in space-based intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance and in space control activities.
The Strategic Defence Review stated that the ability to operate in, from and through space underpins British security, prosperity and daily life, and the Defence Investment Plan committed to the Deep Space Advanced Radar Capability, a trilateral programme with the United States and Australia whose British site is due to begin construction in April 2027 and which will provide continuous radar coverage of geostationary orbit.

articles.title: Britain prepares for war in space as threats grow
articles.body:
Britain is developing capabilities for what it explicitly describes as “orbital warfare”, including systems able to disrupt, degrade and deny hostile activity in space as the Armed Forces prepare for conflict extending beyond the Earth’s atmosphere.
Air Chief Marshal Sir Harv Smyth, Chief of the Air Staff and professional head of the Royal Air Force, set out the direction of travel at the UK Space Power Conference in London, warning that adversaries are not waiting for Britain to complete its preparations.
The conference is delivered by UK Space Command and led in partnership with the Freeman Air & Space Institute. Its programme brings together senior figures from Defence, government, the UK Space Agency and allied military organisations.
Smyth said: “Space has never been more important for our nation’s defence and security, for our prosperity and our daily lives, and our adversaries are not waiting until we’re ready for them.”
He added: “We must now get on with delivery of space capability and operational effect at pace.”
The most direct indication of how far that effort is moving came when Smyth described the development of capabilities specifically intended for operations against hostile activity in orbit.
He said: “To help our nation fulfil the control of space requirement, UK Defence is now developing capabilities for orbital warfare.”
Smyth defined this as “actions and effects conducted within space to achieve military objectives”, alongside electronic warfare, systems intended to counter anti-satellite weapons and other supporting operations.
He said: “These capabilities will help us to deter threats, defend our critical space infrastructure, and reduce an adversary’s freedom to operate against the UK and against our allies.”
The language marks a shift from treating space primarily as a supporting domain for communications, navigation and surveillance towards preparing to contest it directly if necessary.
Smyth said the objective was to secure freedom of action for Britain and NATO while denying an adversary the same advantage.
He said: “Through a whole-of-government approach, the UK will safeguard allied space interests. We will gain and maintain our freedom to operate in space, and we will deny our adversaries that same freedom.”
That effort is being backed by several large investment lines. Smyth said £2.3 billion is being committed to satellite communications between now and 2030, alongside £880 million for space-based intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance and space control, and £440 million for novel space technology.
Skynet remains central to the military communications architecture. Smyth described the satellite system as the backbone of Britain’s sovereign global communications capability and said an additional £50 million had been allocated to extend the life of the existing Skynet 5 satellites.
Skynet 6A is due to join them next year, while allied and commercial satellite communications are also expected to provide additional capacity and resilience.
Britain is also expanding its ability to detect and understand activity in orbit. Smyth pointed to RAF Fylingdales, the planned Deep Space Advanced Radar Capability being developed with Australia and the United States, and a growing network of optical and commercial sensors feeding the National Space Operations Centre.
He said the Borealis command, control and data-processing system had reached initial operating capability six months ahead of schedule under a five-year, £65 million programme, giving commanders a better picture of activity in space.
The UK is also examining newer sensor technologies, including neuromorphic systems intended to search large areas of space for unexpected activity around satellites while using considerably less power and communications bandwidth.
Those surveillance systems are intended to support the wider military effort rather than operate in isolation. Smyth described space as the “connective tissue” of the integrated force, linking communications, surveillance and targeting systems across land, sea and air.
Space-based intelligence is also expected to feed the Digital Targeting Web, a £1.8 billion programme intended to connect sensors, commanders and weapons and reduce the time between detecting a target and acting against it.
Alongside the new technology, Defence is expanding the military organisation responsible for operating it. No. 1 Space Operations Squadron already supports activity through the National Space Operations Centre, while No. 2 Space Warning Squadron carries out operations associated with RAF Fylingdales.
A new No. 3 Space Effects Squadron will provide personnel specifically for offensive and defensive space operations, with Smyth saying it will “disrupt, degrade, and deny hostile activity to defend UK space interests and gain operational advantage for the integrated force.”
Plans are also being developed for further numbered squadrons covering areas including tactics and training, the deep-space radar programme and space defence as part of a wider integrated air, space and missile defence structure.
Smyth was careful to frame the build-up as deterrence rather than an intention to initiate conflict.
He said: “No one wants a war in space. We are positioning to deter this. The UK will always operate responsibly in ways that promote stability and avoid escalation.”
But he also made clear that Defence is preparing for the possibility that deterrence fails.
He concluded that Britain must be able to “monitor space, make effective decisions, deter our adversaries, and, if necessary, prevail in this vital yet increasingly contested domain.”

articles.title: There were 242 combat engagements at the front — the General Staff spoke about the hottest areas
articles.body:
There were 242 combat engagements at the front — the General Staff spoke about the hottest areas
Kyiv • UNN
Over the past day, Russian forces carried out 59 airstrikes, used 190 guided aerial bombs and 4,185 kamikaze drones. The enemy launched more than 180 attacks on the positions of our troops and populated areas.
Over the course of September 23, there were 242 combat engagements on the front. This was reported by UNN, citing the update from the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine.
Details
It is reported that the aggressor carried out 59 airstrikes using 190 guided aerial bombs, deployed 4,185 kamikaze drones for attacks, and carried out 1,801 shelling attacks on the positions of our troops and populated areas.
Situation by direction
On the Northern Slobozhansky and Kursk directions, five enemy assault actions have been recorded since the beginning of the day. The occupiers carried out one airstrike using three guided aerial bombs and shelled the positions of our troops and populated areas 39 times, two of them using multiple launch rocket systems.
On the Southern Slobozhansky direction, the enemy attacked the positions of our units eight times toward the populated areas of Ternova, Starytsia, Vovchansk, Karaichne, and Mala Vovcha.
On the Kupiansk direction, the enemy twice attempted to improve its positions by conducting assault actions toward Kurylivka and Novoosynove.
Thirteen attempts by the invaders to advance were repelled on the Lyman direction in the areas of the populated areas of Novoselivka, Drobysheve, Lyman, Masliakivka, and Dibrova.
On the Sloviansk direction, the Defense Forces stopped five attempts by the invaders to advance in the areas of the populated areas of Yampil, Starodubivka, and Mykolaivka.
On the Kramatorsk direction, the enemy attacked toward Yurkivka.
On the Kostiantynivka direction, the Defense Forces repelled 30 enemy assaults: in the area of the populated area of Kostiantynivka and toward Ivanopillia, Novoselivka, Mykolaipillia, Stepanivka, Novopavlivka, Raiske, Toretske, Vilne, and Stepiv.
The enemy launched twelve attacks on the Pokrovsk direction. The occupiers attempted to advance toward the populated areas of Svitle, Novyi Donbas, Bilytske, Novohryshyne, Hulive, Serhiivka, Molodetske, Muravka, and Novopavlivka.
According to preliminary estimates, 69 occupiers were eliminated here today and 17 were wounded; seven vehicles, one gun, two special-purpose assets, 45 shelters, a fuel and lubricants depot, and four enemy UAV control posts were destroyed. Two vehicles, two artillery systems, six UAV control posts, and 116 personnel shelters were damaged. A total of 149 unmanned aerial vehicles of various types were destroyed or suppressed
On the Oleksandrivka direction, the enemy did not conduct any assault actions.
On the Huliaipole direction, the Defense Forces repelled four enemy attacks near the populated areas of Rizdv'ianka and Kopani.
On the Orikhiv direction, the enemy also attempted five times to advance toward Zarichne, Novoandriivka, and Pavlivka.
On the Dnipro direction, the occupiers attacked toward Marhanets and Dniprovske.
"There have been no significant changes in the situation on the other directions," the General Staff added.
To remind you
More than 50 UN Member States, as well as the EU, called on Russia to agree to a ceasefire and peace talks with Ukraine.

articles.title: 3 killed, over 40 injured as Russia, Ukraine trade accusations about overnight airstrikes
articles.body:
Burc Eruygur
23 September 2026•Update: 23 September 2026
- Ukraine claims it shot down 122 drones launched by Moscow overnight
 
At least three people were killed and over 40 others were injured in Russia and Ukraine as both countries continued to trade accusations concerning overnight airstrikes on Wednesday.
 
In Ukraine, the Kyiv City Military Administration (KMVA) said on Telegram that a warehouse, a fuel station, and an office building in the Holosiivskyi district and another fuel station in the Darnytskyi district were damaged in an overnight attack on the country’s capital, during which drone debris also fell at a location in the Solomianskyi district.
 
“As of 10 am (0700GMT), one person has died and seven others have been injured following a hostile attack on the capital,” it said.
 
*The KMVA later said that the number of those killed in the Ukrainian capital had risen to two, while 23 others were injured.
 
Odesa Governor Oleh Kiper said that one person was killed after Russian strikes targeted port and civilian infrastructure in the southern region, including an Antigua and Barbuda-flagged commercial cargo vessel and an unspecified number of warehouses.
 
“Due to numerous Russian attacks, rescuers from the Mykolaiv region have joined in the efforts to extinguish the fires,” Ukraine’s State Emergency Service (DSNS) said, commenting on strikes in the Odesa region.
 
The DSNS also reported that 12 others were injured due to strikes in the country’s Kharkiv, Zaporizhzhia, and Zhytomyr regions.
 
Ukraine’s Air Force claimed that the country’s air defenses shot down 122 Russian drones overnight.
 
Meanwhile, the Russian Defense Ministry claimed hitting a storage facility and an industrial enterprise in Kyiv and its surrounding region that are allegedly involved in the production of drones and drone components.
 
It also claimed striking three logistics centers in Odesa used to supply Ukraine’s military, a drone warehouse in the Odesa region, and a vessel “while it was delivering military cargo to the port of Odesa.”
 
Earlier, the ministry further claimed that it shot down 514 drones launched by Ukraine overnight over 18 regions, as well as the Black Sea, the Sea of Azov, and Crimea, which Russia annexed in 2014.
 
Alexander Shuvaev, acting governor of Russia’s border region of Belgorod, said in a statement that eight people were wounded in five districts due to Ukrainian strikes over the past day, with two of them in serious condition.
 
In the border region of Bryansk, acting governor Yegor Kovalchuk said two people were injured due to Ukrainian drone strikes in the villages of Kryukov and Churovichi.
 
Ukrainian authorities have not yet commented on strikes in Russia.
 
Both Russia and Ukraine have ramped up strikes in recent months, targeting each other’s logistics centers, ports, and energy infrastructure.
 
Both sides deny deliberately targeting civilian infrastructure, maintaining that their strikes are directed at military targets or facilities linked to military activities.

articles.title: Zelensky calls for pressure on India to stop buying Russian oil
articles.body:
Zelensky calls for pressure on India to stop buying Russian oil
Vladimir Zelensky has attempted to blame New Delhi over the West’s failure to end the conflict in Ukraine, right after the Indian foreign minister discussed peace efforts and bilateral cooperation with his Ukrainian counterpart in New York.
”Russia is basing its economy on India, sometimes Turkey and China,” Zelensky said in an interview with the Wall Street Journal on Tuesday.
The Ukrainian leader is in New York seeking more weapons and cash amid a $27 billion hole in Ukraine’s budget and a frontline collapse. The conflict is now in its fifth year, laying bare the West’s foreign policy failures, and Zelensky seemed to be making a case to US President Donald Trump to use his new sanctions authority to punish Russia’s trading partners.
But in India, the largest buyer of Russian oil besides China, the pitch has come across more as a call to punish New Delhi specifically.
Trump, who is set to meet Chinese President Xi Jinping soon in New York, would be loath to sanction China, especially after Beijing retaliated against earlier US tariffs with restrictions on exports of rare-earth metals and magnets that are crucial to US industries.
“Russia is basing its economy on India” and “ sometimes Turkey and China”. 
How can he make this ridiculous assertion?
China is by far Russia’s biggest trade partner, including in energy.
Turkey is very critical as a country for Russia. Russia and Turkey are connected by major… https://t.co/Jr7IsZzcOS
Russian oil accounted for about 45% of New Delhi’s crude imports in August, at around 2.1 million barrels per day. The numbers were slightly lower in September, tracking at about 1.9 million barrels per day, according to commodity analytics firm Kpler.
India has said it remains committed to securing energy supplies for its 1.4 billion people and will take the necessary measures to protect its trade and economic interests amid repeated US tariff threats. New Delhi has also warned Washington of the sanctions impacting bilateral ties and global energy markets.
”This conflict … will not be solved because somebody is buying or not buying oil or alumina or minerals or metals or fertilizer,” Indian External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar had said earlier this month in Kiev. He had discussed peace efforts, bilateral cooperation, and developments in the Black Sea, affecting markets with his Ukrainian counterpart Andrii Sybiha in New York just before Zelensky gave his interview.
Moscow’s oil revenue has increased amid the disruptions in the Middle East caused by the US-Israeli attacks on Iran, but its non-energy trade with the Global South has also expanded.
Russia remains an important source of minerals and metals throughout the world amid supply chain disruptions. The US, too, has carved out exemptions for Russian uranium in the sanctions law it just passed.
Zelensky’s interview triggered some anger in Indian foreign policy circles. “How can he make this ridiculous assertion?” former Indian foreign secretary Kanwal Sybal posted on X. “China is by far Russia’s biggest trade partner, including in energy. Zelensky is targeting us openly.”

articles.title: Leader’s advisor: Iran fully prepared for defense; US aggression will bring heavy casualties
articles.body:
Leader’s advisor: Iran fully prepared for defense; US aggression will bring heavy casualties
TEHRAN – A senior military advisor to Leader of the Islamic Revolution Ayatollah Seyyed Mojtaba Khamenei, says Iran’s armed forces are fully prepared to defend the country in every field, warning the United States would face heavy casualties in the event of any aggression.
“In the missile, air-defense, and territorial-defense sectors, we have reached a level where, God forbid, if they (American forces) intend to land anywhere in Iran, they will certainly be destroyed,” Major General Yahya Rahim Safavi, said during a televised broadcast on Tuesday.
“We have at least 10 million trained Basij personnel, who can defend all parts of the country through a distributed, mosaic-style approach and asymmetric warfare,” he said.
“People are the main pillar of the Islamic Republic’s power and national security.”
Safavi, a former chief commander of the Islamic Revolution Guards Corps (IRGC), also pointed to Iran’s significant advances in missile, drone and air-defense capabilities, as well as its monitoring of foreign military activity in the region.
“In the maritime domain, whether in the skies over the Persian Gulf or even in the Indian Ocean, we detect with our radar systems the US naval vessels currently in the region…and determine where they are located,” he said.
Safavi said Iran could carry out both defensive and retaliatory operations, adding that the outcome of a conflict would also depend on the resilience and determination of the societies involved.
“What matters is whether their social resilience in the United States is greater than Iran’s. Iran’s is certainly greater. War is a battle of wills,” Safavi said.
“Iran knows its objectives and wants to defend itself, its national interests, and its dignity.”
Safavi’s remarks come amid heightened tensions over US military activity in the region. Iran has repeatedly emphasized deterrence and territorial defense, including the role of missile and drone capabilities and the mobilization of forces across the country.
The advisor also addressed the Strait of Hormuz, saying its reopening would depend, among other things, on the lifting of the United States’ illegal naval blockade.
“The Strait of Hormuz will not be reopened through US military pressure. It is Iran and Oman that can establish the mechanism for this. We are in contact with the Omanis, although public reporting indicates that the United States is preventing this,” he said.
“The reopening of the Strait of Hormuz is conditional on [the US’s] accepting Iran’s terms.”
The strait connects the Persian Gulf to the Gulf of Oman and is a major route for international energy shipments. Its security and freedom of navigation have long been central issues in relations between Iran and the United States.
Safavi said Iran’s broader objective was to establish a Persian Gulf security framework with regional states, without US involvement.
“Our objective is to permanently remove the threat to the Iranian people and, together with the countries of the region, establish lasting security and sustainable development in the Persian Gulf without the presence of the United States,” he said.

articles.title: Taiwan to maintain 'close contact' with US on arms sales ahead of Trump-Xi meeting
articles.body:
Taiwan will continue to keep in close touch with the US to promote the implementation of arms sales according to plan, a defense ministry official said on Wednesday, ahead of a meeting between the US and Chinese leaders in Washington.
China views democratically governed Taiwan as its own territory and has repeatedly demanded US arms sales end.
While US President Donald Trump approved an $11 billion package for Taiwan in December, the largest ever, he said in May after visiting Beijing that a second package, worth some $14 billion, was being kept in abeyance.
Chinese President Xi Jinping is expected to press Trump to halt sales when the two of them meet in Washington this week.
Speaking to reporters in southern Taiwan's Tainan during a media trip, Taiwan defense ministry deputy spokesperson Chiao Fu-chun said maintaining security and stability in the Indo-Pacific region was a "common interest of democratic nations."
"The US government and Congress have repeatedly expressed their support for Taiwan's ability to defend itself," he added.
"Therefore, we will continue to maintain close contact with the US Department of War and continue to promote the implementation of arms sales according to plan."
Taiwan's domestic weapons development
Taiwan President Lai Ching-te has embraced Trump's call for US allies to spend more on their defense.
While the US is Taiwan's most important arms supplier, Taipei has its own weapons development program, covering everything from submarines and fighter jets to long-range missiles.
Taiwan's army on Wednesday showed off its new eight-wheeled armored combat vehicle fitted with a 105mm gun, practicing live-fire exercises to demonstrate the domestically made weapon's fighting abilities.
The military also put on display, but did not fire, some of its US-made weapons, such as Lockheed Martin-made HIMARS rockets.
Taiwan routinely holds live-fire drills and takes reporters to military bases to watch exercises.
China has never renounced the use of force to bring Taiwan under its control, and its military operates around the island on an almost daily basis.
Taiwan's government rejects Beijing's sovereignty claims, saying only the Taiwanese people can decide their future.

articles.title: Poland and Belarus seek thaw in relations as foreign ministers meet for first time in a decade
articles.body:

The foreign ministers of Poland and Belarus have met for the first time in a decade, as both sides indicated that they are open to thawing their long-frosty relations.
The two countries have regularly clashed in recent years, in particular over Minsk’s alliance with Moscow, the migration crisis Belarus has engineered on the Polish border, and the persecution of Belarus’s ethnic Polish minority. Warsaw, meanwhile, has supported the Belarusian democratic opposition.
However, on Tuesday this week, Polish foreign minister Radosław Sikorski confirmed to reporters that he had met with his Belarusian counterpart, Maxim Ryzhenkov, on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly in New York. Sikorski said that the initiative had come from the Belarusian side.
Przełom w relacjach z Białorusią? Sikorski potwierdza "spotkanie zapoznawcze" https://t.co/uDUPM9CiHo #swiat #radoslawsikorski #bialorus #aleksanderlukaszenko #msz #andrzejpoczobut
— Onet Wiadomości (@OnetWiadomosci) September 23, 2026
“When a neighbour wants to unfreeze and improve relations, Poland is the first to reach an agreement,” said Sikorski, quoted by broadcaster RMF.
“This is a first, introductory meeting, but meetings with other ministries and at other levels are also taking place,” he added, noting that Poland will also “soon be opening a new embassy building in Minsk”.
When asked what topics had been discussed, Sikorski said that they had included the border situation and regional security. Asked if he had requested that Belarus not allow Russia to fly drones and missiles through its territory, he said that this was discussed “among other things”.
The last known time that the Polish and Belarusian foreign ministers met was in October 2016, when Belarus’s Vladimir Makei visited Witold Waszczykowski in Warsaw.
Sikorski said that this week’s meeting with Ryzhenkov had been possible because the situation on their shared border – where Belarus has since 2021 encouraged and assisted tens of thousands of migrants, mainly from Asia and Africa, to cross into Poland – is now “more normalised”.
Poland has installed physical and electronic barriers along the border, sent thousands of armed officers to guard it, and has banned asylum claims by migrants who cross irregularly. Following those measures, the number of attempted crossings has fallen dramatically this year.
Sikorski also noted that relations have been improved by Belarus’s recent decisions to release political prisoners, including Polish ones. Most prominent among them is Andrzej Poczobut, a leader of the Polish community in Belarus, who had been imprisoned on trumped-up charges for five years.
The number of attempted illegal crossings by migrants from Belarus to Poland fell from 15,500 in the first half of 2025 to 235 this year – a drop of over 98%
Poland also now claims a 100% success rate in apprehending migrants who manage to cross illegally https://t.co/RFZkd7CeIk
— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 20, 2026
Minsk’s recent actions have provided “more freedom and greater reasons to try to stabilise relations”, said Sikorski. “A snowdrop can bloom if the weather is favorable.”
Belarus’s foreign ministry continued that metaphor in a post on social media on Wednesday, sharing a photo of Sikorski meeting with Ryzhenkov and writing that “snowdrop diplomacy is a nice restart”.
“But we’re in it for the harvest,” added the ministry. “Let’s plant an orchard – it needs nurturing every year, not once a decade. Minsk is ready to host.”
Last year, Belarus called for “dialogue” with Poland in order to “reduce the risk of armed clashes” amid a military build-up around the border. However, it also issued a formal protest to Poland over a demonstration in Warsaw organised by exiled opponents of Belarusian President Alexander Lukashenko.
.@sikorskiradek, snowdrop diplomacy is a nice restart. But we’re in it for the harvest. Let’s plant an orchard 🍎 – it needs nurturing every year, not once a decade. Minsk is ready to host 🇧🇾🇵🇱 pic.twitter.com/WSN5n4uOtE
— Belarus MFA 🇧🇾 (@BelarusMFA) September 23, 2026
News of Tuesday’s meeting was criticised by Stanisław Żaryn, who served as spokesman for the Polish security services under the former Law and Justice (PiS) government and later as an advisor to President Andrzej Duda.
In a social media post, he said that Sikorski and media outlets are “forcibly pushing us into another reset with Belarus (and perhaps even with Russia)”. However, “Belarus chose its strategic path long ago and won’t turn away from Russia”, he added.
He asked if Poles are meant to forget about the death of Mateusz Sitek, a Polish soldier killed by a migrant from a group trying to force its way over the border from Belarus. His suspected killer, a Moroccan national, is believed by Polish prosecutors to still be in Belarus, which has refused to extradite him.
Should “we just move on as if nothing happened regarding Belarus’s involvement in the war against Ukraine and the intelligence war against Poland?” continued Żaryn.
⚠️Radosław Sikorski spotkał się z Szefem MSZ Białorusi. Media już piszą o „przełomie”, a Sikorski zapewnia, że „Polska jest pierwsza do zgody”. Na siłę wtłaczają nas w kolejny reset z Białorusią (a być może i Rosją). Na czym mają polegać przełomy i „zgoda” w stosunkach z… pic.twitter.com/DZ41wSgjL0
— Stanisław Żaryn (@StZaryn) September 23, 2026
Francišak Viačorka, a leading figure in the exiled Belarusian democratic opposition, also expressed scepticism in an interview with Polish newspaper Fakt.
“We believe that the authorities in Minsk cannot be trusted,” he said. “Of course, when the authorities communicate with Western partners, they promise that everything will be fine, that they want dialogue, but then their words fail to match their actions.”
“I understand that Minister Sikorski is doing everything to protect Polish interests and the sovereignty and security of his country, but I think that in Minsk they see it differently.”

Zelensky accuses Putin of using nationals of 47 countries to fight Ukraine war
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky told the UN General Assembly on Wednesday that Russian President Vladimir Putin had enlisted fighters from 47 countries including North Korea, Ghana and India to fight against Ukraine. Zelensky also warned that his forces could target Russian heating and energy facilities in the winter months if Moscow continues to attack Ukraine's energy infrastructure.

Highlighting Russia's growing defence relationship with North Korea, Zelensky also said that two North Korean troops deployed to fight against Ukraine had been captured and sent to South Korea.
"Putin is always looking for someone who can help him kill more, kill more people for every kilometre of land, take more territory and take another country instead of simply stopping and running his own country," Zelensky said at the UN.

"Recently, we sent two North Korean prisoners of war to the Republic of Korea. These guys are not easy to capture alive," he added.

articles.title: Russian Mi-8 Helicopter Briefly Violates Polish Airspace, Poland Scrambles Fighters
articles.body:
A Russian Mi-8 military helicopter briefly violated Polish airspace on Wednesday, flying up to 300 meters (984 feet) into Polish territory near the town of Braniewo, Poland’s Operational Command said.
The helicopter entered Polish airspace from Russia’s Kaliningrad Oblast at 11:08 a.m. local time and remained there for 42 seconds, according to the statement.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Polish military radar systems detected the aircraft, prompting the scrambling of fighter jets. Ground-based air defense forces and other military assets were also placed on standby.
“The nature of the incident indicates that Russia is once again testing the readiness of our air defense,” the Operational Command said.
Polish air defense crews remain on round-the-clock watch, the command added.
Earlier incidents
The incident is the latest in a series of Russian military aircraft and drone incursions into Polish airspace since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
On Feb. 11, 2025, a Russian Su-24MR military aircraft entered Polish airspace over the Gulf of Gdańsk, penetrating about 6.5 kilometers (4 miles) and remaining there for roughly 72 seconds. Russia later acknowledged the incident and attributed it to a navigation-system malfunction.
On April 25, 2025, a Russian military helicopter also entered Polish airspace over the Baltic Sea’s territorial waters. Poland said the incident appeared to be an attempt to test its air-defense readiness.
NATO Keeps Article 5 Trigger ‘Deliberately Ambiguous’
The most serious incident came on Sept. 9-10, 2025, when 19 Russian drones violated Polish airspace during a large-scale Russian attack on Ukraine. Poland scrambled fighter jets and subsequently requested NATO consultations under Article 4.
Most recently, Poland has repeatedly scrambled aircraft in response to Russian attacks on Ukraine and increased military activity near its borders, although not every such incident has involved a violation of Polish airspace.

articles.title: Ukraine’s Vivaldi counteroffensive near Lyman just got help from behind Russian lines: partisans say they cut rail supply to three Russian regiments, no explosion needed
articles.body:
Ukrainian partisans say they have sabotaged the railway signaling that keeps Russian troops supplied on the Lyman front. The ATESH movement reports that its agents disabled four relay cabinets on a line through Voronezh Oblast that carries military cargo to Russian forces there, delaying ammunition to three regiments.
The strike was timed to help Ukraine's Operation Vivaldi, the counteroffensive the Third Army Corps is running near Lyman in northern Donetsk. In its first phase, the operation cleared 75 square kilometers of Russian infiltrators and de-occupied another 10.
Cutting the rail line that feeds the Russian units facing that offensive is, by ATESH's account, part of the same fight, targeting the supply line rather than the front.
Four cabinets go dark
The sabotage hit a rail corridor running through the Voronezh, Novovoronezh, Liski, and Ostrogozhsk areas of Voronezh Oblast, a route ATESH says Russia uses to move military cargo toward the Lyman axis.
Relay cabinets house the switching gear that runs a line's automatic signals. Knocking them out can freeze traffic on a stretch of track without a single explosion, and ATESH says its agents disabled four of them. As with the movement's other claims, the account could not be independently verified.
Ammunition backs up
By ATESH's telling, the signaling failure delayed shipments of ammunition and engineering materiel to the 1st and 15th Guards regiments and the 254th Motor Rifle Regiment. Russian commanders, it said, had to rush in repair crews and divert resources to guard the infrastructure. A delayed shipment, far behind the front, can be felt at it, where an assaulted position waits for the ammunition that does not arrive.
ATESH hunts the supply lines
ATESH is a network of pro-Ukrainian agents operating inside Russia and Russian-occupied territory, and it has increasingly gone after the rail and power infrastructure that sustains Moscow's war. This month, the group also said it knocked out the power supply of a plant in Voronezh that makes components for Russian missiles.

articles.title: Putin restarts battle against Western companies in Russia
articles.body:
Putin restarts battle against Western companies in Russia
After a long pause, Russia’s authorities have renewed their campaign of nationalizing assets held by foreign companies — and they’ve gone big. On Thursday, Vladimir Putin issued a decree putting assets worth €6 billion under external management — specifically, the Russian divisions of retail chains Auchan and Leroy Merlin, food manufacturer Nestle and FM Logistics. Putin appointed an obscure company to manage them, with a former police general as its figurehead.
- Officially, the measure is not nationalization. Putin has imposed external management on the companies, not legally transferred their assets. This scheme was devised in 2023 and formed the basis by which Russia’s authorities seized hundreds of assets from Western owners — from energy firms to brewers and dairy companies. Foreign shareholders retain technical ownership but are stripped of all management rights (the right to repatriate profits was removed in 2022).
- Once a Russian asset is placed under external management, Western shareholders are often forced to sell to a Kremlin-backed owner, as in the case of the Russian subsidiaries of Danone and Carlsberg. To complete the deals, Putin then suspends his own decree. But this is not always the case. Dozens of subsidiaries of Western companies have remained under external management for years.
- By default, Rosimushchestvo (the Federal Agency for State Property Management) takes charge of any assets that are put under local management by a presidential decree. But that route can be overruled. Often, assets are immediately acquired by a third party with the Kremlin's blessing. That is what is happening here. The Russian operations of Auchan, Nestle and FM Logistics went to a special purpose vehicle called LEV Management, a ready-made legal entity purchased by unknown individuals just before Putin issued his decree. The CEO is an obvious figurehead: Police Major General Andrei Krayushkin, who worked as deputy head of the Interior Ministry’s migration department in the late 2010s. Nobody has yet uncovered who is behind him.
- The Kremlin often justifies asset seizure on political grounds. For example, in 2023 many linked the decision to place Denmark’s Carlsberg under external management to Copenhagen’s willingness to supply F-16 fighter jets to Ukraine. Moscow views EU countries — and those in the “coalition of the willing” in particular — as its main opponents. With the exception of Switzerland’s Nestle, most of the affected companies are French. But why France has been singled out is unclear. Right now the Kremlin is in a bigger conflict with Germany, yet Metro Group, a German rival to Auchan, works without problem in Russia.
- Beyond politics, there are economic issues at play. First, amid fresh reports of a budget shortfall in Ukraine, plans to confiscate €200 billion of Russian reserves frozen in Europe since 2022 are back under discussion. This is a highly sensitive issue in Moscow, and all Russia has to threaten in return is the confiscation of foreign assets and funds already frozen in Russia. In this context, placing French companies with assets worth at least 600 million rubles (€6 billion) under external management looks like an attempt to gain a bargaining chip in the event of a future war of asset freezes.
- The Russian government’s own dire need for funds should not be overlooked. Over the first eight months of 2026, the budget deficit has already reached 2.5% of GDP. Placing a company under external management is not the same as nationalization. Russia does not have the right to sell Auchan and FM Logistics, nor plunder funds from their accounts to finance, for example, military expenses. But if Western countries move to confiscate Russian assets, this is the most likely next step.
Why the world should care
For whatever reason, the Russian government is reopening its battle with Western companies, in the biggest cases of de facto nationalization since 2024.

articles.title: How the ‘poisonous tide’ of disinformation spreads division and despair
articles.body:
Russian disinformation campaigns are varied in their falsehoods and strategies.
The narratives range from a deepfake Tom Cruise criticising the Paris Olympics to portraying a recent Russian attack on a train near the Ukraine-Poland border as a false-flag operation.
Some efforts are blatant deepfakes, such as stamping the BBC logo on a video wrongly blaming Ukraine for a deadly missile salvo on its own citizens in Kramatorsk four years ago.
The tactics evolve too, from disseminating deceitful narratives through the Telegram messaging platform to “poisoning” AI systems by littering the internet with false stories in the hope they will be regurgitated by chatbots.
It is systematic and Andy Burnham has seen enough, announcing a new anti-disinformation agency, the National Centre for Information Defence.
“We’re talking about an insidious campaign that reaches into people’s homes and twists what they feel about their own country and community – creating a narrative of decline, stoking division and sowing despair,” he said.
Experts say picking off individual examples is the wrong approach and Burnham is right to tackle what he describes as a “poisonous tide”.
Going after isolated examples of disinformation is a “losers’ game”, says Ned Mendez, head of research at Alliance4Europe, a nonprofit that analyses these destabilising threats.
“You can spend all your time looking for a TikTok or a post on X but it’s not an effective use of your day. It’s the infrastructure that is the problem, so this is a step in the right direction, going after the networks,” he says.
Sophie Williams-Dunning, a cyber analyst at the Royal United Services Institute (Rusi) thinktank, says there is now a “sophisticated ecosystem which exists to exacerbate provokable users for one reason or another”.
Although Burnham is targeting “hostile state information attacks”, this ecosystem does not just include Russia, which likes to amplify “divisive content”, says Williams-Dunning.
It also includes far-right influencers who immediately jump on social flashpoints like the Southport and Belfast riots and individuals simply looking to make money by producing highly engaging content riffing on disruption.
The Burnham announcement is “welcome, if overdue”, says Williams-Dunning, who adds that there will be an accompanying debate about free speech and the right level of government intervention. Inevitably, malign networks will amplify those free-speech concerns, she says.
It is not just Russia deploying information attacks. China and Iran have both used deepfake newscasters to advance their goals.
One recent study, conducted mostly in February by the Social Market Foundation, a British thinktank, found that more than a quarter of posts on X that relate to news were misinformation, a third of which were anti-immigration or Islamophobic.
The UK government defines misinformation as the inadvertent spread of false information, while disinformation is the deliberate creation and spread of falsehoods to create harm or disruption. The two can intertwine to highly disruptive effect.
Labour has become increasingly concerned about Russian disinformation affecting the UK. The Starmer government in May cited information warfare from Moscow when it warned Britain was “confronting an industrial-scale attack on the UK’s and our allies’ information environment, aimed at undermining our security and democratic systems”.
Earlier this year MPs on the foreign affairs select committee called for the creation of a national counter-disinformation centre, in a similar vein to Sweden’s Psychological Defence Agency and France’s Vigilance and Protection against Foreign Digital Interference service.
Experts said Burnham’s announcement at least shows the UK government catching up, although Keir Starmer’s administration showed an awareness of social media’s contribution to unrest by launching the National Internet Intelligence Investigations unit after the Southport disturbances in 2024. Operated by the police, it monitors social media to help local forces “manage public safety threats and risks”.
The UK government has been taking action prior to Burnham’s announcement, however. In May it sanctioned employees of the Social Design Agency and ANO Dialog, Russian entities which it said the Kremlin uses for large-scale interference campaigns.
One example is the Doppelgänger network, so-called due to its technique of imitating the appearance of established media organisations including Le Monde, the Guardian, Der Spiegel and Fox News.
Other examples include the 2023 surge in reports of bedbug infestations in France, falsely blaming Ukrainian refugees. The disinformation leaked into the British press and the French government concluded the stories were being artificially amplified by Russian-linked social media accounts
One of the most longstanding misinformation campaigns has centred on the idea that London is “dangerous” and “lawless”. Analysis of Reddit accounts by King’s College London found the number of such posts rose from 874 in 2008 to 258,444 in 2024.
Robert Topinka, reader in digital media and rhetoric at Birkbeck, University of London, said Russia did not necessarily start such storylines, but enthusiastically amplified them.
He cautioned that counter-disinformation efforts should not assume “people are just being fooled by some sort of outside actor”. Rather, he said, Russia tends to find a point of tension and then create more content around it.
“What really is happening is people are feeling like Britain is run-down – that’s the real source of it,” said Topinka.
AI is adding a new dimension. Mark Zuckerberg’s Meta says AI-generated content is now a “near-standard” part of disinformation campaigns.
The UK thinktank Demos recently highlighted a chatbot “poisoning” campaign where falsehoods published online by a discredited Russian organisation, including the bodies of deceased Ukrainian soldiers being processed into meat products, were repeated by chatbot models.
The National Centre for Information Defence will have a lot of work to do.

articles.title: China Capital stories reveal how ICBC advanced China’s political goals across four continents
articles.body:
PARTNER STORIES
China Capital stories reveal how ICBC advanced China’s political goals across four continents
ICIJ’s media partners uncovered strategic deals and moves the Chinese bank made around the world to further the political priorities of the party-state.
China Capital, an investigation by the International Consortium of Investigative Journalists in collaboration with 23 media partners, provided an unprecedented look into decision-making at the Industrial and Commercial Bank of China, one of the most powerful Chinese institutions, at a time of China’s ascendance on the world stage.
The investigation is based on more than 4.8 million confidential records from two of ICBC’s U.K. units. The records provide rare insight into one of China’s most important financial arms, showing how the government’s influence and political priorities often outweigh ordinary banking protocols.
This is the first time that an international team of reporters has examined the inner workings and lending practices of ICBC– the world’s largest bank by asset size. Like many of its state-owned peers, ICBC is notoriously secretive.
“The ICIJ investigation shows how branch structures can be leveraged by foreign bank headquarters to override local compliance officers when state-backed corporate interests conflict with local regulatory obligations,” said David P. Weber, an accounting professor at West Virginia University and former Chief Investigator of the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission. He urged regulators in the U.S. and the U.K. to implement a cross-border enforcement mechanism that could “reduce oversight fragmentation.”
From New Zealand to Mexico, the 75 journalists who participated in the investigation uncovered previously unknown details about the bank’s involvement in some of their countries’ most important infrastructure projects and natural resources companies, as well as deals with firms linked to China’s military apparatus. Here are some of the revelations they uncovered.
The bank did not respond to reporters’ requests for comment.
How ICBC blended commercial interests with China’s political priorities
ICIJ’s partners across India, New Zealand and Austria found repeated instances where the bank’s political role blended with its commercial interests.
In 2017, Indian and Chinese troops reached a stand-off in the disputed Doklam region at the two countries’ borders, after the Indian government accused Beijing-backed companies of building roads in a territory claimed by China and Bhutan, in violation of a 1980 treaty. The two-month face-off didn’t just have political repercussions, The Indian Express, an ICIJ partner, reported. It also triggered actions inside ICBC’s Mumbai branch, more than 1,200 miles south of the border.
Soon after the news reached the bankers, ICBC “suspended the disbursement of 11 approved but undisbursed loans and bond investments totalling $185 million,” according to internal records. The bank also “organized” Chinese Communist Party members across every department to stay in constant touch with China’s embassy and consulate. The incident exemplifies the bank’s tight links to the party-state and how geopolitical events can influence its lending operations around the world.
Like most Chinese companies, ICBC has a Communist Party committee, an internal cell that ensures its operations advance the party’s interests, and some bankers were internally referred to as “comrades.”
In New Zealand, The Post reported that a Communist Party member who worked as a senior executive at ICBC’s Auckland outpost handled the local accounts of Hikvision, a Chinese surveillance tech company with links to the government. Numerous investigations by researchers and journalists have documented how, since at least 2017, Hikvision has provided surveillance technology to forces in Xinjiang, the Chinese region where Xi Jinping’s government has waged a repression campaign against hundreds of thousands of Uyghurs and other Muslim minorities. In 2020, the U.S. government blacklisted the firm for enabling human rights abuses.
Internal ICBC records describe how Lu Ping, the chief marketing officer of the ICBC subsidiary in New Zealand, “exhibited the outstanding qualities of a communist party member.” “Comrade Lu Ping” was nominated for a company-wide commendation in 2022 for his proactive role “fulfilling cash management needs” in New Zealand for Hikvision and Huawei, one of the bank’s most important clients.
China Capital also uncovered secret links between one of Austria’s most important aviation companies and a top Chinese producer of military aircraft. ICIJ’s partner in Vienna, profil, examined internal 2021 memos that discussed a $230 million loan to Future Advance Composite Components, which is affiliated with the state-owned Aviation Industry Corporation of China.
While FACC, as the firm is known, publicly states that it produces aircraft parts exclusively for the civilian market, its Chinese owner has an “absolute leading position” in China’s defense industry and is the “sole manufacturer of all kinds of military aircraft and airborne equipment” in the country, according to the records.
ICBC bankers also discussed the possibility that the U.S. government could sanction AVIC in the future due to its links to China’s military apparatus. Though some London officers opposed extending the loans due to risk management concerns, they left the ultimate decision to ICBC’s Beijing headquarters. The documents do not state whether the bank approved the loan. AVIC did not respond to inquiries from profil.
Strategic deals revealed across Australia, Ghana, Belgium, the UK and Sweden
As part of China Capital, reporters also examined hundreds of credit application forms and other records that partly explained why ICBC London would want to pursue a deal. The documents revealed the geopolitical nature of some loans.
In Australia, ICBC issued “loss-making or marginal loans” to some of the country’s biggest resources and infrastructure companies, including Rio Tinto, Fortescue and Glencore, as a way of starting long-term relationships that would help advance Beijing’s political goals, the Australian Financial Review found.
The documents show how in 2015, Andrew Forrest, the billionaire CEO of Fortescue, an iron ore miner, made an emergency trip to Beijing to meet with ICBC’s chairman and seek assistance after the company was forced to cancel a $2.5 billion bond issuance because of unattractive interest rates.
Fortescue was struggling financially, but ICBC’s Sydney branch implored the Beijing headquarters to approve the loan at rates close to 30% below those offered by bond investors in the U.S., AFR reported. An internal memo cited Fortescue’s “significant strategic importance for the Chinese steel industry.”
ICIJ media partners in Ghana found evidence of loans awarded for similarly strategic reasons.
Ghana Business News reported how ICBC continued to provide hundreds of millions of dollars to the Ghana Cocoa Board, a government entity that supports and controls the production of cocoa — an important commodity — even though the company lacked transparency and was on a watchlist of borrowers in financial distress.
According to internal records, China stood to benefit from financing the firm, also known as Cocobod, since Chinese trade companies were key buyers and the deal helped cement the political alliance between Beijing and Accra. ICBC’s Brussels branch also participated in the loan to Cocobod, De Tijd reported, suggesting that the overseas units often helped each other when the clients were considered strategic for the bank and the party-state.
ICBC acquired a key role in the China-Africa trade thanks to its 19.7% stake in South African banking giant Standard Bank, The Africa Report found. Chinese authorities have approved the two institutions as joint renminbi-clearing banks — an arrangement that is expected to ease transactions in the Chinese currency across 19 countries where Standard Bank operates, the report said.
The Chinese bank also financed key energy projects in Europe. In the U.K., The Times found that ICBC issued nearly $1.7 billion in loans and borrowing options to U.K. water and energy infrastructure companies, including some that were “highly leveraged, with private owners borrowing heavily against relatively guaranteed incomes to maximise dividends.”
This model could leave water companies at risk should disputes arise over the debts, The Times reported. According to one internal memo, ICBC London’s ability to participate in wind farms financing was “strategically important in order to remain relevant in the UK renewables sector”.
The revelations prompted a debate in the British parliament, with some members of the House of Lords raising concerns about Chinese ownership of water utilities and key local infrastructure.
ICBC also showed an interest in financing Sweden’s top oil producer, Preem, the Göteborgs-Posten found. Internal records show how the bank offered loans to the company, a long-term client, in order to benefit Chinese oil companies and obtain access to Preem’s technology. In an internal document examined by ICIJ’s Swedish reporting partner, a banker noted that the deal allowed ICBC to gain insight into technology used for refining waste oil from cooking and forest biomass into premium oil products — a process of particular interest to China.
Serving Russia’s allies
China Capital also exposed how ICBC used its London operations as a financing hub for companies linked to sanctioned Russian and Belarusian business owners even after Western countries imposed financial sanctions to dent Russia’s military operations in Ukraine.
ICIJ and the Belarusian Investigative Center reported how ICBC London’s clients included a U.K. subsidiary of Zoomlion Heavy Industry Science and Technology, a Chinese construction company. Zoomlion used the subsidiary to partner with Belarusian state-owned company MAZ and build an industrial park near Minsk. The partnership continued even after the European Union and its allies sanctioned MAZ over its ties to Alexander Lukashenko’s regime.
MAZ left the joint venture in 2023, after the U.S. sanctioned the Belarusian firm, but devised a plan to continue supplying heavy vehicles to Zoomlion through an unsanctioned party, according to records obtained by the Belarusian Investigative Center.
MAZ didn’t respond to reporters’ questions. Zoomlion told ICIJ that the company and its subsidiaries operate in compliance with all laws and regulations.
In the Netherlands, Nout Wellink, a former supervisory board member of ICBC who left his post shortly after Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022, questioned the bank’s compliance culture, according to Het Financieele Dagblad. The growing pro-Russian stance within the Chinese government caused him unease during his nearly four-year tenure on the bank’s supervisory board, Welling said, according to ICIJ’s Dutch media partner.
“I don’t have a clear enough picture of the extent to which international sanctions are also being internalized within the bank,” he said. Speaking to a Dutch radio show, Wellink said that the bank is, “to a certain extent, an instrument of the Communist Party.”

articles.title: Sybiha calls for stronger sanctions pressure on Russia, more air defense systems amid attacks on Ukrainian data centers
articles.body:
Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andriy Sybiha said Russia is currently focusing its efforts on strikes against Ukrainian data centers, critical civilian infrastructure, and called for stronger sanctions pressure and more air defense systems.
“Russia has targeted major Ukrainian data centers, seeking to disrupt the flow of information. Rapid warnings about missile and drone threats are crucial – they save lives,” he said in a post on X on Wednesday.
Sybiha stressed that “this is critical civilian infrastructure that provides people with access to life-saving information. It is not a military target. It is necessary for the normal functioning of everyday life.”
“As Russia fails to achieve its goals on the battlefield, it is seeking new ways to destabilize life in Ukraine and terrorize civilians. Increasing sanctions pressure and the number of air defense systems is the only way to stop this terror. These attacks must not become the new normal,” Sybiha said.
The minister said that while the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly is focused on peace efforts and diplomatic measures to end the war, Ukraine is again facing powerful Russian attacks. Two people were killed and more than 40 injured in the Russian strikes, which continued throughout the night and morning, he said. A university building in Kyiv was also hit while students were on campus.

articles.title: Ukraine Hits Russia’s Elite Rubicon Drone Unit, Strikes Warehouse and Command Posts
articles.body:
- Category
- War in Ukraine
Ukraine Hits Russia’s Elite Rubicon Drone Unit, Strikes Warehouse and Command Posts
Ukrainian forces struck a drone warehouse belonging to Russia’s Rubicon unmanned systems unit in the temporarily occupied Donetsk region, along with several UAV command posts and logistics facilities, Ukraine’s General Staff said.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine on September 23, the strikes were carried out on September 22 and overnight into September 23 against Russian military facilities across the Donetsk and Luhansk regions.
Ukrainian forces targeted Russian UAV command posts near Novoselivka Persha and Dachne in the Donetsk region. A separate strike hit a drone warehouse operated by the Rubicon unit near Volnovakha, according to the General Staff.
The operation also targeted Russian military logistics. A fuel and lubricants depot was struck near Kundriuche in the Luhansk region, while logistics warehouses were hit near Hirnyk and Velyka Shyshivka in the Donetsk region.
Near Krasnohorivka, Ukrainian forces also struck a concentration of personnel belonging to a Russian UAV unit, the General Staff said. The extent of the damage at the sites was not immediately disclosed.
Rubicon, formally known as Russia’s Center for Advanced Unmanned Technologies, was established in August 2024 under the Russian Defense Ministry to centralize the development, testing, training, and battlefield deployment of unmanned systems. The unit operates FPV and fixed-wing drones and also maintains dedicated electronic warfare and counter-drone capabilities.
According to a June 2026 analysis by the Foreign Policy Research Institute, Rubicon expanded from roughly 1,450 personnel in 2025 to around 5,000 by spring 2026. Its combat detachments have been used to target Ukrainian drone crews and logistics networks behind the front line while testing new equipment and tactics for wider use by Russian forces.
Earlier, Ukrainian forces struck a Russian attack drone storage and launch site in the Oryol region, damaging five launchers and at least three storage facilities, according to Ukraine’s General Staff. The facility was reportedly used to store, prepare, and launch attack drones against Ukraine.

articles.title: Russia attacked Ukraine with 161 drones, including "Banderols" - how the air defense performed
articles.body:
Russia attacked Ukraine with 161 drones, including "Banderols" - how the air defense performed
Kyiv • UNN
During the night of September 23, Russia launched 161 drones at Ukraine, including 82 jet-powered Shaheds. Air defense shot down or suppressed 122 targets.
Russia attacked Ukraine with 161 drones during the night of September 23; 122 of them were shot down or suppressed, including three "Banderols." UNN reports this, citing data from the Ukrainian Armed Forces Air Force.
What Russia used to strike and where from
According to the Ukrainian Armed Forces Air Force, during the night of September 23 (starting at 18:00 on September 22), the enemy attacked with 161 Shahed-type attack UAVs (82 of them jet-powered), Gerbera drones, Parodiya-type decoy drones, as well as "Banderol"/"Dan-T" drones, launched from the following areas: Oryol, Kursk, Primorsko-Akhtarsk, Millerovo—in Russia; the temporarily occupied territory of Donetsk; and Hvardiiske—the temporarily occupied territory of the Autonomous Republic of Crimea.
How many were destroyed by air defense
The air attack was repelled by aviation, anti-aircraft missile forces, electronic warfare and unmanned systems units, and mobile fire groups of Ukraine’s Defense Forces.
According to preliminary data, as of 08:00, air defense had shot down/suppressed 119 enemy Shahed-type UAVs, Gerbera drones, drones of other types, and three "Banderol"/"Dan-T" drones,
Hits by the enemy’s means of air attack were recorded at 18 locations, as well as the fall of downed targets (debris) at eight locations.
The attack is ongoing; enemy UAVs are in the airspace.

articles.title: NATO chief wants Europeans to fight American wars
articles.body:
NATO chief wants Europeans to fight American wars
European NATO nations should take greater responsibility for security in the Middle East, NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte has said. He also defended the US-Israeli war on Iran and argued that European members should spend less on social programs and more on the military.
Rutte made the remarks at a Chicago Council on Global Affairs event in Iowa on Tuesday after being asked to “make the case” for NATO to Americans by explaining “what’s in it” for them.
He described the Middle East as “Europe’s backyard” and “not the United States’ backyard,” arguing that Washington’s war against Tehran was “necessary” but that the US had to launch it because “somehow the Europeans did not have enough capabilities to do it themselves.”
“In the future, what you get from a stronger NATO is that Europeans can take care of their own backyard,” Rutte said.
The US-Israeli war on Iran, launched in late February, caused major friction within NATO as several European members resisted supporting Washington’s belligerence. Spain refused to allow American warplanes to use its bases for the campaign, drawing US President Donald Trump’s ire. Germany and the UK described the conflict as “not our war,” while stopping short of condemning the US and Israel.
Trump has since repeatedly accused European allies of failing to meet their NATO commitments and claimed the bloc “was not there when we needed them.” In April, US War Secretary Pete Hegseth said NATO’s future was uncertain and Washington could not currently reaffirm its commitment to collective defense.
Rutte also argued on Tuesday that the burden within NATO was unfair because European members spend heavily “on pensions and welfare,” while Washington has to devote more resources to weapons but “would also like to spend more on all these other lofty, beautiful items, but they can’t because they have to spend so much on defense.”
He described raising NATO’s defense spending target from 2% to 5% of GDP as “the fairness element” and part of an “equalizing” process. The remarks come as Washington pushes for a reorganization dubbed NATO 3.0, under which European members would sharply increase military spending and production while assuming “primary responsibility for the conventional defense of Europe.”
Rutte also offered to help “protect the United States from threats of Russia” and China and prevent the Arctic “from becoming militarized by the Russians and the Chinese.”
Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said last month that Moscow was primarily interested in “preserving the Arctic as an area of peace and cooperation” and accused NATO of “driving the region towards militarization.” His comments followed European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen’s proposal earlier this year to use increased EU military spending on “Arctic-ready equipment.”

articles.title: Zelenskyy: Putin is patient zero and has to be stopped
articles.body:
Zelenskyy: Putin is patient zero and has to be stopped
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has called Russian leader Vladimir Putin "patient zero" who is spreading the idea of war around the world.
Source: Zelenskyy's address to the UN General Assembly in New York, as reported by European Pravda
Details: Zelenskyy stressed that Putin "is always looking for someone who can help him kill more people for every kilometre of land, take more territory and attack another country" rather than stopping and running his own country.
"After all of this, can you even imagine him without war? He is 'patient zero' – the one from whom this idea of war keeps spreading further. And wherever it spreads, it brings only pain, instability, new risks and, of course, new crises," the president emphasised.
Zelenskyy said that the more freedom Putin has to act, the more dangerous the world becomes for everyone else.
He explained that Ukraine is targeting Russia's oil industry in an effort to stop Moscow and undermine its ability to finance the war.
"Oil itself is not Ukraine's target. It is not our target. Not gasoline or diesel, not factories or ports as such. Our target is Russia's ability to finance this war, to drag it out, to make it more brutal and more destructive. Russia's finances and Russia's production are what must be stopped if Putin is to be stopped," he stressed.
In this context, Zelenskyy pointed out that when anyone lifts or eases sanctions against Russia, they "give this war more time".
"And when someone in the world weakens sanctions, weakens sanctions against Russian oligarchs, it may make life more comfortable for rich Russians, but it also gives the war more time – more time for Putin to send poor people into the kill zone," he added.
Zelenskyy noted that Russia threatens lives in Ukraine every hour by attacking the country with drones and missiles.
"Would your country survive if, God forbid, you had to face something like this? Ukraine has," the president asked those present, urging them to join efforts to strengthen Ukraine's air defence.
Background:
- Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha stressed during a UN Security Council meeting that Russia's war against Ukraine poses a threat to the entire world.
- It was also reported that 50 countries and the European Union issued a joint statement in support of Ukraine at the UN, calling on Russia to agree to a ceasefire. The United States did not join the statement.
- The previous day, US President Donald Trump called on Putin to "settle the war" against Ukraine.

articles.title: At least 16 senior Russian officials have been killed after going to war in Ukraine, The Insider finds
articles.body:
At least 16 former and serving senior officials in Russia’s regional and municipal executive branches have been killed after going to war against Ukraine, The Insider has calculated based on data from open sources. The tally includes officials ranging from deputy heads of municipal districts or urban districts to deputy governors. Ten of the 16 had been convicted or were facing criminal cases before going to war, mostly on bribery and abuse-of-office charges.
The latest known case is that of former Belgorod mayor and Belgorod Region deputy governor Konstantin Polezhayev. The Kremlin-aligned media outlet Kommersant reported his death on Sept. 22, citing two people close to the former official. One said Polezhayev had served in an assault unit and was killed in a missile strike in the Kharkiv Region.
Polezhayev served as mayor of Belgorod from 2015 to 2019 before becoming a deputy governor. He was detained in 2023 on charges of bribery, with state investigators alleging that a construction company gave him two luxury SUVs, a Porsche Panamera, and a Range Rover worth a combined 18 million rubles ($214,000) in exchange for favorable treatment connected to government contracts. In August 2024, a court sentenced Polezhayev to five years in prison, after which he signed a contract with Russia’s Ministry of Defense.
In April 2025, the independent Belgorod-based outlet Pepel reported that Polezhayev was allegedly only formally listed with a BARS reserve unit and was in fact still living at home. It is not clear when he was actually first sent to the front.
The other casualties
Of the 16 cases of officials’ deaths identified by The Insider, three involved figures who had held positions at the deputy governor level. Sergei Efremov, who was then serving as deputy governor of Primorsky Krai, was killed in early 2025 in Russia’s Kursk Region. He had overseen domestic policy in the region while also commanding the Tiger volunteer unit. Former Khanty-Mansi Autonomous Okrug deputy governor Alexei Zolotukhin, who had been responsible for security in the regional government, volunteered for the war after leaving office and was killed in 2026. The third was Polezhayev.
The Insider found three more cases involving senior city officials. Former first deputy head of Yugorsk Dmitry Krylov signed a contract with the military and commanded an assault platoon before being killed in battles for Avdiivka in February 2024. Former Chelyabinsk Deputy Mayor Sergei Reprintsev went to war after being arrested in a 10 million-ruble ($119,000) bribery case and was killed in May 2025. Former Magnitogorsk Deputy Mayor Dmitry Gavrilov, who had been sentenced to 10 years in prison for bribery, also signed a contract with Russia’s MoD and was subsequently killed in Ukraine. His death became public only in September 2026.
Another 10 cases involved the heads and deputy heads of districts and urban districts. Igor Ustyuzhanin, the former head of Manturovo, was killed after going to war after receiving an 8.5-year prison sentence for corruption. The former head of the Ketovsky District in the Kurgan Region, Alexander Noskov, also joined the Russian army from prison, where he was serving a six-year sentence for abuse of office; he was killed in Ukraine in February 2024. The former head of the Tsimlyansky District in the Rostov Region, Vladimir Svetlichny, had been convicted of abuse and exceeding his authority; he was also killed after being deployed to the front.
Former first deputy head and acting head of the Kortkerossky District in the Komi Republic Alexander Arteyev, who had received an 11-year prison sentence for bribery, embezzlement, and abuse of office, was killed in June 2024. The former head of the Perm Region’s Gornozavodsky District, Alexander Afanasyev, who was sentenced to three years for abuse of authority, signed a contract in December 2024 and was later killed. The former head of the Tselinny District in the Kurgan region, Alexander Sytov, was declared dead in summer 2026. Before the war, he had been sentenced to seven years in prison for bribery, fraud, and embezzlement, including the theft of 100,000 rubles ($1,200) collected for mobilized soldiers.
Fyodor Ivashchuk, head of the Ulchsky District in the Khabarovsk Region, resigned in March 2025, voluntarily signed a contract with the Russian army, and joined the BARS-8 Khabarovsk unit. He was killed that August while carrying out a combat mission. Aidar Zagirov, deputy head of the Uchalinsky District in Bashkortostan, was also serving under contract and was killed during a combat mission. The former deputy head of Novorossiysk’s intracity district, Oleg Skornyakov, signed a contract with Russia’s Ministry of Defense in spring 2025, went missing several months later, and was officially confirmed dead in March 2026.
Former deputy head of the Tugulymsky Urban District in the Sverdlovsk Region Sergei Utkin, who had been sentenced to eight years in prison for taking an especially large bribe, signed a contract with the Russian army while incarcerated and was also killed at the front.
Ten of the 16 were involved in criminal cases
Ten of the 16 officials The Insider identified had faced criminal prosecution before going to war. Nine — Polezhayev, Gavrilov, Ustyuzhanin, Noskov, Svetlichny, Arteyev, Afanasyev, Sytov and Utkin — had been convicted. Reprintsev was under investigation on charges of bribery when he signed his contract.
The Insider reported in 2024 that the war had allowed some former officials to leave prison or put criminal cases on hold, former Vladivostok Mayor Oleg Gumenyuk and former Khakassia Deputy Governor Sergei Novikov prominent among them. Some later returned to Russia after serving their allotted time in the military.
The tally does not, however, include former Krasnodar Region Deputy Governor Sergei Vlasov. Reports of his death surfaced in spring 2026, but Kommersant found that Vlasov was officially listed as missing and that his body had not been found.
The Insider also excluded judges, security officials, election commission members, heads of individual administrative departments, members of parliaments at all levels, and officials killed by shelling or mines while performing their civilian duties. The count includes only serving or former executive officials at the level of deputy district head or higher who entered military service or joined volunteer formations.
A broader count now includes at least 51 dead
If the count is expanded beyond senior executive officials, the number is significantly higher. In February 2025, Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty counted at least 32 Russian government officials who had been killed in Ukraine. That category included election commission officials, members of parliament at various levels, and a federal judge in addition to government officials.
In June 2026, the independent outlet Meduza found open-source reports of at least 16 additional deaths that were published after RFE/RL had completed its project, bringing the minimum estimate to 48. Since the Meduza study was published, at least three more deaths have become publicly known: those of Alexander Sytov in July, Dmitry Gavrilov in September, and Konstantin Polezhayev on Sept. 22. Using the broader definition of “government representatives,” the minimum toll now stands at at least 51, according to The Insider’s calculations.

articles.title: Poland Deploys Military Aviation as Russia Strikes Ukraine, Rzeszów and Lublin Airports Suspend Flights
articles.body:
- Category
- World
Poland Deploys Military Aviation as Russia Strikes Ukraine, Rzeszów and Lublin Airports Suspend Flights
Poland deployed military aircraft, air defense systems, and electronic reconnaissance assets on September 23 in response to renewed Russian strikes on Ukraine, while airports in Rzeszów and Lublin temporarily suspended operations.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Poland’s Armed Forces Operational Command said military aviation had begun operating in Polish airspace as Russia carried out attacks against Ukraine using airborne weapons.
“In connection with the strikes by the Russian Federation on the territory of Ukraine, carried out using airborne assault means, military aviation operations have commenced in Polish airspace,” the command said.
Polish authorities also activated the necessary air defense and equipment to protect the country’s airspace during the Russian attack.
The heightened military activity also affected civilian aviation. The Polish Air Navigation Services Agency reported that airports in Rzeszów and Lublin temporarily suspended operations to ensure military aircraft had sufficient freedom to operate.
Later, both airports resumed normal operations after the Polish military operation concluded.
The September 23 deployment follows a similar response less than a week earlier. On September 17, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said Russian drone strikes had taken place in Ukraine’s Volyn region near the Polish border.
Poland scrambled military aircraft in response, while operations at the same airports in Lublin and Rzeszów were temporarily suspended.
The latest Polish response came as Russia launched another drone attack on Ukraine, including Kyiv. The September 23 strike on the Ukrainian capital killed at least one person and injured seven others, with strikes and falling debris reported across several districts, according to Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko.
Klitschko said one of the victims, who had been hospitalized in serious condition, later died from their injuries. Four other people remained hospitalized following the attack.
