articles.title: Ukraine’s Zelenskyy calls for sustained pressure to end ‘Putin’s crazy war’
articles.body:
Ukraine’s Zelenskyy calls for sustained pressure to end ‘Putin’s crazy war’
Ukrainian president urges world leaders to keep choking Russia’s revenues to impede its war efforts.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has singled out Russian President Vladimir Putin as the reason for the continuing war between the two neighbouring countries, urging world leaders to sustain economic pressure on Moscow during his address at the United Nations General Assembly.
“For nearly five years now, Russia’s generals have tried to carry out Putin’s crazy war,” Zelenskyy said, adding that no one openly supported this war “except for one man”.
Zelenskyy said Russia had lost 248,000 soldiers over the last eight months in Ukraine, managing to capture “a little more than 1,000 square kilometres [386 square miles] of our territory this year”.
“Putin spent 248 people for every kilometre. Does anyone still think he is smart?” he said, adding that the numbers “are not just statistics. This is about people”.
“We have archived footage of thousands and thousands of Russians losing their lives in kill zones. This is what Putin wants,” he said.
“Something always seems to stop Putin from saying, ‘That’s it. Enough. Peace,'” Zelenskyy said. “Can you even imagine him without war? He is ‘patient zero’, the one from whom war keeps spreading further. ‘Patient zero’ must be stopped,” he said.
Zelenskyy said he expects Russia to intensify its bombing campaign on the country in the coming months and that Ukrainians are prepared for a harsh winter.
“Ukrainians understand that this winter could be very harsh for us, but in response we will have no choice but to make it harsh for Russia too,” he said.
This month, Ukraine launched its deepest-ever attack into Russia, targeting two Arctic gas condensate facilities more than 3,000km (1,865 miles) from its border. Another attack on Sunday forced a Moscow oil refinery to halt crude processing.
Russia also slammed jet-powered drones into two petrol stations and other sites in Kyiv, killing one and injuring at least seven people on Wednesday.
Meanwhile, US President Donald Trump has been pushing for an “energy ceasefire” between Russia and Ukraine, blaming the war between the two as one reason behind skyrocketing fuel prices.
Zelenskyy called for sustained economic pressure, saying the money Russia earned through trade “gives this war more time”.
“And that is exactly why we insist on limiting trade with the aggressor, and why we are burning Russia’s revenues ourselves,” he said.
Last week, Trump signed into law a sweeping sanctions package targeting Russia over its war in Ukraine, days after US Congress sent the bill to the White House with rare bipartisan support.
On Wednesday, Zelenskyy also claimed that nationals of 47 countries are fighting alongside Russia in Ukraine, mentioning the two North Korean soldiers captured by Ukrainian forces in Russia’s Kursk region last year, who were sent to South Korea by Kyiv.
“Why should Koreans give their lives in a war in Ukraine?” he asked.
Russia’s Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov told the UN Security Council on Wednesday that Moscow is prepared to negotiate towards a lasting peace with Ukraine, but won’t just “pause” the war, arguing that such a pause would buy Ukraine and its backers time to line up more weapons.
Meanwhile, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio says both Russia and Ukraine have expressed interest in a limited ceasefire that would halt attacks on grain shipments and each country’s energy sectors.

articles.title: Azov Foils Russian Attempt to Encircle Druzhkivka
articles.body:
Within the First Corps Azov of the National Guard of Ukraine’s area of responsibility, defense forces conducted an almost two-month operation to clear Russian troops that had been building up throughout the summer for an offensive toward Druzhkivka and Dobropillia.
The First Corps Azov of the National Guard of Ukraine reported this.
Service members from units directly involved in the operation provided details.
According to the commander of the 12th Special Forces Brigade Azov, callsign Khorus, units of Russia’s 90th Tank Division and 8th Combined Arms Army attempted to reach Ukrainian military logistics routes. This was intended to create conditions for the operational encirclement of Druzhkivka, pose a subsequent threat to the Sloviansk-Kramatorsk agglomeration, and advance toward Dobropillia.
To counter the Russian forces, the Ukrainian command reinforced the units already deployed in this sector of the front. The operation involved the Special Forces Reconnaissance Detachment «Ultima Ratio», the 1st and 6th Battalions of the 12th Special Forces Brigade Azov, the Separate Special Forces Detachment Tuman of First Corps Azov of the National Guard of Ukraine, and the Shkval Battalion of the 425th Separate Assault Regiment Skelya. The National Guard of Ukraine’s Separate Special Forces Detachment Lasar’s Group provided support.
All participating units jointly planned the operation. The initial task was to isolate the area where Russian forces had concentrated and to block the enemy. Ukrainian forces were then to create the conditions for their own assault operations.
According to the commander of the 425th Separate Assault Regiment Skelya, Dmytro, callsign Vodolii, the first Ukrainian assault groups began advancing on August 7. Serhii, commander of the Shkval Battalion, callsign Zamok, explained that the infantry advance followed strikes on Russian positions.
Artillery and strike drones played a significant role. In particular, the Lasar’s Group Detachment supported the Ukrainian assault troops. A service member from the unit’s reconnaissance section, callsign Twister, also spoke about the assistance provided by the results of Operation Ashan.
Militarnyi previously reported that, as part of Operation Ashan, the Ukrainian Defense Forces struck more than 1,000 Russian armored vehicles and artillery systems. The operation had two stages and aimed to reduce the combat capabilities of Russian forces.
The commander of the First Special Forces Group of the Tuman Detachment, callsign Franyk, highlighted the effectiveness of coordination between assault units, artillery, and strike drones. According to him, over nearly two months of operations, his group killed 10 Russian servicemen in small-arms engagements and captured one prisoner. Drones killed another 10 invaders. He also reported numerous wounded Russian servicemen and the destruction of four artillery systems.
Dense vegetation, unconventional movement tactics used by Russian units, and heavy enemy drone activity complicated the operation. The latter, in particular, significantly complicated the evacuation of wounded Ukrainian servicemen.
Despite the challenging conditions, those involved in the operation highlighted the high level of coordination between the units. The commander of the 12th Special Forces Brigade Azov specifically praised the discipline of the Shkval Battalion personnel, who operated alongside National Guard units.
According to the Ukrainian side’s reported results of the operation, Russian forces suffered 237 personnel killed and 44 wounded. Another three Russian invaders were captured.
As a result, Ukrainian units thwarted the Russian attempt to reach the logistics routes needed to advance toward Druzhkivka and Dobropillia. According to the operation’s participants, losing this area is forcing the Russian command to seek alternative avenues of advance, which will require additional time and resources.

articles.title: Canada and UK could merge war chests to fight Russia – media
articles.body:
Canada and UK could merge war chests to fight Russia – media
Canada and the UK are considering merging two major military financing initiatives to help European NATO members and other Kiev backers finance their military buildup against Russia, the CBC reported on Wednesday, citing anonymous officials.
In recent years, European NATO nations have increasingly accused Moscow of preparing an attack on members of the US-led military bloc, using the alleged threat to justify bloated military budgets. Moscow has denied any such intention.
Canada is leading plans for the Defense, Security and Resilience Bank (DSRB), while the UK is pushing for the Multilateral Defense Mechanism (MDM). Both initiatives are intended to make it easier for allied states to finance military purchases and expand arms production.
In July, Carney failed to entice then-UK Prime Minister Keir Starmer to join the DSRB as a founding member. However, Burnham’s government is more aligned with Canada on the issue, the CBC reported, citing an anonymous Canadian official.
Ottawa is confident the two countries will reach a deal to combine their initiatives into a joint institution, the Canadian Press reported last week, citing a senior Canadian official.
So far, Ottawa’s DSRB has attracted support from Albania, Belgium, Greece, Latvia, Luxembourg, Romania, Türkiye, and Ukraine. The Netherlands, Finland, and Poland have backed the UK’s MDM.
The plans come as NATO countries escalate their military spending. Last year, following pressure from US President Donald Trump, bloc members agreed to invest 5% of their GDP annually in their militaries and defense-related areas by 2035.
In the meantime, European NATO members have increasingly touted the Russian threat to militarize and prepare the continent for a potential war with Moscow, all while insulating the US from the consequences of such a conflict.
“European elites… now seek to frighten their populations with a mythical Russian threat,” Russian President Vladimir Putin told journalists at a BRICS summit earlier in September, stressing that Moscow has “no grounds for any conflict with Europe.”

articles.title: Yemen's Houthis to target US interests if supports Saudi strikes
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Yemen's Houthis to target US interests if it supports Saudi-led strikes
A Houthi military adviser said that the group would attack US interests in the region if Washington intervenes in Yemen's war in support of Saudi Arabia or tries to unblock the Bab al-Mandeb strait.
The Iran-backed Houthis seized control of the narrow shipping lane, gateway to the Red Sea, this month, while Saudi Arabia has reportedly requested American and international military assistance against them.
"If America dares to intervene militarily with its fleets or tries to take control of Bab al-Mandeb, it is a red line for them and anyone else... we will fight over it," military adviser Abed Mohammed al-Thawr told AFP in an exclusive interview on Tuesday.
The Houthi blockade has shaken Saudi Arabia, the world's top oil exporter, which was already hit by Tehran's strangehold on the strategic Strait of Hormuz as part of its war with the United States.
The pro-Iran Houthis dislodged Saudi-backed government forces from Yemen's Red Sea coast in fighting that left hundreds dead. Houthi drones and missiles have also targeted Saudi sites, including the capital Riyadh for the first time in years.
Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman requested help from US President Donald Trump in fighting the Houthis, according to US reports. Yemen's government also made the request, a well-placed source told AFP.
The Houthis say Saudi Arabia has conducted hundreds of strikes in Yemen since fighting resumed in July, effectively ending a four-year truce.
'Iron fist'
"If America gambles on supporting Saudi Arabia with airstrikes or air support... We will consider any American interests around us to be targets and we will not exclude anything," Thawr told AFP, adding that they will "close Bab al-Mandeb completely to American ships".
While the Yemen war predates the US-Iran war by years, renewed fighting in Yemen pits allies of Washington and Tehran against each other while the two foes are stalemated in the Gulf.
Thawr denied receiving directives from Iran, but said they are "one alliance and one body".
"Iran is a friendly, allied, and brotherly country to us, but it does not direct us. We are independent in our decisions and in our sovereignty," he said.
The United Nations on Tuesday said the number of people displaced could swell from over 130,000 today to more than 230,000 in the coming months.
"As long as Saudi Arabia insists on and continues killing our country and striking our people, we will strike with an iron fist," Thawr said. "We possess sufficient capability to discipline Saudi Arabia, punish it, and force it out of the game in the fields of oil and the economy."

articles.title: Iran denies dropping preconditions amid ‘very productive’ three-hour UN talks in New York
articles.body:
Iran has pushed back on claims that it dropped former preconditions for reopening the strait of Hormuz in surprise talks held in New York under the mediation of Qatar between Tehran’s foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, and Donald Trump’s envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner.
Trump said the three-hour talks held in a room at the UN headquarters had gone very well and been very productive. He suggested further talks were possible imminently, which led to the price of a barrel of Brent crude to fall to below $100 (£75) for the first time in two weeks. Witkoff said the talks had been “encouraging, constructive and successful”.
In his speech to the UN general assembly, Trump said he had a decision to make very soon on whether to “annihilate the Islamic Republic” or help turn it into one of the great countries of the Middle East, the kind of bombastic threat Trump often deploys during talks with Iran.
In Tehran, the foreign ministry spokesperson, Esmail Baghaei, confirmed the talks had occurred, but appeared not to confirm any shift in the Iranian negotiating position. He said: “The interaction that took place with the American side was through Qatari mediation. This interaction was aimed at conveying Iran’s conditions, including the end of the war in all its dimensions, the cessation of American aggressive actions, the naval siege, and the economic war, the release of Iranian assets and so on.” Aware of the potential domestic backlash, he added that Iran’s conditions had been conveyed.
Iran set seven preconditions before returning to talks, and in a new development over the past 48 hours said the crucial strait of Hormuz could be reopened within seven days if those conditions were met.
It is likely that the US and the Gulf states would have to accept a navigational route for shipping in the strait of Hormuz – a key waterway for transporting oil – that requires commercial shipping to enter through a sea lane mainly in Iranian waters and under Iranian rather than Omani control.
The fact that the talks lasted three hours suggests some progress was made. The US side is under pressure to leverage down oil prices and increase the availability of refined oil before the midterm elections in November. Latest published figures suggest the number of identifiable tankers making it through the strait is fewer than five a day, but estimates of the US navy are much higher.
The blockage in the strait is made worse by the uncertainty surrounding the control by the Houthis’ (the Iranian-backed Yemeni paramilitaries) of a second energy transport chokepoint, the Bab al-Mandab strait that leads from the Red Sea into the Indian Ocean.
There is little sign that Trump wants to relaunch a full-scale war with Iran or indeed with the Houthis as Republicans battle to turn the domestic political agenda away from a hugely unpopular war that the Americans think they are losing.
Iran is under ever more intense pressure from sanctions, and a US naval blockade is making it nearly impossible for Iran to export oil, depriving the country of badly needed foreign currency. Iran’s civilian aircraft on Wednesday faced a potential worldwide grounding owing to the threat of US secondary sanctions on any entity that engaged with Iran’s civilian fleet.
Iranian officials negotiated frantically with neighbouring countries to try to maintain an air bridge, but it appears Oman and Iraq have been forced to close their airspace to Iranian civilian planes.
The president of Iran, Masoud Pezeshkian, is due to address the UN general assembly on Wednesday after arriving in New York on a flight from Tehran as talks were under way.
Pezeshkian is an advocate of negotiations with the US but has not played a direct role in the talks. He has said the memorandum of understanding (MoU), agreed with the US on 17 June, remained the starting point.
Implementation of the MoU fell apart after the two sides accused one another of breaching its terms by trying to take control of the strait. Iran said the MoU clearly left Iran in control of the strait for an interim period before a long-term agreement on its management was reached, including the possibility of Oman and Iran charging fees for navigational services.
Pezeshkian is expected to condemn western double standards over what he regards as an illegal US assault on Iran that has left schoolchildren dead and infrastructure ravaged. Europe’s preparedness to call out Russia for its invasion of Ukraine, and its reticence in criticising the attack on Iran, or Israel’s treatment of Palestinians in Gaza, has been a constant theme of Pezeshkian’s remarks.
Many of the most powerful speeches on Tuesday at the UN general assembly came from European and Arab politicians who decried the inability of the west to enforce peace. In his farewell speech to the UN, the French president, Emmanuel Macron, criticised the attempt to overthrow the Iranian government by the US and Israel, arguing: “Every time a few states, sometimes even in the name of international order, have tried to replace the people in order to change a regime or a system, they have plunged those states into even greater chaos.”
He also said that the west had not imposed a peace in Gaza. “Some boast of a supposed peace. But this peace hasn’t reopened humanitarian routes for a single second. Must we stand by and watch this spectacle that shames us all? Never!”
Macron landed himself in hot water with Israel when he suggested Hamas was not present in the West Bank, as opposed to Gaza.
Netanyahu’s office responded, using the biblical name for the West Bank: “Hamas terrorists carry out attacks against Jews almost every day. They have murdered countless Israeli civilians in Judea and Samaria.”
Jordan’s King Abdullah II attacked the Israeli government for “moving the goalposts”, for continuing attacks and the destruction of civilian infrastructure in Gaza, and for refusing to withdraw from the war-torn Palestinian territory. This has forced the Palestinian population in Gaza into barely one-third of the territory, he said.
Observers must no longer treat Israeli policies as “temporary military measures” or a “consequence of war”, he said.
“Accountability begins when we call things what they are: an attempt to erase Palestinian life and impose a new territorial reality in Gaza,” he added.

articles.title: UK arms broker jailed for 16 years over Libya and Sudan deals
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
UK arms broker jailed for 16 years over missiles and fighter jet deals with Libya and Sudan
A British arms broker who arranged illegal deals to supply ex-Soviet surface-to-air missile systems to South Sudan and fighter jets to Libya during its civil war was on Wednesday jailed in a London court for 16 years.
David Greenhalgh, 68, was convicted in June of 10 counts of involvement in the unlicensed supply of arms, also including AK-47 rifles, battle tanks and hundreds of thousands of rounds of ammunition, between 2009 and 2016.
Greek national Christos Farmakis, 48, was convicted of nine offences, though he was tried in his absence and his current whereabouts is unknown.
Judge Sally-Ann Hales sentenced both men to 16 years' imprisonment, saying they repeatedly sought to breach arms export bans to sell weaponry for significant profits.
Prosecutors said only one charge involved the actual supply of weaponry, with the pair selling a former Ukrainian S-125 Pechora missile system to South Sudan, where Greenhalgh and Farmakis had "very close connections to senior figures."
South Sudan was still formally part of Sudan until it achieved independence in 2011, prosecutor Edmund Burge told jurors at Southwark Crown Court, meaning the semi-autonomous region was subject to a British arms embargo.
Greenhalgh and Farmakis also arranged to supply weapons to Iran, Iraq and Syria in breach of arms embargoes, before Farmakis was arrested in 2016.
Farmakis was caught after using his email address for his job at the government-funded Greater London Enterprise to privately arrange arms deals.
Burge said Farmakis' email account forwarded an email to his boss, which led to the authorities discovering documents relating to plans to sell fighter jets and other arms to Libya in the wake of the 2011 Arab Spring.

articles.title: Latvian trade mission begins in the United States, with meetings planned with global technology leaders
articles.body:
A Latvian business trade mission organised by the Investment and Development Agency of Latvia (LIAA) has begun in the United States. Running alongside Latvian President Edgars Rinkēvičs’s working visit until 27 September, the mission covers New York, Los Angeles and San Diego. Its four sector programmes bring together representatives of start-ups, the film industry, defence and dual-use technology companies, and biomedical and pharmaceutical businesses.
“The United States is Latvia’s strategic partner and trusted ally, and this September marks 35 years since the restoration of diplomatic relations. Successful cooperation with US partners, including those in California, demonstrates the international competitiveness of Latvian companies. The delegation includes representatives of the defence and dual-use sectors, biomedicine, start-ups and the film industry. I hope this visit will help Latvian businesses establish valuable contacts in the United States and, in turn, support Latvia’s economic growth,” said President Edgars Rinkēvičs.
The first business meetings are taking place in New York and Los Angeles on Wednesday, 23 September. Over the following days, Latvian entrepreneurs will meet major US companies, investors, universities and technology transfer centres to pursue export deals, joint technology projects and investment partnerships.
“Trade between Latvia and the United States reached €1.63 billion in 2025, up 13% year on year. This is more than a strong statistical result: it is a foundation for much greater ambition. We need Latvian companies to enter US supply chains, become partners in joint product development, and attract US capital to new projects in Latvia. The United States is a strategically important economic and security partner for Latvia, and the President’s visit lends additional weight to these economic discussions. The goal is clear: new projects, orders and investment,” said Raivis Bremšmits, State Secretary at Latvia’s Ministry of Economics.
Three cities and four sector programmes
In New York, representatives of Latvia’s start-up ecosystem will meet US investors and representatives of ServiceNow, a global developer of enterprise AI and digital workflow platforms. Latvian start-ups will present their solutions at the “Pitch to a President” event, receiving feedback from US investors on their prospects in the market.
In Los Angeles, the film industry programme will begin with a meeting at Paramount. Separate programmes for Latvian defence and dual-use technology, biomedical and pharmaceutical companies are also scheduled in the city over the following days.
“Three cities, four sector programmes and dozens of carefully prepared meetings within just a few days make this one of LIAA’s largest and most complex trade missions. Its pace and scale match the ambitions of Latvian companies in the United States. Last year, Latvia’s services exports to the US rose by 10% to €510 million, with information and communications technology services accounting for more than 40% of the total. Latvian companies have the expertise and technology to sit at the same table as global leaders as equal partners. We will judge the mission’s results by the deals, joint technology projects and investments that follow these discussions,” said LIAA Director Ieva Jāgere.
Latvian delegation includes 44 companies and organisations
The trade mission includes 44 Latvian companies and organisations.
The defence and dual-use technology programme includes Aumeux, SAF North America, Origin Robotics, Raw-tech, SIA Ardlat, Perkons Energy, LMT, LMT Defence, VIC TEC and LAT Security, as well as the Latgale Special Economic Zone, the Latvian Exporters’ Association “The Red Jackets”, the Federation of Security and Defence Industries of Latvia, the Latvian Chamber of Commerce and Industry, the University of Latvia and Riga Technical University.
The biomedical and pharmaceutical programme includes the National Research and Innovation Institute (NIRI), Double Helix Technologies, Rīga Stradiņš University, Riga East University Hospital, Daugavpils University and the University of Latvia.
The film industry programme includes Nafta Films, RED DOT MEDIA, Mistrus Media, Trickster Pictures, Baltic Pine Films, CINEVILLA FILMS, Ierakstu Māja and the Latvian Film Service Producers Association.
BDO Latvia and representatives of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs are also part of the trade mission delegation. The start-up programme includes BirdyChat, Monetizr, Engycell, Submerge, Spotwise, Supliful, Tournated, Capture Study, HoneyB AI, Cellbox and Crowdable.
Los Angeles: From film studios to autonomous defence systems
On 24 September, film industry participants are scheduled to visit the Warner Bros. and HBO studios and meet representatives of Disney and Netflix. Discussions will focus on Latvia’s capabilities in film production, post-production and animation, as well as opportunities for international co-productions.
Defence and dual-use technology companies will take part in a roundtable with representatives of Southern California’s defence industry and visit Anduril, a US defence technology company developing autonomous systems and AI-based solutions. Discussions will focus on using Latvian technology in joint solutions, developing new products and bringing Latvian companies into US supply chains.
Biomedical and pharmaceutical representatives will meet economic development and life sciences organisations in Los Angeles County. They will also visit the Technology Development Group at the University of California, Los Angeles, and the Office of Technology Transfer and Corporate Partnerships at the California Institute of Technology. Discussions with researchers and technology transfer specialists will cover the commercialisation of research, joint product development and cooperation between Latvian companies and US universities.
The day will conclude with a business event hosted by the US Ambassador to Latvia at the Richard Nixon Presidential Library, bringing together the Latvian delegation and representatives of the US business community.
San Diego: Semiconductors, unmanned systems and genomics
On 25 September, the defence and dual-use technology programme will continue in San Diego, a major US centre for defence, aviation and unmanned systems technology.
Latvian companies are scheduled to meet Shield AI, a developer of autonomous aircraft and AI pilot technology, and Kratos, a national security technology company active in unmanned systems, space, hypersonics and missile propulsion. Meetings are also planned with Qualcomm, a global communications, connectivity and semiconductor company; public safety technology company Axon; and Starling Systems.
Representatives of SAF Tehnika and Riga Technical University will meet senior executives at Analog Devices. The global semiconductor company has more than 100,000 customers and reported revenue of $11 billion in its 2025 fiscal year.
“SAF Tehnika regularly takes part in LIAA trade missions to the United States because they allow us to meet senior executives at partner and customer companies and strengthen our reputation with them. For example, during this September’s mission to California, we and Riga Technical University will meet the senior management of a major US semiconductor manufacturer. Opportunities like those offered by LIAA produce results only when a company has done its homework and can say precisely whom it wants to meet and what it hopes to achieve. If you don’t know where you’re going, any road will do,” said Jānis Bergs, Member of the Board and Vice President of Sales and Marketing at SAF Tehnika.
In San Diego, biomedical and pharmaceutical companies will meet Thermo Fisher Scientific, one of the world’s largest suppliers of laboratory, life sciences and pharmaceutical technologies, with annual revenue exceeding $45 billion. Meetings are also planned with Illumina, a leading developer of genomics and DNA sequencing technologies, and DNA sequencing technology company Element Biosciences.
The Latvian delegation will also visit the Technology Transfer Office at San Diego State University and the Office of Innovation and Commercialization at the University of California, San Diego, to discuss research cooperation, technology transfer and bringing new biomedical products to market.
LIAA organises participation in overseas trade missions under the EU co-financed Innovative Entrepreneurship Development Programme for Small and Medium-Sized Enterprises (SMEs), supported by the European Regional Development Fund and national funding. Companies may participate either on a paid basis or with support to cover eligible costs.

articles.title: ADF down 119 drones, three Banderols in overnight Russian attack on Ukraine
articles.body:
ADF down 119 drones, three Banderols in overnight Russian attack on Ukraine
As reported by Ukrinform, the Air Force of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported this on Telegram.
Starting at 18:00 on Tuesday, September 22, the enemy attacked Ukraine with 161 Shahed-type UAVs (82 of them jet-powered), Gerbera drones, Parodiya-type decoy drones, as well as Banderol/Dan-T drones launched from the directions of Oryol, Kursk, Primorsko-Akhtarsk and Millerovo in Russia, as well as temporarily occupied Donetsk and Hvardiiske in temporarily occupied Crimea.
The air attack was repelled by aircraft, anti-aircraft missile forces, electronic warfare units and unmanned systems units, as well as mobile fire teams of the Defense Forces of Ukraine.
According to preliminary data, as of 8:00 on Wednesday, September 23, air defense forces had shot down or suppressed 119 drones and three Banderol/Dan-T drones.
Hits were recorded at 18 locations, while downed targets (debris) fell at eight locations.
The attack is ongoing, with enemy UAVs still present in Ukrainian airspace.
As reported by Ukrinform, in the morning of September 23, a Russian drone struck a gas station in Kyiv’s Holosiivskyi district.

articles.title: Pezeshkian to UN: Iran will never 'bend the knee' to 'US terror'
articles.body:
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian struck a defiant tone at the UN, vowing Iran would never “bend at the knee” to US pressure and accusing Washington of “terrorism” over the killing of former supreme leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei
US President Donald Trump said during a press conference at the United Nations General Assembly that US officials had a "very good" three-hour meeting with Iranian officials. For its part, Iranian state media confirmed that Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi and US special envoy Steve Witkoff met in New York
The war in Yemen between the Iranian-backed Houthis and the Saudi-backed government forces continues with no end in sight
Israel continues to attack Gaza, occupied West Bank, southern Lebanon and south Syria despite any ceasefire agreements
And so we begin our live coverage of the day...
Israeli settlers set fire to Palestinian land near Ramallah
Israeli settlers have set fire to Palestinian land on the outskirts of Burqa, east of Ramallah in the occupied West Bank, according to the Palestinian Wafa news agency.
Burqa has faced repeated attacks by Israeli settlers in recent years amid the expansion of illegal settlements in the area. Incidents have included the burning of crops and farmland, the uprooting of trees and attacks on Palestinian residents and their property.
Israeli air strikes hit two areas in southern Lebanon
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen has pledged continued EU support for Syria after meeting President Ahmed al-Sharaa on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly.
“The EU remains a reliable partner for a peaceful, stable and inclusive transition in Syria, free from harmful foreign interference,” said von der Leyen.
She said the bloc was working to support Syria's reconstruction and the safe and voluntary return of refugees.
“As next steps, we aim to mobilise more investment and upgrade our partnership,” she added.
Earlier, al-Sharaa told the General Assembly that Syria has “moved from crisis to opportunity”, citing progress in rebuilding state institutions, pursuing transitional justice and developing international partnerships.
Israel's Defence Minister Israel Katz said on Wednesday that the Golan Heights would remain under Israeli sovereignty "forever", after Syria's president insisted at the United Nations that it was Syrian land.
"My clear response to the Syrian president, who made bombastic declarations from the UN podium: The Golan under Israeli sovereignty is an inseparable part of the State of Israel forever," Katz said in a video statement.
Israel captured the Golan Heights from Syria in the Six Day War of 1967 and annexed the territory in 1981. The United States had been the only country to recognise the annexation until Colombia recognised Israel's claim last month.
Palestinian villagers wailed over the mangled remains of their olive trees on Wednesday after Israel's military uprooted them with bulldozers, days ahead of the annual olive harvest, normally a source of joy for Palestinians in the occupied West Bank.
Abd Alfattah Tamimi, who owns an olive grove on village land near Ramallah city, watched as a military bulldozer smashed the top of one of his trees and then tore its roots from the ground.
"All our olive trees, including the newly planted ones, were uprooted. Also our neighbours', they uprooted them all," Tamimi said, adding that he and his neighbours own nearly 9 acres of land filled with olive trees.
"They left us with nothing," he said.
Libya's al-Menfi warns Sudan war threatens wider region
Libyan Presidential Council head Mohamed al-Menfi also addressed the ongoing conflict in Sudan, describing the country as Libya's “brotherly neighbour” and saying its people had become the “victims of a devastating war for which they are paying a hefty price”.
“In that war, interests and interventions collide, and its effects extend beyond the borders of Sudan, endangering the security and stability of the region and the unity of its states,” he said.
President tells Trump that Iran will never 'bend the knee'
Iran's president struck a defiant tone at the UN on Wednesday where he spoke for the first time since Washington and Israel launched an all-out war on his country, vowing Tehran would never "bend at the knee."
Masoud Pezeshkian accused Washington of "terrorism" for assassinating former supreme leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei at the start of the conflict, insisting Tehran had never started a war.
On Tuesday, President Donald Trump had told the UN General Assembly that he was weighing whether to "annihilate" Iran but went on to hail renewed talks between Tehran and Washington's negotiators.
Pezeshkian made no reference to the talks to resolve the stalled war in his steely speech.
"(Trump) must know that the resistance of the Iranian people will only increase in the face of sanctions, increased pressure, increased bullying. We will never bow our head or bend at the knee," he said.
Pezeshkian insisted Tehran would not allow the Strait of Hormuz, which it has choked off since the start of the war causing global energy prices to spike, to be used as leverage against his country.
"We cannot let some have free access and bolster their interests from the waterway, while at the same time using that waterway to impose their aggression upon us," he said.
Israel envoy: Golan Heights will 'always' be part of Israel
Israel's UN Ambassador Danny Danon has reiterated Israel's claim to the occupied Golan Heights following Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa's address to the UN General Assembly.
“But no speech will change reality, al-Jolani: the Golan Heights will always be part of Israel,” Danon wrote on X, referring to al-Sharaa by the nom de guerre he used as a militia leader.
During his address, al-Sharaa repeatedly cited UN Security Council Resolution 497, adopted in 1981, which declared Israel's annexation of the Golan Heights “null and void and without international legal effect”.
Israel captured the Golan Heights from Syria during the 1967 war and formally annexed the territory in 1981, a move that is not internationally recognised. The first Trump administration recognised Israeli sovereignty over the occupied territory in 2019.

articles.title: Is NAZA Zionism's worst nightmare or normalisation propaganda?
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Is NAZA Zionism's worst nightmare or normalisation propaganda?
The documentary film NAZA (an acronym for Nezek Agavi; “collateral damage” in Hebrew), written and directed by Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, has created a firestorm of controversy. Though few have actually seen the film, it reportedly contains interviews with 24 anonymous Israeli military and intelligence members who attest to the integration of artificial intelligence (AI) and automated surveillance into military targeting systems used by Israeli forces during the ongoing Gaza genocide.
They also allege government approval of operations in which thousands of Palestinian civilians were killed as “collateral damage.”
Since its premiere at Venice, where Abraham and Szor received a record 25-minute standing ovation, the filmmakers have faced an escalating campaign of official condemnation and deadly threats. Israeli Culture Minister Miki Zohar called for their citizenship to be revoked, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu announced plans for legislation targeting those who “defame” Israeli soldiers, and Israel Defence Force (IDF) Chief of Staff Eyal Zamir said the military would use “every tool at our disposal” against the film.
Far-right activists have gone further, with calls for the filmmakers to be hunted and hanged, with more threats directed at their families.
On the surface, however, it is not clear why the film and its creators have become such a target of hatred and condemnation within Israel and the broader Zionist movement. Documentation of Israel’s genocidal criminality has been readily accessible for years, mostly from Palestinian journalists on the ground in Gaza, and the use of AI in targeting civilians has been detailed by Abraham himself in April 2024.
Furthermore, Israeli soldiers have documented themselves shamelessly committing an array of war crimes. So why the thuggish wrath by Israeli leaders, then dutifully echoed by their fascist supporters? This response is akin to Pavlov blowing his whistle at his trained dogs: the whistle sounds, and the conditioned response follows.
What distinguishes NAZA is that it brings allegations of Israeli genocide from the Palestinian “out-group” and its allies into the Israeli “in-group,” opening a potential space for Israeli voices to confront and challenge its normalisation, potentially leading to accountability.
The intensity of the reaction becomes more intelligible when examined through the mechanisms of escalation and normalisation described by the Wired to Steal (W2S) model, a neurobehavioral framework for understanding colonial expansion.
Normalisation of genocide
Since the events of 7 October, in which Hamas led a military operation resulting in the murder and kidnapping of hundreds of Israeli security forces and civilians, Israel retaliated indiscriminately, obliterating the Gaza Strip and even targeting its own people. The genocide, as international experts and organisations have termed it, is but a recent development in an ongoing Zionist genocidal-colonial cycle, in which Israel has expanded oppression and dispossession in response to acts of resistance by Indigenous Palestinians.
Crucially, Zionism is not exceptional. In its foundations and operation, Israel manifests other white European settler-colonial projects in which extraction and greed by a ruling class drive a cycle of manufactured identity, segregation, fear, dehumanisation and rewards for aggression. This sustains a self-reinforcing system of dispossession of designated out-groups, while escalation and normalisation reproduce it.
In contrast to Zionist narratives which decontextualise the events of 7 October to portray Israel’s subsequent actions as defensive rather than offensive, Palestinian resistance can be understood as being instrumentalised as an essential, albeit tragic, trigger for renewed and expanded aggression. It nourishes the ongoing Zionist settler colonial project which predates the establishment of the state of Israel in 1948.
According to the W2S model, resistance is also used to justify theft under the guise of “defence”. Settler society then normalises this through media institutions, social norms, incentives, and everyday conditioned behaviour, rendering the resulting construct a perceived reality.
In this way, normalisation expands the moral boundaries of what is considered acceptable, and who is considered human, thereby increasing the resources available for theft. This is clear to see in the deliberate and cynical blurring of civilian and militant categories, and the designation of Palestinian children as “future terrorists” by Israeli military and political leaders in recent years.
Furthermore, normalisation constructs a façade of so-called “open debate” among “varying opinions” and, consequently, a plurality of tolerated voices within settler society, while shifting attention from the conduct itself to the boundaries of permissible debate and the legitimacy of individual critics. Without it, the tawdry fabric of settler society is threatened.
Abraham and Szor as collateral damage
Zionist propaganda, also known as Hasbara, is one of the most sophisticated forms of state propaganda greasing expansion and theft. As an essential branch of hasbara, normalisation has evolved into an intricate web of deception, particularly utilised in the tropes of liberal Zionism, which presents the Zionist project and Israel as reformable and compatible with human rights. It includes a right-to-left political spectrum, democratic and progressive values, and a desire for peace and justice.
The fallout from NAZA reflects a conditioned reaction casting Abraham and Szor as traitors to the Zionist narrative, with a distinct propagandistic function.
In contrast to Palestinian journalists, who could be racialised and scapegoated as clear members of the out-group and subsequently targeted for elimination as “terrorists,” Abraham and Szor represent a new kind of threat to Israeli society - a threat from within. They have been singled out as in-group targets to be made an example of, using tactics typically reserved for out-group members (though still mild, for now), with the effect of discouraging other potential in-group whistleblowers from coming forward. Fearmongering and social rewards for their harassment are utilised, while simultaneously clarifying the internal boundaries of Zionist identity.
Thus, rather than approaching the film as new evidence for Israeli criminality, the firestorm around NAZA can be understood as an internal struggle within the Zionist movement over how to respond to evidence of genocide without challenging the underlying Zionist project.
Some liberal Zionists have embraced NAZA as a vehicle for bringing criticism of Israeli conduct in Gaza into Israeli public discourse and encouraging greater scrutiny of existing policies. Establishment Zionists have pushed back against such claims, in part reflecting concerns that their wider acceptance could contribute to a broader crisis of Israeli social cohesion.
In this sense, the debate in its present form serves to normalise Israel’s actions since 7 October: genocide is recast as something “debatable,” maintaining Israel's impunity for the worst crimes against humanity and war crimes, with the identities of those responsible remaining obscured.
Will the Zionist regime permit the film to screen in Israel? The full extent of NAZA's impact is yet to be determined. Already, its reaction should encourage all to adopt the nonviolent Boycott, Divestment and Sanctions (BDS) movement against Israel for its oppression of freedom of speech and the targeting of the filmmakers.
Clearly, for it to have lasting moral impact, NAZA and its creators must give other whistleblowers the courage to step forward. Abraham, Szor and their colleagues can do more than hail the 24 Israeli military personnel featured in the film as courageous. They should urge them to come forward publicly from anonymity, which currently gives opponents an easy basis for dismissing the allegations without addressing their substance. Otherwise, NAZA risks becoming a discredited, normalising propaganda tool at the hands of the very forces it set out to hold accountable, and Abraham and Szor may also be swept into the gruesome machinations of Israel's genocide of Palestinian people as mere collateral damage.
Yoav Litvin is a writer, photographer and doctor of psychology/neuroscience. Litvin’s new book - Wired to Steal: Zionism and the Shaping of the Western Mind (Interlink Books) - co-authored with renowned historian Ilan Pappé, will be released in November 2026.

articles.title: Putin envoy heads to US for talks with Trump officials – Reuters
articles.body:
Putin envoy heads to US for talks with Trump officials – Reuters
Reuters has reported that Kremlin envoy Kirill Dmitriev is heading to the US on Wednesday 23 September for talks with representatives of the Trump administration, including Steve Witkoff, Jared Kushner and others.
Source: Reuters, citing sources familiar with preparations for the talks
Details: The sources told Reuters that Dmitriev's visit to the US, which was agreed with Kremlin ruler Vladimir Putin, will take place in New York during the UN General Assembly and will follow up on Putin's meeting with the US representatives at the Kremlin earlier this month.
One of the agency's sources said the purpose of the visit is to maintain dialogue between Russia and the US and "keep the peacemaking effort going".
The source added that economic cooperation between Russia and the US, energy issues and a peaceful settlement of the situation in Ukraine will be on the agenda of Dmitriev's talks in New York.
Background:
- Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has called Russian leader Vladimir Putin "patient zero" who is spreading the idea of war around the world.
- Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha stressed in an address to the UN Security Council that Russia's war against Ukraine poses a threat to the entire world.
- It was reported that 50 countries and the European Union issued a joint statement in support of Ukraine at the UN, calling on Russia to agree to a ceasefire. The United States did not join the statement.
- The previous day, US President Donald Trump called on Putin to end the war against Ukraine.
- Putin's spokesman Dmitry Peskov also said that the Kremlin "welcomes" the US's decision to invite Putin to the G20 summit in Miami.

articles.title: Zelenskyy: We need peace before AI starts making battlefield decisions
articles.body:
Zelenskyy: We need peace before AI starts making battlefield decisions
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has called on world leaders to curb the rapid development of lethal weapons which have allowed the Russia-Ukraine war to go as far as it has.

articles.title: OpenAI to provide Ukraine with tools to combat cyberattacks
articles.body:
OpenAI to provide Ukraine with tools to combat cyberattacks
Technology giant OpenAI will provide the Ukrainian government with free access to its AI-powered cybersecurity system Daybreak to help protect civilian infrastructure such as hospitals and power plants from cyberattacks.
Source: BBC
Details: According to the Computer Emergency Response Team of Ukraine (CERT-UA), the country's national cyber incident response team, nearly 6,000 attacks were recorded in Ukraine in 2025.
Daybreak can rapidly identify vulnerabilities in digital systems and help develop measures to address them. Under the agreement, Ukraine will gain access to OpenAI's advanced GPT-5.6 Sol model – a competitor to Anthropic's Mythos and Fable.
George Osborne, former UK Chancellor of the Exchequer and now head of OpenAI for Countries, said: "Protecting civilian infrastructure means defending it against both physical and digital attacks, so people can continue to live, work and access essential services."
Reacting to the news, Rafe Pilling, Senior Director of Threat Intelligence at cybersecurity company Sophos, said Russian offensive cyber operations had been a "key component" of the Kremlin's aggression against Ukraine since 2014.
"Any initiative that strengthens Ukraine's already highly capable, but heavily burdened, cyber defence efforts is a welcome development and could provide a valuable force multiplier," he said.
Jamie MacColl, a senior research fellow specialising in cybersecurity at the Royal United Services Institute (RUSI), told the BBC that Western tech companies have been supporting Ukraine for some time – partly for altruistic reasons, but also because they gain highly valuable data and intelligence in an active conflict environment.
He believes access to Daybreak will be useful, particularly given the scale of Russian cyberattacks targeting the country.
Background: Anthropic foiled attempts by hackers to use Claude to conduct a cyber-espionage campaign against Ukraine that was suspected of being linked to Russia.

articles.title: Ethiopia civil war fears escalate after rebel forces ‘seize airport’
articles.body:
Ethiopia civil war fears escalate after rebel forces ‘seize airport’
Forces in Ethiopia’s northern Tigray region have reportedly taken control of the airport in its capital, Mekelle, prompting state-owned Ethiopian Airlines to suspend services to three local destinations. The takeover marks a sharp escalation nearly four years after a peace deal ended a brutal two-year civil war in the East African country.
The carrier announced in a social media post on Wednesday that services to Mekelle, Shire, and Axum have been halted “due to the current situation in Tigray region,” without elaborating. “We sincerely apologize to our valued customers for any inconvenience caused by this suspension. We will inform you when flight operations resume,” the state-owned airline stated.
Two local sources told Reuters that Tigrayan forces have taken control of Mekelle airport from federal police in an overnight operation.
In a statement on Wednesday, Tigray’s regional government said its forces have entered a defensive war against federal troops. It accused the federal government of launching a ground offensive after air and artillery strikes across parts of Tigray on Tuesday.
The federal government has yet to publicly comment on the alleged takeover and the airstrikes.
The development came days after seven armed groups, including the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF), the political party that runs Tigray, announced an alliance seeking to overthrow Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed’s government and establish a transitional administration. In a statement on Sunday, the coalition, known as the Ethiopian Peoples’ Forces Alliance for Survival, accused the ruling Prosperity Party of imposing “dictatorial” rule and pushing the East African country toward disintegration.
On Monday, Abiy’s spokesperson, Billene Seyoum, accused the alliance of collaborating with financial backing from neighboring Eritrea. The authorities in Eritrea have repeatedly denied backing the groups.
Ethiopia has struggled to secure lasting stability in Tigray since a 2022 peace agreement ended the two-year war between federal forces and the TPLF. The conflict killed hundreds of thousands of people. Recent clashes and reported drone strikes have threatened the fragile peace. World Health Organization Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus warned last month that Ethiopia was on the brink of renewed war.
The latest disruption to Ethiopian Airlines schedule follows an earlier suspension of flights to Tigray in January amid reports of renewed military activity. At the time, passengers received cancellation messages citing unplanned circumstances, while a security official linked the interruption to fighting between federal and regional forces.

articles.title: Microamp establishes cooperation with the faculty of electronics at the Military University of Technology
articles.body:
Microamp, a global leader in resilient 5G mmWave connectivity for real-time operations, and the Faculty of Electronics at the Military University of Technology (MUT), a premier academic and research institution based in Warsaw, Poland, have signed a cooperation agreement. The inaugural meeting for this joint initiative took place on 4 September 2026. One of the initial outcomes of this collaboration is the delivery of the Microamp 5G mmWave Starter Kit to the Faculty, which will serve advanced research and educational purposes.
Key representatives from Microamp attended the meeting, including Dr Marcin Góralczyk (Chief Technology Officer) and Adam Olesiński (Head of RAN Solutions). The Faculty of Electronics at MUT was represented by Col. Prof. Jan Kelner (Dean of the Faculty of Electronics), Lt. Col. Dr Jarosław Wojtuń (Deputy Director of the Institute of Communications Systems) and Dr Paweł Skokowski (Head of the Mobile Communications Systems Department) alongside staff members.
The delivered Microamp 5G mmWave Starter Kit is a comprehensive solution enabling the rapid deployment of a fully functional LDI/LPD mobile architecture. The Microamp mmWave wireless platform consists of radio access network elements, mmWave RAN software, a core network and user equipment. Operating in Standalone mode, the system is fully compliant with the 3GPP standard. The network supports n257, n258 and n261 bands across the 24.25-29.5 GHz frequency range, ensuring throughput exceeding 4 Gbps and latency below 5 ms.
The Microamp mmWave network will be extensively utilised in scientific and research activities conducted by the Faculty of Electronics staff, particularly in developing specialised publications and reports for international NATO working groups. Furthermore, the provided solution forms a foundation for joint research initiatives and projects. This Microamp mmWave system will also facilitate commercial scientific research, proactively addressing the current demands of the industrial market and the defence sector. Access to the complete 5G mmWave environment creates an opportunity to practically verify advanced communication scenarios essential for civil and military applications.
Within the academic framework, the Microamp 5G mmWave Starter Kit will support specialised training sessions and laboratory classes dedicated to the latest connectivity standards. The supplied mmWave wireless platform will allow students to acquire practical skills in configuring, deploying and testing 5G mmWave architectures. Access to this Microamp solution will enable the completion of diploma and design projects, including experimental research on wave propagation, network architecture optimisation and the integration of specialised end devices.
Establishing cooperation with the MUT Faculty of Electronics marks a vital step for Microamp in developing expertise within modern telecommunications. The provided mmWave system will enrich the laboratory facilities of the Faculty and integrate academic education with the practical application of modern 5G connectivity.
About Military University of Technology
The Military University of Technology (MUT) in Warsaw is a public academic institution established in 1951. As a military-civilian university, MUT educates cadets and civilian students while conducting advanced research and development in engineering, technical, exact and social sciences. MUT serves as a strategic research and development facility for the Polish Armed Forces and a leading innovation centre for national security and defence.
The Faculty of Electronics at the Military University of Technology is one of the leading academic and research centres in Poland, specialising in advanced technologies across electronics, telecommunications, radar systems, electronic warfare and communication systems. The Faculty conducts scientific research, implementation projects and educational programmes for both the defence sector and civilian industry.
About Microamp
Microamp is a global leader in resilient 5G and 6G mmWave connectivity for real-time operations. The company designs, builds and delivers ultra-high-capacity, near-zero-latency end-to-end networks powered by its own purpose-built radios. By merging deep-tech know-how with a broad portfolio of technology partners, Microamp empowers industries, system integrators, MNOs, DSPs, governments, and research institutions worldwide. Its networks support applications requiring deterministic performance and high-uplink throughput, in both commercial and defence sectors, where resilience, security and jamming resistance are crucial. Engineered for the most demanding environments, the Microamp system supports critical infrastructure, ports, logistics hubs, public transportation, media production, mass events and specialised military missions.

articles.title: Finland and Ukraine sign drone production deal
articles.body:
Finland and Ukraine have signed a defence cooperation agreement that sets the framework for producing drones and other weapons systems in Finland, as Kyiv seeks more production capacity and Helsinki expands cooperation between the two countries’ defence industries.
Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy signed the agreement in New York on Wednesday during the United Nations General Assembly. Stubb had travelled to New York for the UN’s high-level week, which runs from 20 to 24 September.
The agreement covers joint production of defence equipment, transfers of technology and expertise, and industrial projects between Finnish and Ukrainian companies.
Most drones produced in Finland under future projects are expected to go to Ukraine. Stubb said during an August visit to Kyiv that about 90 per cent of drones manufactured in Finland under the planned cooperation would go to Ukraine, while the remainder would stay in Finland or go to other customers.
The agreement itself does not transfer funding. Instead, it provides a framework for companies to negotiate production projects and other contracts.
“Ukraine needs all our support in its fight,” Stubb wrote on X after the signing. He said Finland would also use lessons from Ukraine to develop its own defence capabilities.
Stubb told Finnish media in New York that the speed of implementation would depend on cooperation between Finnish and Ukrainian companies. He said some Ukrainian drone models could be produced in Finland.
The two countries had worked on the agreement for several months. Finland and other Nordic and Baltic countries had already committed in August to expanding joint defence production with Ukraine, including drones, air defence equipment, electronic warfare systems and ammunition.
Finland has also started building company-level links with Ukraine. Stubb travelled to Kyiv in August with representatives from Insta, Boomeranger, Patria, Nokia, ICEYE, Sensofusion and NestAI. Insta, Boomeranger and Patria signed letters of intent with Ukrainian partners during the visit, according to the Finnish president’s office.
The projects under discussion extend beyond aerial drones. Cooperation also covers unmanned ground vehicles and maritime systems.
Defence Minister Antti Häkkänen said the two countries’ defence ministries had negotiated the framework for months. He said it would create opportunities for Finnish defence companies and support Ukraine’s defence capacity.

articles.title: USA Transfers AAV-7A1 Amphibious Vehicles to Indonesia
articles.body:
The first batch of AAV-7A1 amphibious vehicles has been delivered from the U.S. to Indonesia.
Photographer Willymarley posted photos of the vehicles being unloaded at one of Indonesia’s ports on Facebook.
The first shipment consisted of about 10 AAV-7A1 units.
The vehicles are equipped with the Enhanced Applique Armor Kit and the Up-Gunned Weapons Station.
Indonesia has signed an agreement with the United States to deliver approximately 35 AAV-7A1 armored amphibious vehicles.
The vehicles are being transferred from surplus stocks of the U.S. Marine Corps.
They are likely to be officially unveiled on October 5 to mark Indonesian Armed Forces Day.
The AAV-7A1s will supplement the country’s existing fleet, which previously consisted of a limited number—between 10 and 15—of older LVTP-7A1 vehicles transferred by South Korea as military aid in 2009.
In 2025, the U.S. Marine Corps decommissioned the AAV-7 amphibious assault vehicles.
The AAV-7 entered service in 1972. The vehicle was equipped with a waterjet propulsion system and a stern ramp, which sped up troop landings from ship to shore.
As part of a service life extension program in the 1980s, the vehicle received a new engine, transmission, and combat module, after which it was reclassified as the AAV-7A1.
In the late 1990s, the AAVs underwent another phase of large-scale modernization, including the installation of a new engine and an improved suspension.
As a result, the A1-version vehicles were equipped with the same engine as the Bradley infantry fighting vehicles. This provided additional logistical advantages.
In the 1990s, the U.S. Marine Corps began developing a replacement for the AAV.
The U.S. began actively selling surplus vehicles to NATO allies—Romania and Greece—as well as to Taiwan.

articles.title: Who Will Be the Next Leader of the U.N.? Meet the Contenders
articles.body:
With António Guterres’s nearly decade-long tenure as the Secretary-General of the United Nations drawing to a close amid rising conflict around the globe, the race to succeed him as the leader of the world’s most powerful diplomatic body is already underway.
Guterres this week delivered his final address to the U.N. General Assembly, in which he called for a greater focus on climate change, a two-state solution for Israel and Palestine, “de-escalation and dialogue” in the Middle East, and regulations for artificial intelligence.
At the end of his speech, Guterres bid goodbye to a crowd filled with many diplomats and world leaders who he has worked with over his two five-year terms.
"So, on January 1st, when I am no longer Secretary-General, be sure of this. Wherever I will be, whatever I will be doing, I will keep championing the conviction that peace is possible," he said. "I will continue to stand up for the values of the United Nations Charter and I will never, ever give up. Thank you."
Guterres’s successor is set to step in as Secretary-General at a consequential moment for global diplomacy. Research indicates that last year saw the highest number of active global conflicts since World War II and the greatest number of fatalities since the Rwandan genocide. Tensions in other parts of the world are threatening to boil over. Climate change is exacting a growing toll. AI's development is prompting increasing alarm. And the U.N. itself is confronting a growing funding crisis.
Seven candidates are so far in the running to shepherd the U.N. through those challenges. Here’s what to know about the race.
How will the next Secretary-General be chosen?
The process to choose the next Secretary-General began in November, when a joint letter from the presidents of the U.N. General Assembly and Security Council invited the nominations of candidates from member states.
The initiation letter noted “with regret that no woman has ever held the position” and encouraged member states to “strongly consider nominating women as candidates.”
Member states nominate candidates by submitting an application to the U.N. including a personal statement with that candidate’s vision for what they’d do in the role, a resume, and campaign finance disclosures.
The General Assembly then holds “interactive dialogues” in which candidates express their hopes for the position and the U.N. in an opening statement, which is followed by questioning from the assembly. These televised hearings continue as candidates are submitted to the U.N.
Who becomes Secretary-General ultimately comes down to a decision from the U.N.’s 15-person Security Council, which recommends one individual to the General Assembly. The General Assembly then appoints that person to the position.
As part of its selection process, the Security Council holds “straw polls,” in which members of the council select one of three options for each candidate: “encourage,” “discourage,” or “no opinion expressed.” This anonymized process is used to gauge whether candidates would be able to secure the nine votes needed for a formal recommendation by the Security Council.
Who’s in the running?
So far nine candidates have been nominated for the position of Secretary-General. Two of those candidates have withdrawn, leaving seven individuals vying to replace Guterres.
Carolyn Rodrigues Birkett has been Guyana’s permanent representative to the U.N. since 2020 and previously served as foreign minister for her country and held senior roles at the U.N. Food and Agriculture Organization. Nominated by Guyana, her vision statement emphasizes refocusing on the U.N.’s core principles and “a more agile and effective United Nations.”
Rebeca Grynspan is the former vice president of Costa Rica, which nominated her for the position, and current secretary-general of trade and development for the U.N. She named three principles that define the mission she would undertake as Secretary-General: making the U.N. “more useful,” “more agile,” and “more accountable.”
Ivonne A-Baki, nominated by Tonga, is a long-time Ecuadorean diplomat who has twice served as the country’s ambassador to the U.S. She has also served as ambassador to countries including Qatar and France. Her platform highlights her involvement in the 1998 Ecuador-Peru peace settlement. “Where others speak of reform, I speak of renewal,” A-Baki’s vision statement reads. “An institution can be indispensable and in need of renewal at the same time, and ours is both. It is failing to live up to its own Charter, not for want of purpose but for want of focus and discipline.”
María Fernanda Espinosa is the former Foreign Minister and Defense Minister of Ecuador and served as President of the 73rd U.N. General Assembly in 2018. She was nominated by Antigua and Barbuda. Her vision consists of five pillars: “peace and security, development, digital and energy transformation, closing the delivery gap, and rebuilding credibility.” Garcés in her statement contended that “what is now in question is not the relevance of the United Nations, but its credibility.”
Rafael Mariano Grossi is an Argentine diplomat who has served as the Director General of the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) since 2019. “The world does not need more declarations. It needs a United Nations capable of responding to the real demands of our time, with impartiality and a results-oriented approach grounded in facts,” Grossi, who was nominated by his country, wrote in his vision statement.
Olara Otunnu was Uganda’s permanent representative to the U.N. for five years and briefly served as the country’s foreign minister. He was also the U.N. under-secretary-general and the special representative for children and armed conflict. “Reform is no longer an optional choice. It is an imperative,” he said.
Macky Sall was the president of Senegal for twelve years and has served as the chair of the Africa Union, a continental organization spanning 55 member states. He expressed a goal to “restore trust in multilateralism” if chosen as Secretary-General and said that “peace, security and development are intrinsically linked.”
Where does the race stand?
“We're at a moment right now where the race is entering a pretty pivotal phase,” says Daniel Forti, head of U.N. affairs at the International Crisis Group, a non-profit think tank dedicated to preventing deadly crises around the world.
With just over three months remaining in Guterre’s term, it won’t be long before a successor is chosen. The Security Council, though, “is not especially enthusiastic about any of the current contenders,” Forti tells TIME. He cites the last three straw polls, which have favored Greenspan and Birkett, but without “a real consolidation of overwhelming support.”
This lack of consensus, Forti believes, could suggest that other candidates may enter the race late in the game. Although there have been no formal announcements of new candidates, Forti has heard chatter surrounding certain individuals: Nickolay Mladenov, the former Bulgarian foreign minister and former U.N. Middle East envoy who currently serves as the Board of Peace’s High Representative for Gaza; U.N. Deputy Secretary-General Amina Mohammed; and former Mexican Foreign Minister Alicia Bárcena.
“At this late stage, new candidates don't have the luxury of time to really socialize their candidacies, build out their visions, and elaborate very detailed policy platforms and bring them to U.N. member states, and try and win over the P5,” Forti says, referring to the five permanent members of the Security Council. The support of these members—China, France, Russia, the United Kingdom, and the U.S.
—is the most critical because they have the power to veto candidates before being recommended to the General Assembly.
Regardless of the outcome, Forti asserts that whoever is chosen to replace Guterres will inherit a fraught state of international affairs, and certainly be tested.
“You have a really fragmented global landscape,” he says. “The challenges for whoever takes over the office are going to be immense.”

articles.title: Inside NATO’s online propaganda machine
articles.body:
Inside NATO’s online propaganda machine
NATO has spent years researching online influence techniques involving fake profiles, targeted advertising and purchased social media engagement. RT’s America Now has examined the bloc’s experiments and what they could reveal about efforts to shape online narratives.
Host Ben Swann and investigative journalist Elizabeth Lane reviewed NATO promotional material, published research and reports on experiments involving social media manipulation.
One example is a 2024 NATO promotional video featuring predominantly white European women as the alliance’s “future” in a potential conflict, apparently with Russia. Swann and Lane argue that the unusually non-diverse casting could be intended to prepare European audiences for women taking a greater role in a possible confrontation as Ukraine struggles with manpower shortages.
They also examined two 2019 experiments by NATO strategic communications researchers. In one, researchers created fake Facebook pages and profiles, collected publicly available information on military personnel and used targeted advertising to reach them. They reportedly identified around 150 soldiers, tracked troop movements and even induced some personnel to act against orders. The experiment cost roughly $60.
In another test, researchers spent €300 on artificial engagement, buying more than 3,500 comments, 25,000 likes, 20,000 views and 5,000 followers. They identified over 18,000 accounts involved in providing fake engagement. Four weeks later, roughly 80% of the purchased activity remained online, highlighting weaknesses in platforms’ ability to detect manipulation.
NATO described the experiments as defensive research aimed at identifying online threats. Swann and Lane, however, questioned why a military alliance was developing practical expertise in techniques that could also be used to influence public opinion. They also pointed to NATO researchers’ cooperation with Ukrainian social media analytics company Singularex.
The episode also revisited false stories that had circulated during the early stages of the Ukraine conflict, including the “Ghost of Kiev” fighter pilot and initial claims about the “defenders of Snake Island.” Lane argued that journalists who repeat compelling wartime stories without verifying them can amplify false narratives.
Lane also said independent journalists covering Russia and Ukraine regularly face bot attacks, abuse and threats. She said she had received such messages herself, including one stating, “Zelensky sends his love,” which she suggested could point to coordinated activity.
Check out the full episode here.

articles.title: Fifty countries and EU call on Russia to cease fire, US does not support statement
articles.body:
Fifty countries and EU call on Russia to cease fire, US does not support statement
A total of 50 countries and the European Union have issued a joint statement at the UN in support of Ukraine, calling on Russia to agree to a ceasefire. The United States did not join the statement.
Source: European Pravda citing the text of the statement provided by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Ukraine
Details: The statement was released ahead of a UN Security Council meeting on 23 September. The signatories expressed solidarity with Ukraine and deep concern over the escalation of Russian attacks against civilians and civilian infrastructure across the country.
They also voiced concern about attacks in the Black Sea and supported efforts to reach an agreement there to ensure freedom of navigation.
In the statement, the countries reiterated that Ukraine had agreed as early as March 2025 to a full, immediate and unconditional ceasefire.
Quote: "We call on Russia to finally do the same, as a necessary step towards meaningful diplomacy and negotiations leading to peace."
More details: The signatories also called on Russia to ensure the immediate return to Ukraine of all arbitrarily detained, forcibly transferred or deported Ukrainian civilians, including children, as well as the full return of all prisoners of war and all interned persons as important confidence-building measures.
Quote: "Ukraine wants peace. We want peace. Russia must stop its aggression, accept a ceasefire, and engage meaningfully in negotiations towards a comprehensive, just and lasting peace in accordance with international law."
More details: The statement was signed by 50 countries and the European Union (Ukraine, Albania, Andorra, Australia, Austria, Belgium, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Bulgaria, Canada, Costa Rica, Croatia, Cyprus, Czechia, Denmark, Estonia, Finland, France, Georgia, Germany, Greece, Honduras, Hungary, Iceland, Ireland, Israel, Italy, Japan, Latvia, Liechtenstein, Lithuania, Luxembourg, Malta, Monaco, Montenegro, the Netherlands, New Zealand, North Macedonia, Norway, Poland, Portugal, the Republic of Korea, the Republic of Moldova, Romania, San Marino, Slovakia, Slovenia, Spain, Sweden, Switzerland and the United Kingdom).
The United States, which is playing a mediating role in talks between Ukraine and Russia, was not among the signatories.
Background:
- The 81st session of the UN General Assembly is taking place in New York. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy is expected to address it on 23 September.
- The day before, US President Donald Trump urged Russian leader Vladimir Putin to end Russia's war against Ukraine.

articles.title: EU court overturns 2024 and 2025 sanctions decisions against former Russian senator Oleg Tkach (but he remains on the sanctions list)
articles.body:
EU court overturns 2024 and 2025 sanctions decisions against former Russian senator Oleg Tkach (but he remains on the sanctions list)
The General Court of the European Union annulled the Council of the EU’s September 2024 and September 2025 decisions to keep former Federation Council member Oleg Tkach on the sanctions list. An entry for the ruling is posted on the court’s website.
The EU initially imposed sanctions on Tkach in March 2022 because, as a Federation Council member, he had voted to ratify the treaty “on friendship, cooperation, and mutual assistance between the Russian Federation and the Donetsk and Luhansk People’s Republics.”
The court ruled that Tkach’s vote had provided sufficient grounds to impose sanctions on him but was not enough to keep him on the list in subsequent years.
The court concluded that Tkach had “withdrawn from Russian political life”: He did not seek reelection in September 2022 and had also acquired “citizenship in two other countries,” which disqualified him from holding political office in Russia.
The court also rejected the Council’s argument that the former senator had not publicly condemned the invasion of Ukraine. The ruling said his failure to do so could not automatically be taken as a sign of support, particularly given the harsh repression of anti-war views.
The Council also cited Tkach’s ties to the publishing company Olma Media Group, which he founded in 1991, as grounds for extending the sanctions. The group included the publisher Prosveshcheniye, which helped promote anti-Ukrainian narratives through school textbooks.
The Council maintained that although Tkach had formally stepped away from managing the company long ago, he continued to exert influence over it through a trust fund and entities linked to his family. The court rejected this argument because the Council had failed to explain Tkach’s specific role in the company. The court also said VEB.RF, the Russian Direct Investment Fund, and Sberbank had controlled a 75% stake in Prosveshcheniye since 2021.
The court therefore found that the grounds cited in the Council’s September 2024 and September 2025 decisions did not justify keeping Tkach on the sanctions list.
Tkach remains on the EU sanctions list under a March 14, 2026, Council decision. He has already filed a lawsuit seeking to overturn that extension, but the court has not yet ruled on the case. The Council’s September 22, 2026, decision lifting sanctions on billionaires Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman does not mention Tkach.
