articles.title: Is Israel committing genocide in Lebanon? (VIDEO)
articles.body:
Is Israel committing genocide in Lebanon? (VIDEO)
Israel is facing accusations of genocide over its military campaign in Lebanon, where thousands have been killed and large areas devastated. RT correspondent Steve Sweeney reports from Nabatieh, a city in the south of the country that has been repeatedly hit by Israeli strikes.
More than 4,300 people, including over 250 children and 130 medical professionals, have been killed since the latest escalation began in March, according to Lebanon’s Health Ministry.
The Lemkin Institute for Genocide Prevention and Doctors Against Genocide have accused Israel of pursuing what they called a “genocidal policy of absolute destruction,” targeting the foundations of life of Lebanon’s Shia communities. The groups said attacks on medical personnel were part of a sustained pattern affecting “the very systems necessary for civilian survival.”
Around 56,000 hectares of agricultural land have been affected, with losses to the sector estimated at more than $1 billion, according to Lebanon’s Agriculture Ministry.
Israel denies that its campaign targets Lebanon’s Shia population, saying its operations are directed against Hezbollah, the Iran-backed Lebanese armed group. Israeli Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich has warned, however, that Beirut’s predominantly Shia Dahiya district would “look like Khan Yunis,” referring to a war-devastated city in Gaza.
The latest Israeli campaign in Lebanon began in early March, after Hezbollah attacked Israel following the start of US-Israeli strikes on Iran. Israel responded with airstrikes and later expanded its military operations in Lebanon.
Israeli attacks have continued despite a US-brokered framework agreed upon in June aimed at ending the fighting. The deal calls for a progressive Israeli withdrawal from southern Lebanon alongside Lebanese Army deployments and the disarmament of armed groups, including Hezbollah, but implementation has stalled.
Under the 1948 Genocide Convention, genocide requires intent to destroy, in whole or in part, a national, ethnic, racial or religious group. RT looks at whether the destruction and statements accompanying Israel’s campaign could meet that definition.

articles.title: US turns to South Korea to ease ammunition bottlenecks amid global conflicts
articles.body:
Advertisement
US turns to South Korea to ease ammunition bottlenecks amid global conflicts
Depleted stockpiles from the Middle East and Ukraine wars are spurring South Korean arms makers to build US production hubs
4-MIN READ4-MIN
 Listen
Washington is increasingly turning to South Korea to ease ammunition supply bottlenecks triggered by wars in the Middle East and Europe, potentially accelerating Seoul’s integration into the US defence industrial base.
Analysts say the United States may struggle to replenish stockpiles quickly enough if conflicts in Iran and Ukraine drag on, creating opportunities for South Korea’s defence industry to expand its presence in the US market.
Jang Won-joon, a defence science professor at Jeonbuk National University, said the war with Iran and Russia’s invasion of Ukraine had made Washington acutely aware of shortfalls in its domestic defence production capacity.
The US burned through US$22.3 billion worth of ammunition in just four months of the Iran war, according to the Pentagon, putting its defence industry under scrutiny and exposing what critics call a structural problem.
Washington is now expected to build defence production networks with allies across the Indo-Pacific, including South Korea, Japan and Australia to help close the supply gap.

articles.title: Under new deal, U.S. military buys non-standard weapons
articles.body:
- Global Military Products won a spot on a new five-year, $19.5 million USSOCOM contract for U.S. and foreign weapons, ammunition, and protective equipment.
- GMP has historically supplied Soviet-pattern weapons like AK-platform rifles and RPG-7 launchers for training and partner-force support.
Global Military Products has been selected as one of several contractors on a new U.S. Special Operations Command indefinite delivery, indefinite quantity contract for U.S. and foreign weapons, ammunition, and personal protective equipment, the Tampa, Florida-based company said Sept. 21.
The five-year contract has a ceiling of $19.5 million, and GMP will compete against other contract holders for individual delivery orders as the command’s needs arise.
The company has not disclosed which specific weapons this contract will cover. But GMP’s business has long centered on sourcing non-standard, foreign-made military equipment through a separate line of contracts known as Special Ammunition and Weapon Systems, or SAWS, which the company has held with the Army for over a decade. Those items typically include Soviet and former-Eastern-Bloc-pattern hardware not in the standard U.S. arsenal: Kalashnikov-pattern rifles such as the AKM and AK-74, PKM and RPK machine guns, RPG-7 rocket launchers, SVD-pattern sniper rifles, and mortars in non-NATO calibers such as 82mm, along with the ammunition that feeds them. The U.S. military uses this kind of foreign-made equipment to train special operations forces on weapons they may encounter in the field, to equip foreign partner forces already using Soviet-era arms, or for testing.
This is the second consecutive USSOCOM IDIQ contract for weapons and ammunition procurement that GMP has held. The company said its work on the earlier agreement, which involved sourcing and delivering weapons and ammunition through its international supplier network, factored into its selection this time.
“Special operations forces require speed, flexibility and dependable access to equipment,” said Austin Gouveia, associate program manager at Global Military Products. “This award reflects Global Military Products’ commitment to providing U.S. and allied forces with reliable access to critical defense equipment and capabilities.”
“This award also reflects our ability to perform under the previous USSOCOM IDIQ contract, where we excelled at sourcing and delivering weapons and ammunition while leveraging our global network and supply chain capabilities to respond to evolving operational requirements and support USSOCOM missions,” Gouveia said.
GMP, a subsidiary of Global Ordnance, has built its business around supplying this kind of non-standard hardware to the U.S. military and its allies, including mortar systems, sniper rifles, assault rifles, machine guns, grenade launchers, anti-armor weapons, ammunition, electro-optics, and weapon accessories. The company separately holds a $639.8 million Army contract for 155mm artillery rounds awarded in 2025.

articles.title: "General Winter" may go over to Ukraine’s side this year – Zelenskyy
articles.body:
"General Winter" may go over to Ukraine’s side this year – Zelenskyy
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has warned Russia that Ukraine will make the winter painful for Russia if it continues to strike Ukraine's energy system.
Source: Zelenskyy's address to the UN General Assembly in New York on 23 September
Quote: "Ukrainians understand that this winter could be very harsh for us, but in response, we will have no choice but to make it painful for Russia too.
No Russian official ever imagined that Army General Winter, which had fought on Russia's side for centuries, would one day switch sides and support those defending themselves from Russia. We will make that happen this winter if Russia continues to target our energy system and our heating." [The idiom General Winter refers to the severe Russian winter weather that has historically hindered military invasions of Russia – ed.]
Details: The president stressed that this is precisely why steps towards de-escalation are needed before the winter.
Zelenskyy also reminded the assembled world leaders that Ukraine did not choose the war, but is simply choosing not to die and is defending itself.
Background: In the same address, Zelenskyy called Russian leader Vladimir Putin "patient zero" who is spreading the idea of war around the world.

articles.title: EU extends Russia sanctions for three years, lifts restrictions on billionaires Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman
articles.body:
The Council of the European Union has agreed to extend sanctions against Russian individuals and entities for another three years, according to a council statement issued on Sept. 22. As part of the agreement, Russian billionaires Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman were removed from the sanctions list.
The remaining restrictions were extended for three years, through Sept. 22, 2029. The existing measures cover more than 3,000 individuals and entities that Brussels says are linked to Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
The document separately notes that the council “decided not to renew the listings of three individuals and one entity.” The council statement did not name those delisted, but their identities appear in a document published in the EU’s Official Journal. They are:
- Alisher Usmanov, founder of USM Holdings;
- Mikhail Fridman, co-founder of Alfa Group;
- Andrei Falaleev, former rector of Vernadsky Crimean Federal University;
- and Redbird Corporate Services Ltd, a company linked to a vessel belonging to Russia’s “shadow fleet,” the network of ships used to transport Russian oil and other cargo while evading Western sanctions and a price cap designed to limit the Kremlin’s revenue amid the ongoing war.
Multiple media outlets and international news agencies had previously reported that EU countries were discussing the removal of the 62-year-old Fridman and 73-year-old Usmanov from the sanctions list, with reports appearing in The Guardian, Euronews, and Reuters. France and Slovakia had sought Usmanov’s removal, according to the Financial Times, while Luxembourg supported lifting sanctions on Fridman. Latvia was among the countries that opposed the moves.
A spokesperson for Ireland, which currently holds the rotating presidency of the EU Council, told The Guardian that the decision was the result of a “difficult compromise” — one that saw the above-mentioned figures removed from the list in exchange for a procedural switch that will significantly extend the time between renewals of the larger sanctions regime:
“Until now, these listings have been reviewed and assessed on a six-monthly basis; today’s decision to renew on a 36-month basis enhances the durability and predictability of the EU sanctions framework.”
Uzbekistan-born Usmanov, who according to Forbes has a net worth of $14 billion (placing him 224th on its list of global billionaires as of Sept. 23), amassed his wealth in the mining, industry, telecoms, and media sectors. He was sanctioned by both the EU and the U.S., as well as Canada, the UK, and multiple other countries in the wake of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
In its sanctions announcement, the EU described Usmanov as having “particularly close ties to Russian President Vladimir Putin” and referred to him as “one of Vladimir Putin’s favorite oligarchs.” Usmanov has denied any association with Putin.
A number of court cases involving Usmanov in Germany have seen the oligarch get the upper hand, with a court in Hamburg upholding a libel lawsuit filed by the billionaire against the newspaper Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung (FAZ) this past January. Prosecutors in Munich dropped an investigation into suspected sanctions violations by Usmanov after he made a sizeable charitable payment in 2025, while the Frankfurt am Main public prosecutor’s office closed a separate money laundering investigation into the billionaire in November 2024 after he paid a fine of €4 million.
The Ukraine-born Fridman, co-founder of Alfa Bank, Russia’s largest privately owned bank, has an estimated net worth of $16.6 billion, according to Forbes, which puts him 175th on in its list of global billionaires. Fridman, who also holds Israeli citizenship, was first sanctioned by the European Union on Feb. 28, 2022, four days after Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine. He was added to the same sanctions list as Usmanov. The UK followed on March 15, 2022, while the United States designated him on Aug. 11, 2023.
After the invasion, Fridman stepped down from his Luxembourg-based holding company LetterOne and also reduced his stake. British authorities have frozen his London properties, including the Athlone House estate, valued at around $100 million.
Fridman founded commodities trader Alfa-Eco in 1989 with entrepreneurs German Khan and Alexei Kuzmichev. The group later formed oil venture TNK-BP by uniting with British energy giant BP in 2003 before selling its stake in 2013 in a deal that brought Fridman about $5.1 billion in cash. Ukraine opened a criminal case against Fridman in August 2023 over alleged fraud linked to Alfa Bank Ukraine and placed him on an international wanted list that December.

articles.title: The Fixer: Amjad M. Tadros on a life in Middle East journalism
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
The Fixer: Amjad M. Tadros' extraordinary 30-year journalism journey through the Middle East
For more than three decades, Amjad M. Tadros was one of the people behind some of American television’s most important coverage of the Middle East.
A Jordanian journalist and the son of Palestinian refugees, Tadros joined CBS News in 1990 almost by accident after a job in Saudi Arabia fell through in the aftermath of Iraq’s invasion of Kuwait.
He went on to spend more than 30 years as CBS News’ Middle East producer, working across Iraq, Yemen, Syria and the wider region and helping correspondents from CBS News and 60 Minutes report from some of the world’s most difficult and dangerous environments.
His career placed him at the centre of stories that shaped American understanding of the region. He was in Baghdad when a US cruise missile struck his hotel in 1993, leaving him injured and unexpectedly face-to-face with Saddam Hussein in an Iraqi hospital.
In Yemen, he pursued stories about al-Qaeda and Osama bin Laden’s network. He worked on reporting about the abuse of prisoners at Abu Ghraib, the Arab Spring and Syria’s war, among many other major stories.
Yet Tadros never saw himself simply as a producer. For much of his career, he was known as a "fixer" — the person who could open doors, find sources, arrange access, navigate bureaucracy and help foreign correspondents understand the places they were reporting from.
That experience is at the heart of his new memoir, The Fixer: A Journalist’s Accidental Journey Through the Middle East. He spoke to The New Arab about his memoir, the extraordinary experiences that shaped his career and what has happened to American coverage of the Middle East.
The New Arab: Your memoir is called The Fixer: A Journalist’s Accidental Journey through the Middle East. Why did you choose that title, and what does being a “fixer” mean to you?
Amjad M. Tadros: I decided to call the book The Fixer because although I had many titles during my career, I had no problem with being called a fixer. We don’t really have this term in Arabic; the Americans called us “fixers,” and we do everything from getting the coffee to arranging interviews.
Some of my colleagues did not like the term, and eventually I got called a producer. But I was proud to be called a fixer. I was the best at it, and I fixed for all the major US networks. Plus, it was a nice title.
The book was actually going to be called The Accidental Journalist for a long time because I really did become a journalist by accident. But The Fixer felt more honest.
Being a fixer was not just a job title for me. It was about adapting, surviving and connecting — about being the bridge between two worlds.
One of your assignments was to go to Iraq, and it ended with you being caught up in a US missile attack on Baghdad while you were in a hotel. You ended up in hospital, where you met the then Iraqi President Saddam Hussein. Most people would have quit after that, but you kept going back to Iraq. What happened, and why did you keep going back?
It was in January 1993, and back then the Iraqis didn’t trust us Jordanians because we could speak the language. So when American reporters would go out on assignment, I stayed behind in the Baghdad hotel.
We didn’t think this would happen, as the hotel was meant to be a safe place. But we were hit by an American cruise missile, and I was injured.
I was taken to the hospital screaming. I was worried that people would go to my hotel room to see blood, see I was not there and assume I was dead. My parents would then see the news and think I was dead too.
Nobody knew where I was. After being stitched up, the hospital refused to let me go because they got word that Saddam Hussein was going to visit the injured. He wanted to show people he was still alive, which is why he was coming. I had only a few minutes to decide what to say to him, and I chose to avoid politics and just thank him for the humanitarian gesture.
When he came into the hospital, I pulled myself up and leaned forward to greet him with a kiss on the cheek. Iraqi television took a photograph of us, and that image was widely circulated. It became a defining moment in my career because Iraqi officials began to assume that I had a connection to Saddam. After that, I was able to work in Iraq largely uninterrupted for years and gained access that allowed me to pursue stories other journalists could not.
Up until a few years after the US-led invasion of Iraq in 2003, American media was always interested in Iraqi stories, but you also tried to get more interest going in Yemen too. What was it like trying to get the US media to cover Yemen?
Yemen was a hard sell. I have three chapters in the book about Yemen and the stories I covered there.
The first story that brought me to Yemen was about a Yemeni guy in Guantanamo Bay; while there, I discovered a guy who was Osama Bin Laden’s bodyguard.
I got CBS to greenlight the story, and after that one, I kept going back to cover more stuff. It was always hard to get American editors to approve these stories, though, but I managed it; I got CBS Evening News, 60 Minutes, and the website to do stories on Yemen.
I love the country; the Yemeni people are the nicest, and it's so scenic and fascinating. Dangerous at the same time, but very beautiful. There are over 40 million people who live there; they are part of an important global access point, and you can’t just ignore them.
Do you think your journalism made a difference in how the US saw the Arab World, and how would you assess where we are today with American coverage of the region?
I hope I made a difference. Journalists often like to take the moral high ground and believe they are making an impact, so I hope I made a difference.
I believe we covered stories that no one else did, and especially with something like 60 Minutes, where we could cover a story with great depth, I like to think this made a difference.
Unfortunately, in recent coverage, I think certain technological changes have challenged how things are covered. Things like social media and AI have created a demand for more news to be produced in less time.
But this approach doesn’t work for understanding developments in the Middle East; these are old societies with long histories, and you cannot convey this with these incentives.
I also believe news coverage has become shallower and more opinionated; this is not how I was taught journalism.
One of the reasons I wrote the book was to push back on claims that we are legacy media, fake news and so on. We did important stories like the US abuse of prisoners in Abu Ghraib, which had an impact in America; we were certainly not joking around.
While some outlets still do good work, unfortunately they are being pushed in the wrong direction.
Usman Butt is a multimedia television researcher, filmmaker and writer based in London who read International Relations and Arabic Language at the University of Westminster and completed a Master of Arts in Palestine Studies at the University of Exeter

articles.title: EU court strikes down sanctions extension against former Russian senator
articles.body:
EU court strikes down sanctions extension against former Russian senator
The EU has failed to provide sufficient evidence to keep a former Russian official on its sanctions blacklist, the bloc’s General Court ruled on Wednesday. The decision came a day after the EU removed two Russian businessmen from the list as part of a deal to extend restrictions on thousands of others.
The court annulled the September 2024 and September 2025 extensions of sanctions against former Russian Senator Oleg Tkach, who represented Kaliningrad Region in the Federation Council from 2004 to 2022. He was also involved in publishing, founding and chairing Olma Media Group.
The EU first sanctioned Tkach in March 2022 over his vote to ratify treaties with the Donetsk and Lugansk People’s Republics, which later became part of Russia following referendums rejected by Ukraine and most Western countries. The case centered on whether the EU Council had grounds to keep extending the restrictions after Tkach left office.
According to Wednesday’s ruling, the Council failed to demonstrate that Tkach retained close ties to Russian authorities. The court also found that his failure to publicly oppose Russia’s military operation in Ukraine did not, by itself, constitute continued support for the authorities.
Brussels had also cited Tkach’s publishing background, including his links to Olma Media Group and textbook publisher Prosveshcheniye. However, the court found the evidence insufficient to establish his current role or influence at the companies.
The ruling does not affect the EU’s most recent sanctions extension from March 2026, which Tkach is challenging separately. He argues that condemnation based on his former Senate position is outdated and that the Council’s evidence is unreliable and lacks a “sound factual basis.” He has also argued that the measures are disproportionate.
A day before Wednesday’s ruling, the EU agreed to remove Russian businessmen Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman from its sanctions list. Both had previously mounted legal challenges related to EU restrictions, while Fridman has also filed a multibillion-dollar arbitration claim against Luxembourg.
Their removal came as part of a compromise to renew sanctions against around 3,000 other individuals and entities for three years, until September 2029, replacing the bloc’s usual six-month renewal cycle.
